1.title: Overview
1.description: Igris helps engineers run AI tasks with governed, verifiable execution.
1.content: Igris Request -> Execute -> Verify Request Execute Verify What To Expect From The Current Product Recommended Path Find By Goal Advanced Directions # Igris Igris helps engineers run AI tasks with governed, verifiable execution. Direct provider calls are still the right tool for simple chat or one-off prompting. Igris becomes useful when AI output starts doing work: calling tools, crossing system boundaries, touching customer data, or triggering decisions that need to be reviewed later. The simplest mental model is: 1. **Request** through one Igris API surface. 2. **Execute** with governance, routing, events, and failure handling. 3. **Verify** with signed records and verification-ready receipts. --- ## Request -> Execute -> Verify ### Request Send a request once. The surface can be OpenAI-compatible chat, a task submission, or another documented Igris endpoint. The point is not "many products." The point is one execution system that can accept work in a stable, inspectable way. ### Execute Igris decides how the run should proceed for the deployment you have configured. That can include routing to a runtime, applying capability and policy boundaries, capturing execution events, and surfacing failure paths instead of hiding them behind a plain model response. ### Verify Igris returns more than output text. The system can also return execution metadata, signed execution records, and receipt material that can be checked after the run. That is the difference between "the model answered" and "the execution can be inspected." --- ## What To Expect From The Current Product **Governed execution.** Igris is built for runs that need boundaries, not just completions. Capability checks, policy controls, and execution-state visibility are part of the product story. **Execution visibility.** The system tracks route decisions, execution metadata, and receipt-oriented records so engineers can inspect what happened after a run. **Verification-ready records.** Signed envelopes and receipts are part of the product today, and the local unified proof demonstrates signature and hash verification on the proof-backed path. **Honest proof status.** The strongest proven path today is the local unified proof with a mock upstream. Real-provider mode is wired, but it requires sanctioned credentials and was not proven in the prior environment. Advanced areas such as local GGUF fallback, checkpoint recovery, fleet failover, robotics, and multimodal should be treated according to their page-level proof labels. ## Recommended Path Start

2.title: Agent Lifecycle
2.description: Every agent running on the execution engine has a tracked lifecycle. State transitions are deterministic, signed, and queryable through the local runtime state API.
2.content: Agent Lifecycle States State Transitions Querying Agent State Get the state for one local runtime agent Lifecycle Records Canceling In-Flight Work Safe Idle (Human-in-the-Loop) Recovery # Agent Lifecycle Every agent running on the execution engine has a tracked lifecycle. State transitions are deterministic, signed, and queryable — giving you a full audit trail of every agent's history from initialization to termination. --- ## States | State | Meaning | |---|---| | `INIT` | Agent registered, not yet started | | `RUNNING` | Actively processing a request | | `IDLE` | Waiting for the next request | | `DEGRADED` | Repeated failures; execution continues with reduced confidence | | `SAFE_IDLE` | Paused pending human review or approval | | `RECOVERING` | Restarting after a violation or crash | | `TERMINATED` | Permanently stopped; no further requests accepted | --- ## State Transitions INIT → RUNNING RUNNING → IDLE (request completed normally) RUNNING → DEGRADED (error threshold exceeded) RUNNING → SAFE_IDLE (human approval required) IDLE → RUNNING (new request received) DEGRADED → RECOVERING (recovery triggered) RECOVERING → IDLE (recovery succeeded) RECOVERING → TERMINATED (recovery failed) SAFE_IDLE → RUNNING (approval granted) SAFE_IDLE → TERMINATED (approval denied) * → TERMINATED (explicit shutdown or fatal error) --- ## Querying Agent State bash # Get the state for one local runtime agent curl http://localhost:8080/v1/runtime/agent/agent-abc/state \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "state": "IDLE", "created_at": "2026-03-01T10:00:00Z", "last_transition": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "total_requests": 47, "violations": 0 } The current local runtime API exposes state for a single known agent ID. Fleet-wide runtime lists are available through the swarm and fleet coordination APIs rather than the agent lifecycle endpoint. --- ## Lifecycle Records Each state transition is recorded as a signed lifecycle event: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "from_state": "RUNNING", "to_state": "IDLE", "trigger": "request_completed", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "signature": "sha256:d4e1..." } Lifecycle records are hash-chained and included in the audit log alongside execution receipts. --- ## Canceling In-Flight Work bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/runtime/task/task-abc/cancel \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Cancellation is task-scoped in the current runtime API. A canceled task is recorded in the runtime task history and its receipt/WAL evidence remains available for reconciliation. --- #

3.title: Agents
3.description: Igris supports four agent patterns: reflection, planning, tool use, and swarms. All run inside the execution envelope with full governance applied.
3.content: Agents Reflection Agents Planning Agents Tool-Use Agents Multi-Agent Swarms MCP Swarm Mode Agent Lifecycle Choosing the Right Agent Pattern Mode Flags Monitoring Agent State Context Engineering # Agents Igris supports four agent patterns: reflection, planning, tool use, and swarms. All run inside the execution envelope with full governance applied. --- ## Reflection Agents A reflection agent generates an initial response, evaluates its own quality, and regenerates if the quality score falls below a threshold. **Execution loop:** 1. Generate initial response 2. Score response on a 0.0–1.0 quality scale 3. If score ≥ threshold: return response 4. If score < threshold: regenerate with critique feedback 5. Repeat until threshold met or `max_steps` reached **Configuration:** json { "mode": "reflection", "reflection_threshold": 0.8, "max_reflection_steps": 3 } **When to use:** Tasks where response quality must meet a minimum bar before the result is returned — code generation, structured output, reasoning tasks. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Planning Agents A planning agent breaks down complex tasks into steps, executes each step, observes the result, and adjusts the plan before proceeding. **Execution loop:** Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect → Plan (repeat) The agent maintains a working plan that is revised after each step. Planning steps consume `max_steps` from the execution envelope. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "planning", "max_steps": 10 } **When to use:** Multi-step tasks where the approach depends on intermediate results — research, code generation with testing, multi-stage workflows. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Tool-Use Agents A tool-use agent can call external tools as part of inference: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. Tool calls are governed by the execution envelope's capability grants. Available tools (each requires an explicit capability grant): | Tool | Capability | What it does | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | GET/POST to external APIs | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands (sandboxed) | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, list files | Tool calls are recorded in the execution receipt including the call parameters, response, and latency. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "tools", "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": true } } [Tools →](/docs/tools) · [Capability Model →](/docs/capability-model) --- ## Multi-Agent Swarms A swarm executes a task using multiple specialized agents in parallel. 10.title: API Authentication
10.description: Authentication models for cloud and local API use.
10.content: Authentication Tenant API Keys Session Cookies Runtime-local Auth Choosing a Credential Bearer Example Example JSON # Authentication Which credentials belong to automation, browser sessions, and runtime-local deployments, and how to choose the right one for each route. ## Tenant API Keys Customer automation should use tenant API keys with the `igris_` prefix. These keys are the default credential for server-side integrations, CI jobs, backend workers, and any script that is calling the hosted API outside the browser. Supply the key as `Authorization: Bearer ...` or `X-API-Key` if the endpoint allows it. Endpoint pages call out the expected model explicitly, so treat the endpoint page as authoritative over any generic assumption. ## Session Cookies Browser-driven console workflows use session cookies. These routes are designed for an authenticated user session rather than headless automation, so they should not be treated as generic bearer-token endpoints unless the endpoint page says an API key is also accepted. If you are building automation, prefer routes that are documented with API-key access. ## Runtime-local Auth The local runtime API follows the runtime `auth` configuration. Some deployments intentionally keep that surface inside a trusted network boundary with minimal local auth, while others front it with stricter controls. Because that access model depends on deployment, do not assume that a local runtime route behaves like the hosted API. ## Choosing a Credential Use tenant API keys for server-to-server automation. Use session cookies for browser experiences that are already inside the Igris console. Use runtime-local authentication only when the endpoint is explicitly local and you control the deployment boundary. ## Bearer Example text curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" \ https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/models ## Example JSON json { "error": "unauthorized", "code": "INVALID_API_KEY" } API authentication bearer api key session cookie runtime auth

23.title: API Errors
23.description: Error handling and common response codes.
23.content: Errors Status Codes Validation Errors Authentication Failures Server Errors Handling Strategy Error Envelope Example JSON Common Status Codes # Errors How to read error responses across the API reference and what to expect from validation, authentication, throttling, and server failures. ## Status Codes The HTTP status code tells you what class of failure happened before you look at the JSON body. Treat 4xx responses as request, authentication, or access problems that your client should handle directly, and treat 5xx responses as server-side failures that may require retry, fallback, or operator attention. The most common patterns are 400 for invalid request shape, 401 for missing or invalid credentials, 403 for an authenticated request that still is not allowed, 404 when the addressed resource does not exist, 429 when throttling is applied, and 500-level codes when the server cannot complete a valid request. ## Validation Errors Validation failures usually mean the request shape was wrong for the route you called. Many handlers return a compact JSON envelope with `error` and sometimes a more specific `message` or `code` value that tells you what part of the request could not be accepted. ## Authentication Failures Authentication failures typically return HTTP 401. Session-based handlers often use codes such as `MISSING_SESSION` or `INVALID_SESSION`, while API-key handlers more commonly return `INVALID_API_KEY`. ## Server Errors Server-side failures commonly return a generic error such as `internal_error` or a route-specific code such as `registration_failed` or `STORAGE_FAILED`. These responses indicate that the server accepted the route contract but could not complete the operation. ## Handling Strategy Good clients do not handle every error the same way. Fix the request for 400-class validation issues, refresh or replace credentials for 401 responses, stop and inspect authorization assumptions on 403 responses, and apply controlled retry or fallback only for the routes and statuses that are documented as retry-safe. ## Error Envelope text { "error": "invalid_request", "message": "Failed to parse request body" } ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 400 | Bad Request | The route was reached, but the request body, query, or path data did not match the endpoint contract. | | 401 | Unauth API errors error codes invalid request unauthorized internal error

26.content: GET /v1/receipts/export When To Use Integration Guidance Common Mistakes Related Endpoints Related Guides Query Parameters Notes Code Examples cURL JavaScript Go Rust Sample Response Status Codes 401 Example 500 Example # GET /v1/receipts/export Streams execution receipts as a downloadable attachment. It is designed for export and downstream processing, not for interactive paging or ordinary list views. Method GET Path /v1/receipts/export Base URL https://overture.igrisinertial.com Auth Session cookie or igris_ API key Surface Cloud API Stability stable Support supported Deployment cloud ## When To Use Use this endpoint when receipt data needs to leave the product boundary for BI, compliance, archive, or offline analysis. Choose NDJSON for machine pipelines and CSV for spreadsheet-oriented workflows. ## Integration Guidance Retry transient 5xx or 429 responses with backoff, but treat export like a batch operation rather than a request you fire repeatedly from an interactive client. ### Common Mistakes - Expecting a JSON metadata payload instead of a streamed attachment response. - Using export for ordinary UI pagination when the list and detail routes are the correct interactive surfaces. - Starting repeated large exports without narrowing the time range or planning downstream retention. ### Related Endpoints - [GET /v1/history/events](/docs/api-reference/execution-history-and-receipts/get-v1-history-events) - [GET /v1/receipts](/docs/api-reference/execution-history-and-receipts/get-v1-receipts) - [GET /v1/receipts/:id](/docs/api-reference/execution-history-and-receipts/get-v1-receipts-id) ### Related Guides - [API Authentication](/docs/api-reference/authentication) - [API Errors](/docs/api-reference/errors) - [Receipts and Audit Workflow](/docs/receipts-audit-workflow) ## Query Parameters | Field | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `format` | `string` | No | Export format. `jsonl` is the default; `csv` streams comma-separated rows. | | `from` | `string` | No | RFC3339 lower time bound. | | `to` | `string` | No | RFC3339 upper time bound. | ## Notes - The default format is NDJSON (`application/x-ndjson`) with filename `receipts.jsonl`. - When `format=csv`, the same route streams `text/csv` with filename `receipts.csv`. ## Code Examples ### cURL bash curl -X GET https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=jsonl \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" ### JavaScript javascript const response = await fetch('https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=jsonl', { method: 'GET', headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer $ `, }, }); GET /v1/receipts/export Exports receipts as JSONL or CSV.

36.title: API Introduction
36.description: Overview of the customer API contract.
36.content: Introduction Two Product Surfaces How Endpoint Pages Work SDK Guidance Support Labels and Deployment Modes Base URLs Example JSON # Introduction How the Igris API reference is organized, when to use each access point, and how to move from guides into endpoint-level integration work. ## Two Product Surfaces Igris is documented here as one product with two access points. Use the hosted API at `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` when your integration needs account, fleet, billing, receipt, or policy capabilities. Use the local runtime API at `http://localhost:8080` by default when the request belongs on the machine where Igris is running. This split is about where the request executes, not about two different products. The API reference groups endpoints by capability so you can navigate by task first and only think about the base URL when you are ready to make the call. ## How Endpoint Pages Work Every endpoint has its own page. That page tells you what the route is for, which authentication model it expects, the path and query parameters it accepts, the request body fields that matter, and the status codes you should plan for in a real client. Use the overview page to browse by capability, then switch to endpoint pages when you are implementing or debugging a specific call. ## SDK Guidance JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, and Python are the first-class SDK languages today. When an endpoint is covered by a native SDK, prefer that SDK for application code because it gives you a cleaner call surface and reduces request-shape drift over time. Some management routes are still best treated as direct HTTP integrations. In those cases, the endpoint page is the primary contract: use the request and response examples, confirm the authentication model, and wire your own client behavior around the listed status codes. ## Support Labels and Deployment Modes Each endpoint page carries both a support label and a deployment mode. **Core** routes are the primary customer contract. **Supported** routes are part of the shipped product surface but may not be the first endpoint a new customer should start with. **Preview** routes are available, but they should be adopted deliberately. Deployment mode tells you where the route belongs operationally. **Cloud** routes are served by the hosted API, **Local** routes are served by `igris-runtime`, and **Hybrid** routes are used when the hosted product and one or more runtimes are working together. ## Base URLs text Cloud API https://overture.igrisinertial.com Loc API introduction base URL surfaces overview contract

74.title: API Rate Limits
74.description: Rate limit behavior and retry expectations.
74.content: Rate Limits Global Control-plane Limit Runtime Download Limit Client Behavior 429 Example Example JSON Common Status Codes # Rate Limits What throttling exists today, where it applies, and how clients should behave when they receive a 429 response. ## Global Control-plane Limit The hosted API currently applies a default limiter of 100 requests per minute. Endpoint pages call out the exceptions that matter more than the global default. Response headers are only guaranteed on the 429 path right now. Clients should not assume that every successful response carries full rate-limit metadata. ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime download endpoints use a tighter subscription-aware throttle. Treat binary download as a provisioning or rollout action, not as a hot-path request that your application makes repeatedly during normal traffic. ## Client Behavior Build clients so that a 429 is expected and handled, not treated as an exceptional edge case. Honor `Retry-After` when it is present, apply backoff with jitter for repeated retries, and avoid running parallel request bursts that all wake up at the same second. ## 429 Example text Retry-After: 60 X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 429 | Too Many Requests | Retry after the advertised cooldown window. | API rate limits retry-after 429 throttle

90.title: GET /api/v1/runtime/commands

90.content: GET /api/v1/runtime/commands When To Use Integration Guidance Common Mistakes Related Endpoints Related Guides Query Parameters Code Examples cURL JavaScript Go Rust Sample Response Status Codes 400 Example 404 Example # GET /api/v1/runtime/commands Fetches queued runtime commands for a registered machine and clears the queue atomically. Runtimes use this after heartbeat to pick up config-push and OTA update commands. 109.title: Human-in-the-Loop Approvals
109.description: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval pauses an execution run before it completes a high-stakes action. A reviewer must explicitly approve or reject the run before execution continues.
109.content: Human-in-the-Loop Approvals How Executions Get Paused for Review Finding Runs Waiting for Approval Reviewing in the Console Approving a Run → {"status": "RUNNING", "approved": true} Rejecting a Run → {"status": "REJECTED", "reason": "action_out_of_scope"} What Gets Recorded in the Receipt Replaying a Rejected Run → {"status": "replayed", "new_execution_id": "exec-01HABC"} Monitoring the Approval Queue Best Practices # Human-in-the-Loop Approvals Human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval pauses an execution run before it completes a high-stakes action. A reviewer must explicitly approve or reject the run before execution continues. The full approval event — who made the decision, when, and why — is recorded in the signed execution receipt and cannot be altered after the fact. --- ## How Executions Get Paused for Review The execution engine evaluates review triggers as each run progresses. Triggers are configured in your policy and can match on tool call targets, output classifications, capability combinations, or custom conditions. When a trigger fires, the run transitions from RUNNING to **PAUSED** with `pause_reason: human_review_required`. The run holds open in that state indefinitely — it does not time out and does not progress — until a human makes a deliberate approve or reject decision. The execution envelope remains intact while the run is paused. Resources are reserved and the agent's context is preserved. Once a decision is made, the run either continues (approve) or terminates (reject) from exactly the point where it was paused. --- ## Finding Runs Waiting for Approval Query paused runs via the API: bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/execution/runs?status=PAUSED" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "execution_id": "exec-01HXYZ", "agent_id": "agent-abc", "status": "PAUSED", "pause_reason": "human_review_required", "paused_at": "2026-03-31T10:14:22Z", "prompt_preview": "About to POST to https://payments.example.com/disburse with amount: 4500", "runtime_id": "runtime-01" } ] The `prompt_preview` field is a brief description of what the execution was about to do at the point it was paused. It is generated by the execution engine and is not the raw model input — it is a structured summary of the pending action, designed to give a reviewer enough context to make an informed decision. --- ## Reviewing in the Console The **Execution Runs** page in the console shows all paused runs in a dedicated review queue at the top of the list. Each row shows a **Review** badge and the time the run has been waiting. Click a paused run to open its detail panel. You will see: - **Prompt preview** — the pending action description - **Agent ID** — which agent initiated this run - **Pause reason** — always `human_review_required` for HITL items - **Paused

110.title: Architecture
110.description: Igris is one execution system for AI tasks. This page maps the Request -> Execute -> Verify model onto the hosted and runtime components that implement it.
110.content:
Architecture System Overview Coordination Layer (Cloud Gateway) Core Capabilities Data Layer API Surface Igris Runtime (Edge Engine) Core Capabilities Trust Chain Deployment Topologies # Architecture Igris is one execution system for AI tasks. The best way to read the architecture is not "which product do I buy?" but "how does a request move through Request -> Execute -> Verify?" At a high level: - **Request** enters through an Igris API surface. - **Execute** happens on the configured hosted or runtime path, with policy, capability, and routing decisions applied along the way. - **Verify** happens through execution metadata, signed records, and receipt-oriented audit material after the run. The hosted control plane and the runtime are implementation components inside that unified model. They matter for deployment and operations, but they should not be your first mental model. --- ## System Overview Start from the execution flow, then map it to components. A request enters Igris, execution happens on the configured path, and verification data comes back with the result. Hosted and runtime surfaces are deployment choices, not separate product identities. | Layer | Responsibility | |---|---| | **Application** | Sends requests through an Igris API surface | | **Execution Control** | Applies routing, policy, runtime selection, and failure-path handling | | **Hosted Providers** | Execute hosted model work when the configured path stays in cloud infrastructure | | **Runtime** | Executes governed local or hybrid work, returns execution artifacts, and emits signed receipt material | Registration, heartbeat, receipt sync, and task handoff connect the hosted and runtime layers when you run Igris in hybrid mode. mermaid graph TD App["Your Application

(OpenAI-compatible API)"] LLM["Local LLM
(GGUF models)"] BT["Behavior Tree Engine"] Tools["Tool Sandbox
(HTTP, Shell, FS)"] Receipts["Signed Receipts
(cryptographic chain)"] MCP["MCP Server/Client"] Server --> LLM Server --> BT Server --> Tools Server --> Receipts Se

112.title: Deploying Igris on Edge Devices
112.description: Step-by-step guide for deploying the Igris runtime on Raspberry Pi, Jetson, and other edge hardware.
112.content: Deploying Igris on Edge Devices Supported Edge Platforms Install The Runtime 1. Download the archive 2. Extract and install 3. Download a model 4. Configure the runtime 5. Start the runtime Run As A Service Health And Monitoring # Deploying Igris on Edge Devices Running `igris-runtime` on edge hardware gives you local inference, local policy enforcement, and a clean path to hybrid cloud coordination. --- ## Supported Edge Platforms | Platform | Architecture | Minimum RAM | Recommended starting model | |---|---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4/5 | ARM64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano | ARM64 | 8 GB | Mistral 7B (Q4) | | Generic x86_64 host | x86_64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | GPU-backed x86_64 host | x86_64 | 16 GB | 7B to 8B GGUF | --- ## Install The Runtime ### 1. Download the archive bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-arm64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the checksum output before extracting. ### 2. Extract and install bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ### 3. Download a model bash mkdir -p /opt/igris/models wget -O /opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf \ "https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-gguf/resolve/main/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf" ### 4. Configure the runtime Create `/etc/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf", n_gpu_layers: 0, threads: 4, context_size: 4096 } } Platform tuning: - **Raspberry Pi**: keep `n_gpu_layers` at `0`; tune `threads` to the available CPU cores - **Jetson**: raise `n_gpu_layers` for GPU offload and keep `threads` conservative - **GPU-backed x86_64**: increase `n_gpu_layers` based on VRAM capacity ### 5. Start the runtime bash igris-runtime serve If you want the device to appear in Fleet, also set `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` before startup. --- ## Run As A Service Example `systemd` unit: ini [Unit] Description=Igris Runtime After=network.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=/home/igris/.local/bin/igris-runtime serve Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 User=igris Group=igris [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target --- ## Health And Monitoring bash curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health curl http://localhost:8080/

113.title: Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates
113.description: A practical guide to configuring capability grants, monitoring violations, and iterating on your agent policies.
113.content: Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates The Capability Model Available Capabilities Start Restrictive, Expand as Needed Step 1: Deploy with No Capabilities Step 2: Review Violations Step 3: Grant Legitimate Capabilities Step 4: Iterate Capability Patterns by Agent Type Read-Only Analyst API Integration Agent Automation Agent DevOps Agent Monitoring and Alerting Console Monitoring API Monitoring Reviewing Violations Common Pitfalls Over-Granting Capabilities Ignoring Violations Not Using Shadow Mode # Building Safe Agents with Capability Gates When agents can make HTTP requests, execute shell commands, or access the filesystem, the risk surface grows significantly. Igris's capability gates ensure that agents can only perform operations you explicitly authorize. --- ## The Capability Model Every execution in Igris runs with a **capability grant** — a declarative list of what the agent is permitted to do. The engine enforces these grants before any operation executes. ### Available Capabilities | Capability | Controls | |---|---| | `allow_http` | Outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | Specific domains the agent can call | | `allow_shell` | Shell command execution | | `allowed_shell_commands` | Specific commands the agent can run | | `allow_filesystem` | File read/write operations | | `allowed_filesystem_paths` | Specific paths the agent can access | | `max_file_write_bytes` | Maximum bytes the agent can write | --- ## Start Restrictive, Expand as Needed The safest approach is to start with no capabilities granted and add them incrementally: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 1: Deploy with No Capabilities Deploy your agent with all capabilities disabled. Run it against real traffic in **shadow mode** to observe what it would do without actually executing. ### Step 2: Review Violations Check the **Proof → Violations** page in the console. Each violation shows: - Which capability was attempted - Which agent attempted it - When it happened ### Step 3: Grant Legitimate Capabilities For violations that represent legitimate agent behavior, grant the specific capability: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allowed_http_domains": ["api.example.com", "cdn.example.com"], "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 4: Iterate Repeat steps 2–3 until your agent operates without violations. This process typically takes 1–3 iterations for well-designed agents. --- ## Capability Patterns by Agent Type ### Read-Only Analyst An agent that analyzes data and produces reports: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } No tools needed. The agent works purely with its training knowledge and the provided context. ### API Integration Agent An agent that calls external APIs: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": tr

114.title: How Adaptive Routing Works
114.description: How Igris automatically routes requests to the best provider for your workload based on real-time performance data.
114.content: How Adaptive Routing Works The Problem How It Works Why This Matters for Your Workload Automatic Adaptation Handles New Providers Gracefully Balances Cost and Performance Configuration Monitoring # How Adaptive Routing Works When you configure multiple AI providers with Igris, you face a fundamental question: which provider should handle each request? The answer depends on constantly changing factors — provider latency, error rates, cost, and your specific workload patterns. Igris solves this automatically using an adaptive routing algorithm that learns from every request. --- ## The Problem Imagine you have three providers configured: | Provider | Avg Latency | Cost per 1K tokens | |---|---|---| | Anthropic Claude | 280ms | $0.015 | | OpenAI GPT-4 | 350ms | $0.030 | | Google Gemini | 200ms | $0.010 | A naive approach might always pick the fastest (Gemini) or the cheapest (Gemini). But what if: - Gemini occasionally times out under load? - Claude produces higher-quality responses for your specific prompts? - OpenAI is faster for certain model types? Static rules can't adapt to these dynamics. Igris's adaptive routing can. --- ## How It Works Igris maintains real-time performance statistics for each configured provider: latency, success rate, and cost. On each request, the routing engine selects the best provider based on recent observations — automatically balancing between providers it knows are reliable and occasionally trying others to keep its data fresh. After each request completes, the provider's statistics are updated with the observed result. A provider that performs well receives more traffic. A provider that degrades is automatically routed around. --- ## Why This Matters for Your Workload ### Automatic Adaptation If a provider's latency degrades, the router automatically reduces its traffic share. No manual intervention needed. When the provider recovers, traffic gradually returns. ### Handles New Providers Gracefully When you add a new provider, the router explores it to gather performance data, then settles into a steady pattern once it understands the provider's characteristics. ### Balances Cost and Performance The algorithm naturally finds the sweet spot between cost and performance for your specific workload. If a cheaper provider is "good enough," it will receive more traffic. If quality matters most, higher-performing providers dominate. --- ## Configuration Adaptive routing is the default. You can also select a specific strategy: json { "routing": { "strategy": "thompson-sampling", "fallback_chain": ["anthropic", "openai", "local

115.title: Audit
115.description: Igris produces a tamper-evident audit record for every execution. This page covers the implemented cloud receipt and proof APIs used to access, query, export, and verify audit data.
115.content: Audit Execution Receipts Lineage Querying Receipts List receipts from the cloud ledger Get a specific receipt by execution ID Filter by time range Export Export as JSONL Export as CSV Retention Proof API GET /proof/receipts POST /proof/receipts/verify → {"valid": true, "execution_id": "exec-01HXYZ"} GET /v1/proof/violations Compliance Use Cases # Audit Igris produces a tamper-evident audit record for every execution. This page covers how to access, query, and export audit data. --- ## Execution Receipts Every execution produces a signed execution receipt. The receipt is the primary audit artifact. A receipt contains: - **Request identity**: request ID, tenant ID, timestamp - **Inputs**: full prompt, system message, and parameters - **Outputs**: full model response - **Resource usage**: tokens consumed, wall time, tool calls - **Capability grants**: what the execution was permitted to do - **Capability violations**: any operations that were blocked - **Tool calls**: parameters, responses, and latency for each tool invocation - **Signature**: cryptographic seal over the canonical envelope The signature is computed over a deterministic serialization of all fields. An altered receipt will have an invalid signature. [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) --- ## Lineage Each receipt includes a `request_id` that traces back to the originating API call. For executions that went through the cloud coordination layer, the `request_id` links the routing decision to the execution record: API call → routing decision (request_id: abc123) │ ▼ Execution receipt (request_id: abc123, provider: anthropic) │ ▼ Signed envelope (canonical hash: sha256:...) Full lineage is queryable end-to-end by request ID. --- ## Querying Receipts Receipts are queryable through the cloud audit surfaces: - **Cloud receipt API** (`overture.igrisinertial.com`) — the central execution ledger - **Proof API** (`overture.igrisinertial.com/proof`) — verification and policy violation review The current runtime build returns execution receipt data from local execution responses, but it does not expose a public local receipt listing endpoint. bash # List receipts from the cloud ledger curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # Get a specific receipt by execution ID curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/exec-01HXYZ \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # Filter by time range curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts?from=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z&to=2026-03-02T00:00:00Z" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" --- ## Export Export receipts in bulk for external audit workflows: bash # Export as JSONL curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?fo

116.content: Behavior Trees 1. Cloud Definition Schema 2. Runtime Execution Schema Using the JavaScript SDK Using the Go SDK Practical Rule Durable Execution # Behavior Trees Igris currently exposes **two** behavior-tree schemas. Treat them as different layers of the product: - The **definition schema** used by the cloud control plane and console editor - The **runtime execution schema** used by the runtime API and native SDKs If you mix them up, validation will fail. --- ## 1. Cloud Definition Schema The coordination layer stores graph-style definitions using `nodes` and `edges`. json { "name": "shutdown-guard", "description": "Temperature-triggered shutdown sequence", "nodes": [ , , ], "edges": [ , ] } This is the schema used by: - `GET /v1/bt/templates` - `GET /v1/bt/definitions` - `GET /v1/bt/definitions/:id` - `POST /v1/bt/definitions` - `DELETE /v1/bt/definitions/:id` --- ## 2. Runtime Execution Schema The runtime and native SDKs use a nested tree representation with lowercase node types. json { "type": "sequence", "name": "shutdown-guard", "children": [ { "type": "condition", "name": "check_temp", "key": "sensor.temperature", "expected": "80" }, { "type": "action", "name": "shutdown", "tool": "http_post", "args": { "url": "http://localhost:9000/shutdown" } } ] } This is the schema accepted by the local runtime endpoints: - `POST /v1/btree/validate` - `POST /v1/btree/run` - `POST /v1/btree/deploy` --- ## Using the JavaScript SDK typescript import { Runtime, BehaviorTree, SequenceNode, ConditionNode, ActionNode, } from '@igris-inertial/sdk'; const runtime = new Runtime( ); const tree = BehaviorTree.fromJson( new SequenceNode('shutdown-guard', [ new ConditionNode('check_temp', 'sensor.temperature', '80'), new ActionNode('shutdown', 'http_post', ), ]).toJSON(), runtime, ); const result = await tree.validate(); console.log(result.valid); --- ## Using the Go SDK go package main import ( "context" "log" igris "github.com/igris-inertial/go-sdk" ) func main() { runtime := igris.NewRuntime("http://localhost:8080") treeDef := igris.NewSequenceNode("shutdown-guard", igris.NewConditionNode("check_temp", "sensor.temperature", "80"), igris.NewActionNode("shutdown", "http_post", map[string]interface{}{ "url": "http://localhost:9000/shutdown", }), ) tree := igris.NewBehaviorTree(treeDef, runtime) if _, err := tree.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } --- ## Practical Rule Use `nodes` / `edges` only when you are talking to the cloud definition API. 117.title: Capabilities & Limits
117.description: The execution engine enforces a capability model: every execution runs with an explicit set of permissions. If an agent tries to do something outside those permissions, the operati
117.content: Capabilities & Limits Capability Fields Configuration Enforcement Points Violation Records Violation Types # Capabilities & Limits The execution engine enforces a capability model: every execution runs with an explicit set of permissions. If an agent tries to do something outside those permissions, the operation is blocked before it executes and the violation is recorded in the signed receipt. --- ## Capability Fields | Capability | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `allow_http` | bool | Allow outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | string[] | Allowlist of domains for HTTP calls | | `allow_shell` | bool | Allow shell command execution | | `allow_filesystem` | bool | Allow filesystem read/write | | `max_file_write_bytes` | int | Maximum bytes the execution may write | --- ## Configuration Set capability limits in your `config.json5`: json5 { capabilities: { allow_http: true, allowed_http_domains: ["api.openweathermap.org", "api.github.com"], allow_shell: false, allow_filesystem: true, max_file_write_bytes: 1048576 // 1 MB } } Capabilities can also be set per-request via the `X-Igris-Capabilities` header for tenants with override permission. --- ## Enforcement Points **HTTP tool calls** — before each outbound request, the engine checks `allow_http` and that the target domain is in `allowed_http_domains`. Blocked calls produce a `HttpDomainNotAllowed` violation. **Shell commands** — if `allow_shell` is false and an agent attempts a shell invocation, the call is rejected with a `ShellNotAllowed` violation before the command is spawned. **Filesystem operations** — write operations are counted against `max_file_write_bytes`. Reads beyond the allowed path prefix produce a `FilesystemNotAllowed` violation. --- ## Violation Records Every blocked operation is recorded as a violation in the execution receipt: json { "capability_violations": [ { "kind": "HttpDomainNotAllowed", "detail": "Domain 'evil.com' not in allowed_http_domains", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:00:01Z" } ] } Violation records are included in the signed receipt and cannot be removed or suppressed. Compliance auditors can verify that policy enforcement was applied to every execution. --- ## Violation Types | Kind | Trigger | |---|---| | `HttpNotAllowed` | HTTP tool called but `allow_http` is false | | `HttpDomainNotAllowed` | Domain not in `allowed_http_domains` | | `ShellNotAllowed` | Shell command attempted but `allow_shell` is false | | `FilesystemNotAllowed` | Path outside allowed prefix |

119.title: Circuit Breaker
119.description: The circuit breaker is an advanced failure-aware execution mechanism that reduces traffic to unhealthy upstream paths.
119.content: Circuit Breaker Core States Why It Matters What It Does Not Mean How To Operate It Monitoring Related Pages # Circuit Breaker The circuit breaker is an advanced failure-aware execution mechanism. Its purpose is to reduce traffic to an upstream path that is repeatedly failing, then probe cautiously to see whether that path has recovered. This helps make failure paths more visible and controlled during execution. --- ## Core States The common state model is: - **closed** when the path is healthy enough for ordinary traffic - **open** when the path should stop receiving ordinary traffic - **half-open** when the system is probing recovery carefully This is a classic control mechanism, but in Igris it matters because it shapes which execution paths remain eligible during failure conditions. ## Why It Matters Without a breaker, the system may keep sending work into a failing path longer than it should. With a breaker, operators get: - clearer failure handling - reduced repeated attempts against a path that is already misbehaving - a more deliberate recovery probe before normal traffic resumes ## What It Does Not Mean The breaker is not a blanket guarantee that every execution survives every upstream issue. It is one mechanism in the larger Execute-stage control stack. Other layers still matter: - policy - health - trust - explicit deployment choices ## How To Operate It Use breaker settings to match your tolerance for: - repeated upstream failures - recovery probe frequency - flapping behavior If a path is bouncing rapidly between states, that is an operational signal worth inspecting rather than something to hide behind automation language. ## Monitoring Use console and API health views to inspect breaker state and recent failure behavior. Treat those views as execution diagnostics, not as proof that all survival scenarios are fully covered. ## Related Pages - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Provider Trust →](/docs/provider-trust) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) - [SLO Enforcer →](/docs/slo-enforcer)

120.title: Cloud Coordination
120.description: Hosted coordination is the part of Igris that manages provider-backed execution, runtime lifecycle surfaces, and customer-facing receipt workflows.
120.content: Cloud Coordination What Hosted Coordination Does Hosted Request Entry Provider Configuration Runtime Lifecycle Surfaces Receipt And Audit Surfaces Routing Details Belong Lower In The Stack Related Guides # Cloud Coordination Cloud coordination is the hosted part of the Igris execution system. Its job is to coordinate provider-backed execution, expose customer-facing management surfaces, and connect runtimes into the broader execution model when hybrid workflows are enabled. That is useful when you want: - a stable hosted entry path for applications - provider-backed execution without custom client-side routing logic - runtime lifecycle and fleet-oriented operator surfaces - customer-facing receipt and audit workflows --- ## What Hosted Coordination Does Hosted coordination can cover: - application-facing request entry - provider-backed execution setup - runtime registration and lifecycle surfaces - receipt and proof-oriented query surfaces - account, policy, and key-management workflows This is part of one execution system. It should not be read as a separate product introduction. ## Hosted Request Entry For many teams, the first hosted path is the OpenAI-compatible surface: text https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1 That keeps the application contract simple while letting Igris own the execution path behind it. ## Provider Configuration Hosted execution depends on provider credentials stored through the vault API. For customer traffic today, use `openai` or `anthropic`. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' Provider-backed execution is configurable and supported. Proof claims about specific real-provider flows should still follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status). ## Runtime Lifecycle Surfaces When hybrid workflows matter, runtimes coordinate with the hosted layer through the runtime lifecycle routes. 121.content: Routing Advisor How It Works Proposals GET /v1/cognitive/proposals GET /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id POST /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id/apply → {"status": "applied", "applied_at": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z"} Auto-Apply Configuration GET /v1/cognitive/config PUT /v1/cognitive/config # Routing Advisor The Routing Advisor analyzes your routing history and proposes configuration changes — adjusting provider weights, enabling speculative execution, or switching routing strategy — based on observed performance. Auto-apply can be configured to apply proposals automatically when they meet your confidence and risk thresholds. --- ## How It Works 1. The advisor monitors routing telemetry continuously 2. When it detects an optimization opportunity, it generates a **proposal** with a confidence score and a risk score 3. You can review and apply proposals manually, or configure auto-apply thresholds 4. Applied changes take effect immediately; a rollback window is available --- ## Proposals ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals List pending and recent proposals. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "id": "prop-01HXYZ", "type": "routing_strategy", "description": "Switch to latency-optimized routing — Anthropic p50 has dropped 18% over 24h", "confidence": 0.91, "risk_score": 0.12, "estimated_improvement": "~18% latency reduction", "proposed_at": "2026-03-01T12:00:00Z", "status": "pending" } ] | Field | Description | |---|---| | `confidence` | 0–1 — how certain the advisor is this change helps | | `risk_score` | 0–1 — estimated risk of degradation | | `status` | `pending`, `applied`, `rejected`, `rolled_back` | --- ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id Get a single proposal with full detail. --- ### POST /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id/apply Apply a proposal immediately. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals/prop-01HXYZ/apply \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # → The change takes effect on the next request. If performance degrades within the rollback window, you can revert via the console or by applying the previous configuration manually. --- ## Auto-Apply Configuration The advisor can apply proposals automatically when they meet configured thresholds. Set `enabled: true` in the auto-apply config to activate. ### GET /v1/cognitive/config Returns the current auto-apply configuration. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/config \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "enabled": false, "confidence_threshold": 0.85, "max_risk_score": 0.25, "eval_interval_mins": 60, "rollback_window_mins": 30,

122.content: Console User Guide Dashboard Execution Runs Proof, Receipts, And Violations Execution Environments Policy And Governance Views Billing And Account Areas How To Read The Console Related Pages # Console User Guide The console is the operator view for Igris. Its main job is to help teams inspect and operate: - execution events and run history - signed records and receipt-oriented workflows - execution environments - account, policy, and billing surfaces This page focuses on the practical operator reading of the console rather than trying to document every advanced feature as if it were equally central. --- ## Dashboard The dashboard is the summary view. Use it to get a quick answer to questions like: - are execution runs active - are violations or alert-worthy events increasing - are registered environments still visible - are we approaching an environment-capacity limit Treat it as an operator snapshot, not as the source of truth for deep execution analysis. ## Execution Runs The most important console surface for many teams is the run view. Use it to inspect: - current run status - pause, cancellation, or review state - run metadata - links into receipt and follow-up workflows This is the console surface that maps most directly to the Verify stage of the product model. ## Proof, Receipts, And Violations The proof-oriented areas of the console help operators inspect: - signed or receipt-oriented records - policy-violation follow-up - what should be verified before evidence leaves the product boundary Use these views together with: - [Verification](/docs/verification) - [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Receipts and Audit Workflow](/docs/receipts-audit-workflow) ## Execution Environments The console also shows registered execution environments and their visibility state. That is useful for: - checking whether a runtime environment is registered - confirming heartbeat visibility - staging rollout work carefully The console should not be read as proof that all environment-management automation is broadly ready across every workflow. Use [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) when rollout or update claims matter. ## Policy And Governance Views Console policy and governance views are operator tools for: - checking whether boundaries are behaving as expected - investigating violations - reviewing the effect of permission and policy changes They are useful because policy only matters if the run and its results can still be inspected afterward. ## Billing And Account Areas The console also includes account and billing surfaces. 123.description: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what the model should see, what the runtime should remember, and what the product should preserve across steps, failures, and depl
123.content: Context Engineering Start With The Smallest Useful Context The Context Layers In Igris 1. Request-local context 2. Retrieval and memory 3. MCP and shared context 4. Durable task state 5. Receipts and audit context Choosing The Right Layer Implementation Checklist Common Patterns Hosted inference with light context Agent workflows with reusable state Hybrid deployments with shared device state Long-running workflows A Practical Product Pattern Common Mistakes What Good Context Engineering Looks Like Code And Workflow Quality Signals Related Guides # Context Engineering Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what the model should see, what the runtime should remember, and what the product should preserve across steps, failures, and deployments. In Igris, that choice matters because context can live in several different places: - the request itself - memory systems - MCP and shared context - durable-task checkpoints - receipts and audit records If you put the wrong information in the wrong layer, the system still works, but it becomes harder to reason about, more expensive to operate, and more fragile across retries, restarts, and handoffs. --- ## Start With The Smallest Useful Context The default rule is simple: give the model only the context required to succeed at the current step. That means: - put request-specific instructions and inputs in the request - put reusable knowledge in retrieval or memory - put shared operational state in an explicit shared context layer - put recovery-critical workflow state in durable tasks What you want to avoid is using the prompt as a dumping ground for everything the product knows. ## The Context Layers In Igris ### 1. Request-local context Request-local context belongs in the request payload itself: messages, task inputs, or tool-call inputs. This is the right place for information that matters only to the current call. Use this for: - the current user instruction - short-lived execution constraints - immediate tool-call inputs - one-off routing intent Do not use request-local context as a substitute for shared memory or durable state. ### 2. Retrieval and memory Use memory systems when context should survive beyond one request but does not need to become part of the durable workflow protocol. This includes: - semantic retrieval from vector memory - short-lived working state in KV-style memory - shared blackboard-style state when multiple agents need the same view Use this when the question is: "what should the next step be able to recall?" Use durable tasks instead when the question is: "what must survive an interruption and resume safely?" ### 3. MCP and shared context Use MCP when context should be shared across tools, sessions, or runtime instances in a structured way. MCP is the right layer for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented context - cross-instance context in swarm or multi-device operation Use MCP when context is part of the operating en

124.title: Data Privacy
124.description: Igris is designed with privacy as a core principle. This guide explains how your data is handled, stored, and protected across the platform.
124.content: Data Privacy Data We Collect Account Data Execution Data Fleet Data Provider Keys How We Handle Your Data Data Storage Data Retention Data Isolation Your Rights Data Access Data Deletion Data Portability Privacy by Deployment Mode Cloud API Mode Edge / Offline Mode Hybrid Mode Third-Party Data Sharing Cloud Providers Billing Analytics Compliance GDPR Data Processing Agreement Security Measures Contact # Data Privacy Igris is designed with privacy as a core principle. This guide explains how your data is handled, stored, and protected across the platform. --- ## Data We Collect ### Account Data - Email address and account information - Subscription tier and billing history - API key metadata (prefix only — full keys are never stored after creation) ### Execution Data - Request inputs (prompts, messages) - Model outputs and responses - Resource usage metrics (tokens, latency, cost) - Capability violations and enforcement actions - Signed execution receipts ### Fleet Data - Runtime instance identifiers and registration details - Health metrics and telemetry - Configuration state - Topic mappings (for ROS2 integrations) ### Provider Keys - Cloud provider API keys (encrypted at rest) - Key validation status and rotation history --- ## How We Handle Your Data ### Data Storage - **Cloud API users**: Execution data is stored in our managed infrastructure with encryption at rest - **Edge/Offline users**: All data stays on your device. Nothing is transmitted to Igris servers unless you explicitly export it ### Data Retention Execution records are retained according to your tier: | Tier | Retention Period | |---|---| | Seed | 7 days | | Horizon | 30 days | | Infinite | 90 days (customizable) | After the retention period expires, execution data is automatically purged. ### Data Isolation All data is strictly scoped by tenant. Your data is never accessible to other tenants, and Igris staff cannot view your execution content without explicit authorization. --- ## Your Rights ### Data Access You can access all data associated with your account at any time: - Export execution receipts via the API - Download your fleet configuration - View your complete audit log bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?range=30d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" ### Data Deletion You can request deletion of your account and all associated data: 1. Navigate to **Settings → Account** 2. Click **Delete Account** 3. Confirm the deletion Account deletion is permanent and irreversible. All execution records, fleet data, and configuration will be removed within 30 days. ### Data Portability You can export all your data in a structured format for migration to another system. Contact [support@igrisinertial.com](mailto:support@igrisinertial.com) for a full data exp

125.title: Deploy Local Runtime
125.description: Use this workflow when execution should happen closer to the machine, device, or environment where the work actually runs.
125.content: Deploy Local Runtime 1. Download The Runtime Archive 2. Install The Binary 3. Configure Auth And Local Execution Behavior 4. Start And Verify The Runtime 5. Send A Local Request What To Say Carefully Common Mistakes Related Guides # Deploy Local Runtime Use this workflow when Igris should execute closer to where the work happens. Local runtime is not a separate product identity. It is an execution surface for workloads that benefit from locality, device-level boundaries, or reduced dependence on a hosted path. Choose this path when you need: - execution near the machine or device doing the work - local policy enforcement or bounded task handling - offline or low-connectivity operation - runtime-local behavior tree or tool execution If those properties are not central to the workload, start with the hosted integration first. --- ## 1. Download The Runtime Archive Use the runtime distribution endpoints for your platform and treat download as provisioning, not application traffic. bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-amd64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the archive checksum before installation. ## 2. Install The Binary bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ## 3. Configure Auth And Local Execution Behavior Create `~/.config/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0 } } This configuration expresses how the runtime should execute work locally. Treat local GGUF fallback carefully in public claims: the code path exists, but reproducible proof should be checked against [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before you present it as a guaranteed behavior. ## 4. Start And Verify The Runtime bash igris-runtime serve curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health Once the runtime is healthy, use the runtime base URL for local requests: text http://localhost:8080/v1 ## 5. Send A Local Request typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'http://localhost:8080/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'phi3', messages: [ ], }); This is still the same execution model: - **Request** through an Igris API surf

126.title: Deployment
126.description: Choose the Igris deployment mode based on where execution should run: hosted, local, or hybrid.
126.content: Deployment Hosted Deployment Local Deployment Hybrid Deployment Local Models And Fallback Language Verifying A Deployment Common Deployment Issues Related Guides # Deployment Choose your deployment mode based on where execution should run. Igris is one execution system with multiple deployment modes: - **hosted** when provider-backed execution through the managed surface is enough - **local** when work should run closer to your machine or device - **hybrid** when hosted coordination and runtime participation both matter The deployment choice changes where execution happens. It does not create separate products. --- ## Hosted Deployment Use hosted deployment when you want the fastest provider-backed path with the least operational overhead. python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1", api_key="your-api-key" ) Hosted deployment is a good fit when you want: - managed API entry - provider-backed execution - simpler onboarding - customer-facing receipt and audit surfaces without local runtime operations Proof claims for specific real-provider paths should still follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status). ## Local Deployment Use local deployment when execution should happen closer to the environment doing the work. Typical reasons: - device or infrastructure locality - local tool or workflow integration - low-connectivity or offline-sensitive operation - runtime-side governance near the workload Start the runtime on your own infrastructure and point the client at the runtime base URL when the request belongs there. ## Hybrid Deployment Use hybrid deployment when you want one application-facing contract while allowing runtime participation underneath. This mode is useful when you need: - a hosted entry path for applications - runtime-backed execution in selected environments - operator visibility into registered execution environments Keep the proof language careful: - hybrid architecture is supported - not every failover or recovery behavior should be described as proven without the matching artifact See [Hybrid Deployment Workflow](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow) for the staged operator view. ## Local Models And Fallback Language Local model configuration is part of the deployment story, but language here should stay disciplined: - local execution is real - local fallback paths exist in the product model - failure-to-local-model proof should follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before being described as proven behavior ## Verifying A Deployment After you deploy,

127.title: Durable Task Execution
127.description: Use durable tasks for long-running AI work that needs state, boundaries, and records that survive beyond a single synchronous request.
127.content: Durable Task Execution What Durable Tasks Add How To Think About The Lifecycle Submitting A Task Example Tracking Task Status Checkpoints And Recovery Language Durable Streaming Common Mistakes Related Guides # Durable Task Execution Durable tasks are for long-running AI work that should not be treated like a single short request. Use them when the workload needs: - multiple steps - explicit state progression - bounded execution over time - records that remain inspectable after the task completes or fails This page explains the durable-task model in practical terms and keeps recovery claims aligned with current proof status. --- ## What Durable Tasks Add Compared with a short synchronous request, a durable task adds: - task identity - execution-state tracking across steps - checkpoint and WAL-oriented structures - follow-up inspection through task status and receipt-oriented workflows That makes durable tasks the right fit for longer-running governed work. ## How To Think About The Lifecycle The durable-task lifecycle is still Request -> Execute -> Verify: - **Request** submits the task definition - **Execute** runs the task step by step under boundaries - **Verify** inspects task status, execution outcome, and receipt-oriented records ## Submitting A Task bash POST /v1/tasks/submit Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Content-Type: application/json The product supports different submission shapes, but they all become one durable execution workflow underneath. ### Example json { "task_type": "agent_workflow", "task_definition": { "steps": [ { "step_index": 0, "model": "gpt-4.1-mini", "messages": [ ] }, { "step_index": 1, "model": "gpt-4.1-mini", "messages": [ ] } ] }, "idempotency_key": "report-q3-2026-run-1" } ## Tracking Task Status bash GET /v1/tasks/TASK_ID Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY Typical statuses include: | Status | Meaning | |---|---| | `pending` | Awaiting runtime assignment | | `dispatched` | Assigned and executing | | `checkpointed` | Mid-execution with checkpoint state recorded | | `completed` | All steps finished successfully | | `failed` | Execution ended with a non-recoverable error | | `recovering` | Recovery handling is in progress | Use these states to understand where the work is, not as proof that every recovery path has been demonstrated end to end. ## Checkpoints And Recovery Language Checkpoint, WAL, and recovery structures are part of the durable-task model, but proof language matters: - 129.title: Routing Engine
129.description: The routing engine is an advanced path-selection layer inside Igris execution, combining policy, health, trust, and strategy-specific selection logic.
129.content: Routing Engine What It Is What It Considers Strategy Layer Relationship To Other Controls Console And Inspection Proof Language Related Pages # Routing Engine The routing engine is an advanced path-selection layer inside Igris execution. Its job is to choose among the execution paths that remain allowed and usable after policy, health, and trust have already narrowed the field. This makes it important to advanced operators, but it should not be read as the primary product identity. --- ## What It Is At a simple level: text Request -> policy and boundary checks -> health and trust filters -> routing engine -> selected execution path That means the routing engine is not a standalone product story. It is one layer inside the broader Execute stage. ## What It Considers Depending on configuration, the engine may consider: - latency behavior - success or failure history - cost signals - availability - strategy-specific selection logic Different deployment modes may expose different routing behavior, but the core idea is the same: choose an execution path under governance, not by ad hoc client-side guessing. ## Strategy Layer Different strategy modes can exist on top of the engine, such as adaptive, cost-aware, or latency-aware selection. Those strategies are advanced operator tools and should be evaluated with workload-specific evidence rather than broad assumptions. ## Relationship To Other Controls The engine sits behind: - policy - health - trust - circuit-breaker state That ordering matters. Advanced path selection should not override the safety and governance layers that determine whether a path should even be considered. ## Console And Inspection Routing dashboards can help explain which path was chosen and why, but they should be treated as advanced execution diagnostics. They are useful after you already understand the main product model. ## Proof Language The routing engine is a real advanced control layer, but this page should not promise globally optimal provider choice, automatic savings, or universal reliability gains without evidence for the specific workload and environment. ## Related Pages - [Semantic Routing →](/docs/semantic-routing) - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination)

131.title: Execution Model
131.description: This page explains the Igris execution model as Request -> Execute -> Verify, with governed boundaries and signed records around the run.
131.content: Execution Model Request Execute Boundaries Verify Signed Records Deployment Modes Fit Under The Same Model What To Treat Carefully # Execution Model The Igris execution model is: 1. **Request** 2. **Execute** 3. **Verify** Everything else on this page is a more detailed explanation of those three stages. --- ## Request Request is how work enters Igris. That can be an OpenAI-compatible call, a task-oriented request, or another documented surface. The key idea is consistency: the request enters one execution system, not a collection of unrelated product identities. At request time, Igris establishes the context that matters for the run: - identity and tenant scope - input payload and parameters - capability expectations - applicable limits or policy boundaries ## Execute Execution is where the request becomes governed work. During execution, Igris can: - apply capability and policy checks - enforce budgets and other boundaries - capture execution events and state - run on the hosted or runtime-backed path configured for the workload - record violations or failure outcomes instead of hiding them This is the layer that turns a plain model response into an inspectable run. ### Boundaries Typical execution boundaries include: | Boundary | What it restricts | |---|---| | Capability gates | What the run is allowed to do | | Token or resource limits | How much work the run can consume | | Time limits | How long execution is allowed to continue | | Tool restrictions | Which external actions are allowed | If execution exceeds an allowed boundary, that outcome should be recorded as part of the run. ## Verify Verification is how you inspect what happened after execution. Depending on the path, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt hashes - proof-status information That is what makes the system useful for review, governance, and post-run analysis. ## Signed Records The model is not complete until the run produces something you can inspect later. In Igris terms, that can include: - the execution envelope for the run context - the execution receipt for the final record - hash-linked receipt material for downstream audit workflows Use [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) and [Verification](/docs/verification) for the public-facing receipt and proof workflows. ## Deployment Modes Fit Under The Same Model Hosted, local, and hybrid setups all fit under the same execution model: - the request still enters through Igris

132.content: Execution Receipts Current Query Surface List Receipts Export Receipts Proof Verification # Execution Receipts Execution receipts are the customer-facing audit record for what ran, where it ran, and whether policy violations occurred. --- ## Current Query Surface The current customer query surface for receipts lives in Overture: - `GET /v1/receipts` - `GET /v1/receipts/:id` - `GET /v1/receipts/export` - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` The current runtime build does **not** expose a public local `GET /v1/receipts` listing endpoint. 133.content: First Hosted Integration 1. Create A Tenant API Key 2. Add A Provider Key 3. Send A Hosted Request 4. Inspect What You Need Next Proof Language For Hosted Execution Common Mistakes Related Guides # First Hosted Integration Use this workflow when you want the shortest path from the Request -> Execute -> Verify model into a provider-backed hosted integration. Hosted execution is one deployment mode for Igris. It is a good fit when the team wants to start with a managed API surface, keep the application contract simple, and prove that governed execution is useful before adding local runtime infrastructure. The basic sequence is: 1. Create a tenant API key 2. Add at least one provider key 3. Send a request through the hosted Igris API surface 4. Inspect execution metadata and decide whether you need deeper Igris-native features --- ## 1. Create A Tenant API Key Create one tenant API key for the environment that will call the hosted surface. Treat it like any other production secret and keep it in your standard secret store. - [Trial & Billing →](/docs/trial-billing) - [API Authentication →](/docs/api-reference/authentication) ## 2. Add A Provider Key Hosted execution depends on provider credentials stored in the Igris vault. For customer traffic today, use `openai` or `anthropic`. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' ## 3. 134.content: First Verified Run What This Run Proves Prerequisites Run The Demo What The Script Does What To Inspect What Is Proven Locally What Is Not Proven By This Demo Real Provider Mode # First Verified Run This page walks through the narrowest honest proof-backed path in the repo today. Use it when you want to see Igris do real execution work and return verification-ready artifacts, without assuming unproven provider, fallback, or robotics behavior. --- ## What This Run Proves The local proof demonstrates: - one request sent through Overture - execution handed off to Runtime - signed `execution_envelope` returned from the run - signed `execution_receipt` returned from the run - receipt hash recomputation and receipt-log chain verification - route-decision metadata showing the request was forwarded to Runtime This is a **proven locally** path based on the current proof artifacts. ## Prerequisites - A checkout of this repository - `node`, `go`, `cargo`, `curl`, and `lsof` - Free ports `8080` and `8081` - Free port `18090` for the default mock-provider mode ## Run The Demo From the repo root: bash ./scripts/unified_execution_proof_demo.sh Expected output shape: text Unified execution proof succeeded. Mode: mock Provider: local-mock-cloud Route decision: forwarded_to_runtime_task Receipt execution_id: ... Receipt hash: ... Artifacts: /tmp/igris-unified-proof.XXXXXX ## What The Script Does 1. Prepares local proof artifacts, including an offline license artifact and local signing material. 2. Builds or reuses the Runtime binary. 3. Builds the Overture binary. 4. Starts a local mock OpenAI-compatible upstream on `127.0.0.1:18090`. 5. Starts Runtime on `127.0.0.1:8080`. 6. Starts Overture on `127.0.0.1:8081`. 7. Sends one `/v1/infer` request through Overture. 8. Fails if Overture falls back away from Runtime. 9. Verifies the returned `execution_envelope`. 10. 135.description: Use fleet management to register, inspect, and coordinate execution environments that participate in Igris workflows.
135.content: Fleet Management 1. Register Execution Environments 2. Track Heartbeats And Coordination Surfaces 3. Inspect Registered Environments 4. Treat Config Push Carefully 5. Treat OTA-Style Updates Carefully What Fleet Management Means In Practice Common Mistakes Related Guides # Fleet Management Use fleet management when you need visibility into the execution environments that participate in Igris workflows. This page is about operating registered runtime environments. The reliable, practical use cases today are: - registering execution environments - monitoring whether they remain visible and healthy enough to participate - inspecting runtime coordination surfaces - using queued command and rollout features carefully --- ## 1. Register Execution Environments The stock runtime attempts registration automatically when both `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` are present at startup.
