136.title: Fleet Rollout Workflow
136.description: Use this workflow when you want to introduce Igris execution environments gradually and verify behavior before expanding rollout.
136.content: Fleet Rollout Workflow 1. Start With A Small Environment Set 2. Observe Execution Before Expanding 3. Roll Configuration Deliberately 4. Expand In Stages 5. Keep Rollback Simple Common Mistakes Related Guides # Fleet Rollout Workflow Use this workflow when you want to introduce runtime-backed execution environments in stages instead of turning on broad rollout all at once. The goal is simple: 1. start small 2. observe execution behavior 3. verify the records that matter 4. expand only after the first slice is stable This page is about staged rollout of execution environments. --- ## 1. Start With A Small Environment Set Before expanding rollout, make sure each target environment can: - start cleanly - register successfully - remain visible through heartbeat reporting - execute the workload shape you care about If those basics are not healthy, rollout is the wrong next step. ## 2. Observe Execution Before Expanding Do not treat rollout as a blind infrastructure action. Use the first slice to inspect: - whether environments stay registered - whether requests route the way you expect - whether execution events and receipts remain available - whether customer-facing traffic is unaffected This is the practical operator version of Request -> Execute -> Verify. ## 3. Roll Configuration Deliberately If you use config-push surfaces, separate configuration changes from binary updates whenever possible. That makes it easier to answer: - did the environment change break execution behavior - did the binary change introduce the issue - which step should be rolled back first Config-push surfaces exist, but broad rollout success should still be described carefully unless you have reproducible evidence for the exact pattern you are using. ## 4. Expand In Stages A safe rollout sequence looks like: 1. one environment or a small canary group 2. inspect runtime visibility and execution behavior 3. check receipts or proof-oriented inspection where the workflow depends on them 4. expand to the next slice only after the first slice is stable Avoid language that implies failover or recovery is already proven across the whole environment set. ## 5. Keep Rollback Simple Plan rollback before expansion: - keep the previous known-good runtime version available - avoid mixing config changes and binary changes in the same rollout stage - use staged expansion so rollback scope stays small Rollback should be an explicit operator action, not an assumption hidden behind marketing language. ## Common Mistakes - Expanding rollout before checking the first slice for stable registration and execution b

137.title: Governance
137.description: Governance in Igris means applying boundaries, permissions, execution events, and signed records around the Request -> Execute -> Verify lifecycle.
137.content: Governance What Governance Covers Before Execution: Permissions And Scope During Execution: Boundaries And Events After Execution: Signed Records Capability Boundaries Review And Follow-Up What To Avoid Claiming Related Guides # Governance Governance in Igris starts with the Request -> Execute -> Verify model. - **Request** defines what work is being asked for and under which context. - **Execute** applies permissions, boundaries, and runtime checks while the work runs. - **Verify** makes the resulting events and signed records available for inspection later. This page is about the practical controls around execution, not about broad unsupported governance claims. --- ## What Governance Covers Governance answers four operator questions: 1. what was requested 2. what the run was allowed to do 3. what happened during execution 4. what record is available afterward That maps directly to: - permissions and capability checks - execution boundaries - execution events and outcome state - signed records and receipt-oriented inspection ## Before Execution: Permissions And Scope Before the main work runs, Igris can apply controls such as: - tenant or deployment scope - capability grants - allowed tools or access paths - duration or resource expectations This is the part of governance that decides whether the request is allowed to become execution at all. ## During Execution: Boundaries And Events While the run is active, governance is about keeping execution inside its declared boundaries and making the outcome inspectable. Examples include: - capability checks during tool or action attempts - resource boundaries such as duration or token limits - recording violations or rejected actions - surfacing execution events that help operators understand what happened That is why governance belongs to execution itself, not just to a static policy document. ## After Execution: Signed Records Governance is only useful if the result can be checked later. Depending on the path, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt-oriented audit records Use these pages for the public-facing workflow: - [Verification →](/docs/verification) - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status) ## Capability Boundaries Governance often starts with capability scope. 139.description: Use this workflow when one Igris execution model needs to span hosted coordination and local runtime execution.
139.content: Hybrid Deployment Workflow 1. Keep One Application-Facing Contract 2. Start Runtimes With The Right Registration Context 3. Verify Hosted And Runtime Health Separately 4. Decide What Must Stay Hosted Versus Local 5. Treat Failure Paths Carefully Common Mistakes Related Guides # Hybrid Deployment Workflow Use this workflow when one Igris execution model needs to span hosted and local environments. Hybrid deployment is still one product story: - **Request** enters through a stable application-facing Igris surface - **Execute** can involve hosted coordination and runtime-backed execution - **Verify** stays tied to the same records, receipts, and inspection workflows This model is useful when you care about: - governance across hosted and local environments - running execution closer to devices or private infrastructure - clearer failure-path handling between application traffic and runtime operations - verification-ready records even when execution topology is mixed --- ## 1. Keep One Application-Facing Contract In most hybrid setups, the application still points at the hosted base URL: text https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1 That keeps the application contract stable while allowing runtime participation underneath. ## 2. Start Runtimes With The Right Registration Context Hybrid deployment only works when the runtime can start and register correctly. bash export IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY="YOUR_LICENSE_KEY" export IGRIS_API_KEY="YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" igris-runtime serve This is the operational step that makes runtime-backed participation possible. It does not create a second product surface for the application team. ## 3. Verify Hosted And Runtime Health Separately Check both sides of the system deliberately: - hosted API calls succeed with your tenant API key - the runtime answers `http://localhost:8080/v1/health` - runtime registration and visibility succeed where your workflow depends on them Hybrid works best when execution traffic and runtime operations are both observable. ## 4. Decide What Must Stay Hosted Versus Local Use hosted coordination when you want: - the simplest application-facing entry path - provider-backed execution without device-local routing decisions in the client - centralized operator workflows Use runtime-backed execution when you want: - locality - device-level governance - execution near private infrastructure or tools The important point is that the workflow still belongs to one execution system. ## 5. 140.title: Identity & Access
140.description: How Igris handles console identity, tenant API keys, tenant roles, and higher-assurance access controls.
140.content: Identity & Access Two Access Planes Console Identity Tenant API Keys Tenant Roles Higher-Assurance Access Controls 2FA SSO Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Identity & Access Igris separates **human access** from **programmatic access**. - **Console identity** is for people using the web app - **Tenant API keys** are for applications, automation, and deployed runtimes Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Two Access Planes | Plane | Used by | Primary credential | Scope | |---|---|---|---| | **Console** | Human operators | Session cookie | Browser session tied to a tenant user | | **API** | Apps, agents, runtimes | `igris_` API key | Tenant-scoped machine access | Console cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. For scripts and integrations, use tenant API keys. --- ## Console Identity The console uses a session-based sign-in model. A user signs in once, receives a session cookie, and then operates inside one tenant context at a time. Current product behavior: - Console access is designed for interactive human use - Session state is separate from tenant API-key auth - Tenant context is applied before policy, billing, and audit logic This keeps browser access and machine access cleanly separated. --- ## Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys are the automation contract for the coordination layer. Accepted forms: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Use tenant API keys for: - server-side application calls - CI/CD or operational automation - provisioning and runtime registration flows - customer-visible integrations that should not depend on browser cookies Do not reuse one tenant's API key across other tenants. Keys are tenant-scoped by design. --- ## Tenant Roles Igris distinguishes between ordinary tenant access and elevated administrative access. In practical terms, roles matter for: - tenant administration - sensitive configuration changes - identity and security operations - management actions that should not be available to every authenticated caller When you design operational workflows, treat roles as part of the product boundary that customers and operators can reason about directly. --- ## Higher-Assurance Access Controls Igris includes stronger access controls for deployments that need more than basic session auth plus API keys. ### 2FA Two-factor authentication is available for tenant-level console access hardening. Use it when console operators can perform security-sensitive actions such as reviewing paused executions, rotating provider keys, or chang

141.title: Key Management
141.description: Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer.
141.content: Key Management What The Current Public API Supports Add A Provider Key Rotate, Validate, Remove Security Properties # Key Management Igris stores provider keys in the vault used by the cloud coordination layer. --- ## What The Current Public API Supports The current public vault API accepts these provider identifiers: | Provider | Intended use | |---|---| | `openai` | Customer cloud traffic | | `anthropic` | Customer cloud traffic | | `benchmark` | Synthetic or test traffic | Do not assume broader provider coverage on the public vault API unless it is explicitly documented in the current contract. --- ## Add A Provider Key bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/vault/keys \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "provider": "openai", "key_name": "production", "api_key": "YOUR_OPENAI_KEY" }' Current request fields: | Field | Description | |---|---| | `provider` | Provider identifier such as `openai` | | `key_name` | Human-readable name for the key | | `api_key` | Provider secret to encrypt and store | --- ## Rotate, Validate, Remove Current routes: - `GET /v1/vault/keys` - `GET /v1/vault/keys/:provider` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/rotate` - `POST /v1/vault/keys/:provider/validate` - `DELETE /v1/vault/keys/:provider` The current response contract returns masked values only. Raw provider secrets are never returned after creation. --- ## Security Properties - Provider keys are encrypted before storage - Key operations are tenant-scoped - API responses expose masked key material only - Vault operations are available through authenticated control-plane APIs --- [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) · [Security →](/docs/security) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

142.title: Licensing & Activation
142.description: How Igris licenses are activated, validated, and kept alive across the console, coordination layer, and deployed runtimes.
142.content: Licensing & Activation Product Model Tenant Activation Runtime Admission Device Identity And Heartbeats What The License Controls Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Licensing & Activation Igris licensing is not just a billing flag. It is part of the runtime bootstrap path. There are two distinct surfaces: - **Tenant activation in the console** associates a purchased license with a tenant - **Runtime validation and heartbeat** determine whether a deployed runtime is allowed to stay active Treat those as one lifecycle. --- ## Product Model At a high level, the licensing flow works like this: 1. A tenant activates a license key from the console. 2. The runtime validates that license during startup. 3. The runtime registers a device identity under that license. 4. The runtime sends periodic heartbeats to remain counted as active. If validation fails, the runtime should not be treated as fully admitted into the platform. --- ## Tenant Activation The console exposes a tenant-facing activation flow so an operator can bind a license to the current tenant account. From a product perspective, that does three things: - sets the active plan for the tenant - determines the feature set and quota envelope - establishes the license record that runtimes will validate against The console also exposes plan and quota state, including: - current plan - license status - request quota - device quota - active device count That means licensing is visible to both finance and operations, not just procurement. --- ## Runtime Admission The runtime performs license validation during startup before it proceeds with its normal cloud-registration path. In practical terms, runtime admission depends on: - a valid license key - a generated device identity - the runtime version reported during validation The runtime then attempts device registration under that license. This is important operationally because a license is not only "valid" or "invalid"; it also tracks how many active devices are attached to it. --- ## Device Identity And Heartbeats Each runtime derives a device ID from local machine characteristics and registers that device against the license. Once registered, the runtime sends periodic heartbeats. This gives Igris an operational answer to questions like: - which runtimes are still alive - how many devices are currently consuming the license - whether a device should be treated as stale or deregistered If you are operating a fleet, heartbeats are part of capacity accounting, not just health reporting. --- ## What The License Controls Lice

143.description: igris-runtime can serve GGUF models locally and participate in hybrid deployments where cloud routing falls back to on-device inference.
143.content: Local LLM Fallback What Exists Today Configuration Fields Hybrid Behavior Supported Model Format Operational Notes # Local LLM Fallback `igris-runtime` can serve GGUF models locally and participate in hybrid deployments where cloud routing falls back to on-device inference. --- ## What Exists Today The current runtime config surface is `local_fallback`. The shipped config supports local model loading and tuning knobs such as context size, threading, GPU layer offload, and prompt caching. json5 { local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/mistral-7b.Q4_K_M.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0, max_tokens: 512, temperature: 0.7 } } Optional fields also available in the current runtime: - `main_gpu` - `prompt_cache_dir` - `batch_size` - `lora_adapter_path` --- ## Configuration Fields | Field | Description | |---|---| | `enabled` | Enables the local fallback subsystem | | `model_path` | Path to the GGUF model on disk | | `context_size` | Runtime context window size | | `threads` | CPU threads for local inference | | `n_gpu_layers` | Number of model layers offloaded to GPU | | `max_tokens` | Default local generation cap | | `temperature` | Default local sampling temperature | There is no dedicated pure-local fallback toggle in the current runtime config. For pure local deployments, point clients directly at `http://localhost:8080/v1` and do not rely on cloud routing. --- ## Hybrid Behavior In a hybrid deployment: 1. Your application calls Overture 2. Overture routes normally across cloud providers 3. If the runtime is registered and selected by your routing configuration, local execution can participate in the request path In a fully local deployment: 1. Your application calls the runtime directly 2. The runtime answers from the local model 3. Signed execution receipts are returned with the response payload when enabled by the runtime path --- ## Supported Model Format The current runtime expects GGUF model files on disk. 144.content: MCP Guide Pages Transport Surfaces Method Families Session and Transport Context and Resource Operations Tooling and Agent Workflows How MCP Fits In # MCP MCP is the structured context layer in Igris. Use it when context belongs to the operating environment and must move between tools, agents, sessions, or runtimes without becoming accidental prompt state. This section documents MCP as part of the product contract. Start with the overview pages below if you are orienting yourself, then move to the transport and integration guides when you are shaping production workflows. ## Guide Pages - [MCP Server](/docs/mcp-server): customer-facing transport and method model - [MCP Swarm Mode](/docs/mcp-swarm): how shared context behaves in multi-agent execution - [MCP Integration Patterns](/docs/mcp-integration-patterns): practical patterns for durable, auditable context usage ## Transport Surfaces - [`POST /v1/mcp`](/docs/mcp-server): hosted transport for customer-facing MCP requests - [`POST /v1/mcp/stream`](/docs/mcp-server): streaming transport when MCP exchange needs incremental output ## Method Families ### Session and Transport - initialize session state - advertise capabilities - establish request and response shape ### Context and Resource Operations - list available context resources - read resource content - push or refresh context into the shared working surface ### Tooling and Agent Workflows - expose tools to participating agents - share execution context across swarm members - coordinate working context without confusing it with receipts or durable checkpoints ## How MCP Fits In Use MCP for shared working context. Use durable tasks for long-running progress. Use receipts for audit evidence. Keeping those three concerns separate is what makes the system understandable and operable at scale. --- [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering) · [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

145.title: MCP Integration Patterns
145.description: This guide shows how to use MCP as part of a production integration rather than as an isolated protocol feature.
145.content: MCP Integration Patterns Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Related Guides # MCP Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use MCP as part of a production integration rather than as an isolated protocol feature. --- ## Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Use MCP for working state that tools, agents, or runtimes need to share. Do not use MCP as the place where audit evidence lives. Keep audit and receipt workflows separate so the system remains understandable. ## Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Avoid dumping arbitrary JSON into a few generic keys. Define stable keys and value shapes for shared context that your application team can reason about. Good: - `mission_state` - `dispatch_plan` - `device_role` Weak: - `state` - `payload` - `latest_data` ## Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately MCP and durable tasks solve different problems: - MCP shares structured state - durable tasks preserve progress and resume semantics Use both when a long-running workflow needs shared context and safe recovery. Do not force one to replace the other. ## Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Your application should still think in terms of one product: - hosted coordination when the application contract belongs in the cloud - runtime-local execution when work belongs on-device - MCP for shared operational state across those boundaries ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Durable Tasks →](/docs/durable-tasks) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

146.title: MCP Server
146.description: This page documents the MCP server surface that Igris exposes through the product.
146.content: MCP Server What The MCP Server Is For Customer Contract Request Shape Core Method Families Integration Guidance Related Guides # MCP Server This page documents the MCP server surface that Igris exposes through the product. Treat MCP as part of the product contract rather than as a generic tool-call side channel. --- ## What The MCP Server Is For Use the MCP server when context needs to move between agents, tools, sessions, or runtimes in a structured way. That makes it useful for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented working context - multi-agent coordination - runtime-local or cross-runtime context exchange If the problem is only one request deep, keep the data in the request instead. Use MCP when the context belongs to the operating environment. ## Customer Contract The customer-facing hosted entry points are: - `POST /v1/mcp` for request/response JSON-RPC calls - `POST /v1/mcp/stream` for streaming MCP interactions The product forwards those calls to the appropriate runtime MCP server where needed, so the customer can keep thinking in terms of one product surface. ## Request Shape The MCP request body follows JSON-RPC 2.0: json { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "context/write", "params": { "key": "mission_state", "value": { "step": 3, "status": "navigating" } }, "id": 1 } ## Core Method Families The main MCP method families exposed through Igris today are: - `context/*` for structured shared context - `tools/*` for tool discovery and invocation Treat the specific method contract as part of your application integration, not as an undocumented side channel. ## Integration Guidance - keep request-local prompt data out of MCP unless it truly belongs in shared state - prefer explicit keys and schemas for shared context - do not mix audit evidence with working context - use durable tasks when progress recovery matters more than context recall ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering) - [Hybrid Deployment Workflow →](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow)

147.title: MCP Swarm Mode
147.description: MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network.
147.content: MCP Swarm Mode What It Solves Operational Model Configuration Design Boundaries Common Mistakes Related Guides # MCP Swarm Mode MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network. Use it when context must move between devices or runtime instances without turning every exchange into an application-managed synchronization problem. --- ## What It Solves Swarm Mode is useful when: - multiple runtimes need the same operational context - one runtime should be able to continue after another runtime wrote the latest shared state - distributed planning or robotics coordination needs a shared context layer ## Operational Model In Swarm Mode: - runtimes discover peers - shared context is replicated across the swarm - reads can be served from a peer that did not originate the write That makes Swarm Mode a context-sharing mechanism, not a replacement for durable workflow recovery or audit evidence. ## Configuration toml [mcp_swarm] enabled = true discovery = "mdns" encryption_key_path = "/path/to/swarm.key" ## Design Boundaries Use Swarm Mode for shared operational state. Do not use it for: - signed audit records - long-term business data retention - progress recovery that should be modeled as a durable task ## Common Mistakes - treating swarm replication as if it were a durable checkpoint protocol - storing too much request-local prompt state in the shared swarm context - using swarm state where one runtime-local value would be simpler ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

148.title: Memory
148.description: Igris supports three memory systems: vector store for semantic retrieval, KV cache for fast key-value lookup, and cross-instance context via MCP Swarm Mode.
148.content: Memory Vector Store KV Cache Cross-Instance Context (MCP Swarm Mode) Agent Blackboard API GET /v1/agents/memory/ GET /v1/agents/memory/:key PUT /v1/agents/memory/:key DELETE /v1/agents/memory/:key → 204 No Content On-Device Training # Memory Igris supports three memory systems: vector store for semantic retrieval, KV cache for fast key-value lookup, and cross-instance context via MCP Swarm Mode. --- ## Vector Store The vector store indexes embeddings and retrieves semantically similar documents at query time. It gives agents access to a long-term knowledge base without including everything in the context window. **How it works:** 1. Documents are embedded and stored in the local vector index 2. At query time, the agent provides a query string 3. The vector store returns the top-K most similar documents 4. Retrieved documents are injected into the agent's context **Configuration:** json { "memory": { "vector_store": { "enabled": true, "top_k": 5, "similarity_threshold": 0.75 } } } **Supported embedding models:** - Any GGUF-format embedding model - External embedding APIs (via the HTTP tool) The vector index is stored on device. Embeddings do not leave the device unless you configure an external embedding endpoint. --- ## KV Cache The KV cache provides fast key-value storage for agent state that must persist across steps or across executions. **Use cases:** - Storing intermediate results between planning steps - Persisting agent state across tool calls - Caching frequently accessed data to reduce tool call latency **Access:** json { "kv_cache": { "set": }, "get": , "ttl_seconds": 3600 } } KV entries expire after `ttl_seconds`. The cache is local to the engine instance unless MCP Swarm Mode is enabled. --- ## Cross-Instance Context (MCP Swarm Mode) MCP Swarm Mode enables execution context to be shared across multiple engine instances. Any instance in the swarm can access context written by another instance. **How it works:** - Instances auto-discover each other via mDNS on the local network - Context is written to shared encrypted storage (AES-256-GCM) - Any instance can read context written by any other instance - Context is available within milliseconds of being written **Use cases:** - Multi-robot coordination: one robot updates mission state, others read it - High-availability: if one instance goes offline, another continues the execution - Distributed agents: agents on different nodes share a working memory **Configuration:** json { "mcp_swarm": { "enabled": true, "discovery": "mdns", "encryption_key_path": "/path/to/swarm.key" } } The encryption key is device-specific and must be dis

149.description: > Infinite Tier — Federated model aggregation is included with the Infinite plan.
149.content: Model Aggregation What It Is Architecture Aggregation Rounds Round Configuration Privacy API GET /v1/federated/status GET /v1/federated/participants GET /v1/federated/rounds POST /v1/federated/rounds/start GET /v1/federated/config PUT /v1/federated/config Console # Model Aggregation > **Infinite Tier** — Federated model aggregation is included with the Infinite plan. Igris supports federated learning across your fleet of Runtime devices, enabling collaborative model improvement without sharing raw data between devices. --- ## What It Is Model Aggregation (federated learning) allows multiple Runtime devices to train local model updates (LoRA adapters) and aggregate them into a global model improvement — all without sending training data off-device. Device A: trains local adapter ──┐ Device B: trains local adapter ──┼──► Aggregator → Global model update Device C: trains local adapter ──┘ Each device: 1. Trains a LoRA adapter on its local execution history 2. Sends only the adapter weights (encrypted) to the aggregator 3. Receives the aggregated global model update 4. Applies the update to its local model Raw execution data never leaves the device. --- ## Architecture ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer (Cloud) │ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Federated Coordinator │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ Round Manager → Aggregator → Model Distributor│ │ │ └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ │Device A │ │Device B │ │Device C │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ --- ## Aggregation Rounds Federated learning operates in rounds: 1. **Round Start** — The coordinator triggers a new aggregation round 2. **Local Training** — Each participating device trains its LoRA adapter 3. **Weight Upload** — Devices upload encrypted adapter weights 4. **Aggregation** — The coordinator computes a weighted average of all adapters 5. **Distribution** — The aggregated model is sent back to all participants 6. **Application** — Each device loads the updated model ### Round Configuration json { "federated_learning": { "enabled": true, "min_participants": 3, "round_interval_mins": 60, "max_rounds_per_day": 12, "privacy_budget": 1.0, "noise_scale": 0.1 } } | Field | Type | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `enabled` | bool | `false` | Enable federated learning | | `min_participants` | int | 3 | Minimum devices required to start a round | | `round_interval_mins` | int | 60 | Time between aggregation rounds | | `max_rounds_p

150.title: Multi-Tenancy
150.description: Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail.
150.content: Multi-Tenancy Architecture Isolation guarantees Tenant Identification Tenant Configuration Resource Quotas Cross-Tenant Isolation Data isolation Network isolation Key isolation Billing # Multi-Tenancy Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail. --- ## Architecture Multi-tenancy in Igris is enforced at every layer: ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer │ │ │ │ Tenant A │ Tenant B │ │ Tenant C │ Tenant D │ └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ Runtime A │ │ Runtime B │ │ Runtime C │ │ (Tenant A) │ │ (Tenant B) │ │ (Tenant C) │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ ### Isolation guarantees | Layer | Isolation method | |---|---| | **Inference** | Separate API keys, separate provider configurations | | **Execution** | Separate execution envelopes with tenant-scoped IDs | | **Data** | Tenant-scoped storage — no cross-tenant data access | | **Policies** | Per-tenant policy envelopes | | **Audit** | Per-tenant receipt chains | | **Keys** | Per-tenant vault — keys are never shared | --- ## Tenant Identification Every request is associated with a tenant via the API key used for authentication. The API key maps to exactly one tenant. There is no cross-tenant key. API Key → Tenant ID → Execution Context The tenant ID is embedded in every execution receipt, ensuring full traceability from receipt back to tenant. --- ## Tenant Configuration Each tenant has an independent configuration: json { "tenant": { "id": "tenant-abc123", "name": "Acme Corp", "tier": "horizon", "providers": ["anthropic", "openai"], "policy": { "max_tokens": 4096, "max_steps": 10, "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false }, "slo": { "latency_p99_ms": 2000, "max_cost_per_request_usd": 0.05 } } } --- ## Resource Quotas Tenants are allocated resource quotas based on their tier: | Resource | Seed | Horizon | Infinite | |---|---|---|---| | Runtime instances | 3 | 50 | 500 | | Receipt retention | 7 days | 30 days | 90 days | | Federated learning | — | — | ✓ | | SLO enforcement | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | Routing advisor | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | When a tenant exceeds its quota, requests are rejected with HTTP 429. The `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header indicates remaining capacity. --- ## Cross-Tenant Isolation ### Data isolation - Execution receipts are scoped to tenant — no tenant can query another tenant's receipts - Vector store indexes are tenant-scoped - KV cache entries are tenant-scoped -

Check [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before promoting multimodal behavior beyond preview language. --- ## How It Fits Multimodal work still belongs under the same Request -> Execute -> Verify model: - **Request** includes text plus one or more additional modalities - **Execute** depends on the configured multimodal-capable path - **Verify** depends on the execution record that comes back from that run The preview status is about maturity, not about a different product identity. ## What To Expect This surface is appropriate for evaluation when teams want to explore: - text-plus-image workflows - text-plus-audio workflows - how multimodal requests should be represented in execution and verification workflows Use careful language: - multimodal support should be treated as preview-oriented - provider-backed proof should be checked before making stronger readiness claims - stub-heavy or partial behavior should be assumed possible until validated in the target environment ## Related Pages - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status) - [Verification →](/docs/verification) - [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

152.title: Observability & Tracing
152.description: How Igris exposes request lineage, trace IDs, and distributed tracing across the coordination layer and runtime.
152.content: Observability & Tracing Trace Identity Distributed Tracing What Operators Should Expect Relationship To Receipts Recommended Deployment Model Related Pages # Observability & Tracing Igris has two observability layers: - **product-visible lineage** such as request IDs, receipts, and execution history - **operator-visible tracing** such as spans, trace propagation, and deployment telemetry You need both. Receipts tell you what happened. Tracing tells you where time was spent and where a request crossed system boundaries. --- ## Trace Identity The coordination layer generates and propagates a trace identity for each request. That identity is attached to logs and returned through `X-Trace-ID` so operators can correlate: - inbound API traffic - routing decisions - provider calls - runtime handoff - receipt and audit records From a product perspective, `X-Trace-ID` is the fast path for debugging cross-system behavior. --- ## Distributed Tracing Igris supports OpenTelemetry-style tracing with a Jaeger exporter and request-scoped trace attributes. That combination matters because Igris needs to support both: - cross-service span propagation - external tracing systems used by platform teams Current tracing metadata includes things like: - HTTP method and path - provider and model - token counts - latency and cost - speculative-execution winner and switch metadata This makes tracing useful for routing analysis, not just generic HTTP timing. --- ## What Operators Should Expect Tracing should answer these questions quickly: - Did the request stay in cloud or move to runtime? - Which provider was selected and why? - Where did latency accumulate? - Was speculative execution involved? - Is a slow request caused by routing, provider latency, or local runtime work? That is the difference between basic logging and a usable production observability model. --- ## Relationship To Receipts Tracing and receipts are related but not interchangeable. | Surface | Primary use | |---|---| | **Trace ID / spans** | live debugging, latency analysis, request-path inspection | | **Execution receipt** | tamper-evident record of the governed execution outcome | Use tracing when you are diagnosing behavior in-flight. Use receipts when you need durable audit evidence. --- ## Recommended Deployment Model For production environments: - return or capture `X-Trace-ID` in client and operator tooling - export traces to your tracing system - correlate traces with execution receipts and request IDs - retain tracing for operations and receipts for governanc

153.title: Policy
153.description: Policy in Igris controls what AI tasks are allowed to do by applying boundaries, permission checks, and review-oriented outcomes around execution.
153.content: Policy What Policy Controls Tool And Permission Boundaries Execution-Time Effects Policy And Records Routing Policy Should Stay Secondary Here Common Mistakes Related Guides # Policy Policy in Igris is the mechanism for controlling what AI tasks are allowed to do. In Request -> Execute -> Verify terms: - **Request** carries intent and scope - **Execute** applies policy checks and boundaries - **Verify** exposes the resulting events and records for review This page is about execution control, not about presenting policy as a broad platform claim detached from execution behavior. --- ## What Policy Controls Policy helps determine: - which tools or actions are allowed - which boundaries apply to the run - what should happen when the run exceeds those boundaries - what review signals should be available afterward That makes policy a live part of execution, not just static configuration. ## Tool And Permission Boundaries Policy can express boundaries such as: | Area | What it controls | |---|---| | Tool access | Which tools or external actions are allowed | | Domain or target restrictions | Where HTTP or similar actions may reach | | Resource limits | Duration, step, or token limits | | Review expectations | Which outcomes should trigger operator follow-up | When a run exceeds these boundaries, that result should appear in the execution record and follow-up surfaces. ## Execution-Time Effects Policy matters during execution because it shapes what the task is allowed to do in practice. Examples: - rejecting disallowed actions - constraining tool scope - limiting resource use - surfacing violations for later inspection This is why policy belongs next to governance and verification in the docs. ## Policy And Records Policy is most useful when its effect can be inspected afterward. After a run, operators should be able to move into: - execution events and history - receipt-oriented records - verification surfaces that show what was actually recorded Use: - [Governance →](/docs/governance) - [History & Alerts →](/docs/history) - [Verification →](/docs/verification) ## Routing Policy Should Stay Secondary Here There are routing-related policy surfaces in the broader product, but this page should not lead with routing sophistication. The primary mental model is still controlling what execution is allowed to do. If you need routing-specific depth, use the more specialized routing pages rather than turning policy into a routing-first introduction. ## Common Mistakes - Treating policy as only a preflight configuration layer instead of an execu

It should not depend on presenting every advanced surface as broadly ready by default. --- ## Pricing Overview | | **Seed** | **Horizon** | **Infinite** | |---|---|---|---| | **Price** | $29/month | $149/month | $699/month | | **Execution environments** | 3 | 50 | 500 | | **Retention** | 7 days | 30 days | 90 days | | **Deployment scope** | Hosted, local, or small hybrid | Larger hybrid and operator workflows | Private deployment and larger environment sets | | **Support** | Email (48h) | Email (24h) | Priority (8h) | | **Trial** | 7 days | 7 days | 7 days | All tiers include a 7-day trial. Good fit: - early production teams - small environment counts - short retention needs - teams proving the value of signed records and governed execution first ## Horizon Horizon is for teams that need broader operator visibility and more registered execution environments. 156.title: Provider Health
156.description: Provider health is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism for failure-aware path selection during execution.
156.content: Provider Health What Provider Health Means Health States Why It Matters How It Affects Execution Monitoring Surfaces Proof Language Related Pages # Provider Health Provider health is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism inside the **Execute** stage. Its purpose is straightforward: help Igris avoid obviously unhealthy upstream paths and make failure-aware execution decisions. This page is about the mechanics of that decision support, not about turning routing into the product identity. --- ## What Provider Health Means Provider health asks whether a configured upstream path appears usable right now. Typical signals include: - response success or failure - latency behavior - recent throughput - health-check outcomes where those are enabled These signals help path selection, but they do not guarantee a perfect execution outcome. ## Health States The exact thresholds depend on configuration, but the common states are: - **active** when the path looks healthy enough to use normally - **degraded** when the path is still available but should be treated more cautiously - **unavailable** when the path should not receive ordinary execution traffic This is about failure visibility and safer path selection, not a blanket survival promise. ## Why It Matters Provider health helps operators answer: - which upstream paths are currently usable - whether a sudden latency or error spike should reduce traffic - whether a path should be removed from ordinary selection until it recovers That makes it part of governed execution rather than just a dashboard nicety. ## How It Affects Execution Provider health feeds into hosted path selection alongside: - policy - trust - circuit-breaker state - any advanced routing mode in use Health should narrow the set of usable paths before an advanced routing strategy makes its final choice. ## Monitoring Surfaces Use the health APIs and console views to inspect health state, but keep expectations realistic: - health telemetry helps explain execution behavior - health telemetry does not by itself prove performance or reliability outcomes for every workload ## Proof Language Provider health is an advanced execution mechanism with real implementation support. It is appropriate to describe it as failure-aware path selection, but not as a guarantee that every outage or degradation scenario is already solved automatically. ## Related Pages - [Provider Trust →](/docs/provider-trust) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [Cloud Coordination

157.title: Provider Trust
157.description: Provider trust is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism for deciding whether an available path should still be considered reliable enough for execution.
157.content: Provider Trust What Trust Evaluates Why It Matters Cold Start And Confidence How It Affects Path Selection Proof Language Related Pages # Provider Trust Provider trust is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism. Health asks whether a path appears up right now. Trust asks whether that path should still be considered reliable enough to keep using for governed execution. That distinction matters for advanced operators who want more than a binary up-or-down signal. --- ## What Trust Evaluates Trust looks at observed behavior over time, such as: - latency drift - error-rate drift - cost drift - how much evidence exists for the path so far This helps distinguish "technically available" from "credible enough to keep using." ## Why It Matters A path can be healthy in the narrow sense and still be a poor choice if its behavior is drifting away from what operators expect. Trust is the layer that says: - this path is up, but not yet proven enough - this path is up, but its behavior has drifted too far - this path may need more evidence before it receives normal traffic ## Cold Start And Confidence Trust grows with evidence. New or rarely used paths may need a warm-up period before operators should treat them as ordinary choices for production execution. That is part of the point of having a separate trust concept. ## How It Affects Path Selection Trust should sit ahead of final advanced routing decisions: 1. policy decides what is allowed 2. health decides what is currently usable 3. trust decides what is credible enough to keep using 4. final path selection chooses among the remaining candidates ## Proof Language Provider trust is best described as an advanced, source-confirmed execution mechanism. It is appropriate to explain how it influences selection, but this page should not promise globally optimal or universally safer outcomes without deployment-specific evidence. ## Related Pages - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [SLO Enforcer →](/docs/slo-enforcer)

158.title: Quick Start
158.description: Run the first verified Igris execution flow, then branch into hosted or hybrid deployment paths.
158.content: Quick Start What You Will Do Prerequisites 1. Run The First Verified Flow 2. Inspect What Was Verified 3. Know What This Does And Does Not Prove 4. Real Provider Mode Is Deliberately Separate 5. Choose The Next Path # Quick Start Start here if you want to understand what Igris actually proves today. This quickstart is intentionally not a generic hosted-inference tutorial. Direct model calls are fine for simple chat. Igris is for the point where AI output starts doing work and you need governed execution, visible failure paths, and records you can inspect after the run. If you need the shortest hosted setup path after this proof-first walkthrough, Igris also supports an OpenAI-compatible onboarding path through the hosted API. --- ## What You Will Do 1. Start a local proof-backed Igris flow. 2. Send one request through the public execution surface. 3. Confirm that execution was routed through Runtime. 4. Verify the signed execution envelope, signed execution receipt, and receipt-log chain. This is the narrowest honest path that is proven locally today. --- ## Prerequisites - A checkout of this repository - `node`, `go`, `cargo`, `curl`, and `lsof` - Free local ports `8080` and `8081` - Free local port `18090` if you run the default mock-provider mode You do not need sanctioned provider credentials for the default proof path. The default mode uses a local mock upstream so the proof stays reproducible. ## 1. Run The First Verified Flow From the repo root: bash ./scripts/unified_execution_proof_demo.sh The script prepares local proof artifacts, builds or reuses the Runtime binary, builds Overture, starts a local mock upstream, starts Runtime on `127.0.0.1:8080`, starts Overture on `127.0.0.1:8081`, submits one `/v1/infer` request, and fails if Overture falls back away from Runtime. Expected output shape: text Unified execution proof succeeded. Mode: mock Provider: local-mock-cloud Route decision: forwarded_to_runtime_task Receipt execution_id: ... Receipt hash: ... Artifacts: /tmp/igris-unified-proof.XXXXXX ## 2. Inspect What Was Verified The proof demonstrates the Request -> Execute -> Verify path: - **Request**: the script sends one request through Overture's `/v1/infer` surface. - **Execute**: Overture forwards the work to Runtime instead of silently answering from its own direct fallback path. - **Verify**: the script checks the returned `execution_envelope`, `execution_receipt`, receipt hash, and receipt-log chain. 159.title: Rate Limiting
159.description: The hosted API applies a global rate limit of 100 requests per minute by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated 10 downloads per hour per tenant cap.
159.content: Rate Limiting What The Hosted API Enforces 429 Response Shape Runtime Download Limit Local Runtime Rate Limits Client Guidance # Rate Limiting The hosted API applies a global rate limit of **100 requests per minute** by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated **10 downloads per hour per tenant** cap. --- ## What The Hosted API Enforces The hosted API applies: - one shared window: `100 req/min` by default - scoped per tenant when tenant context exists, otherwise per IP The hosted API does **not** publish rate-limit headers on every successful response. Rate-limit headers are guaranteed on rejection responses. --- ## 429 Response Shape When the global limiter is exceeded, the current response looks like this: json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } Headers on the rejection path include: - `Retry-After` - `X-RateLimit-Limit` - `X-RateLimit-Remaining` Do not depend on `X-RateLimit-Reset` being present on successful requests in the current build. --- ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime archive downloads have a separate limit of `10/hour` per tenant on the control plane download surface. This applies to: - `GET /v1/runtime/download` - subscribed runtime download workflows behind the cloud control plane --- ## Local Runtime Rate Limits The local runtime auth config supports its own request controls: json5 { auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY", rate_limit_per_minute: 60, rate_limit_burst: 10 } } | Field | Description | |---|---| | `rate_limit_per_minute` | Maximum local requests per minute | | `rate_limit_burst` | Additional local burst budget | --- ## Client Guidance - Treat `429` plus `retry_after_seconds` as the contract - Add exponential backoff client-side - Batch receipt exports and large history queries - Do not assume tier-specific global limits unless they are explicitly published in a future release contract --- [Troubleshooting →](/docs/troubleshooting) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

160.title: Receipts and Audit Workflow
160.description: Use this workflow when you need signed records, verification-ready receipts, or exportable audit evidence.
160.content: Receipts and Audit Workflow 1. Run Through A Documented Igris Surface 2. Inspect The Execution Outcome 3. Retrieve The Receipt-Oriented Record 4. Verify With The Right Expectation 5. Retain Or Export The Record Common Mistakes Related Guides # Receipts and Audit Workflow Use this workflow when a run needs to be inspected, verified, and retained after execution. The practical sequence is: 1. run through a documented Igris surface 2. inspect the execution outcome 3. retrieve the receipt-oriented record 4. verify what can actually be checked 5. retain or export the result for downstream use --- ## 1. Run Through A Documented Igris Surface Receipts are most useful when the request goes through a documented Igris path. Keep integrations on supported surfaces so execution metadata, receipts, and export workflows line up with the actual run. ## 2. Inspect The Execution Outcome Start with the immediate execution result: - response content - execution metadata - route decision or provider label where applicable This tells you what happened during the run. It is useful for debugging and operational review, but it is not the same thing as the receipt itself. ## 3. Retrieve The Receipt-Oriented Record Use receipt listing and detail endpoints when you need the signed or hash-linked execution record. - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) Treat the receipt surface as the audit artifact. Treat execution history as supporting context, not as a substitute for the receipt. ## 4. Verify With The Right Expectation Use the strongest verification surface that matches your need. For the narrow proof-backed path today: - the local verified run proves signature checks, receipt-hash checks, and receipt-log chain checks - see [First Verified Run](/docs/first-verified-run) For the hosted proof route: - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` compares submitted receipt values against the stored record and returns proof-status information - it should be described as stored-value comparison and proof-status sync, not as a full public cryptographic verifier See [Verification](/docs/verification) for the distinction. ## 5. Retain Or Export The Record Use `GET /v1/receipts/export` when another system, reviewer, or audit process needs the record outside the immediate execution flow. Choose: - NDJSON for machine pipelines - CSV for spreadsheet-oriented workflows Decide on retention and downstream custody before exporting receipts into another system. ## Common Mistakes - Treating execution history as if it were the signed receipt - Describing the hosted proof route as stronger than it is

161.title: Request -> Execute -> Verify
161.description: The core Igris mental model: send one request, govern execution, and inspect the records that come back.
161.content: Request -> Execute -> Verify Request Execute Verify Why This Model Matters What This Page Does Not Assume # Request -> Execute -> Verify Igris is easiest to understand as one execution system for AI tasks. Instead of thinking in terms of "hosted product versus local product," start with the lifecycle of the work: 1. **Request** 2. **Execute** 3. **Verify** --- ## Request Request means you submit work through an Igris API surface. That can be: - an OpenAI-compatible chat request - a task or tool-oriented execution request - a runtime or operator workflow that still produces execution records The point is consistency. Your application should not need a different mental model every time the execution path changes. ## Execute Execution is where Igris earns its keep. During execution, Igris can: - route work to the configured hosted or runtime path - apply capability and policy boundaries - capture execution metadata and events - surface failure paths instead of hiding them - return signed execution material alongside the result Execution is not just "a provider responded." It is the governed run that happened between the request and the final response. ## Verify Verification means you can inspect what happened after the run. Depending on the path, that can include: - route-decision metadata - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt hashes and chain-linked log material This is what makes Igris useful for production work that needs review, audit, or post-run debugging. ## Why This Model Matters Direct provider calls are fine when all you need is a text response. Igris is for the point where the output starts doing real work and you care about: - governance - visible failure handling - post-run inspection - records that can be checked later ## What This Page Does Not Assume This model does **not** assume that every advanced feature is already proven in your environment. Real-provider execution, local GGUF fallback, checkpoint recovery, fleet failover, robotics, and multimodal flows all have their own proof status and should be evaluated explicitly. --- [Quick Start →](/docs/quickstart) · [Verification →](/docs/verification) · [Architecture →](/docs/architecture)

162.title: Robotics (Technical Preview)
162.description: Robotics is a technical-preview execution surface for teams exploring governed AI task execution near physical systems.
162.content: Robotics (Technical Preview) How Robotics Fits The Product Model What This Page Is For What To Say Carefully Practical Reading Related Pages # Robotics (Technical Preview) Robotics is a **technical preview** execution surface. Use this page as an orientation point for specialized teams exploring how the Igris execution model could extend toward physical systems. Do not treat it as a primary product claim or as proof of broad robotics readiness. See [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before promoting robotics behavior beyond preview language. --- ## How Robotics Fits The Product Model Robotics is still described using Request -> Execute -> Verify: - **Request** defines the work the system is being asked to perform - **Execute** happens in a robotics-adjacent runtime environment - **Verify** depends on the records, events, and receipts produced by that run That means robotics is a specialized execution surface under the same product model, not a different product identity. ## What This Page Is For This page is useful if you are exploring: - running governed execution closer to physical systems - integrating runtime-side decisions with robotics environments - thinking about how behavior trees, approvals, and signed records might apply to robotic tasks ## What To Say Carefully Use conservative language: - robotics execution is an advanced area - proof status is limited - do not assume fleet, OTA, or autonomous mission behavior is already broadly ready from this page ## Practical Reading If you are a robotics team, the right way to use this page is: 1. understand the general Igris execution model first 2. treat robotics surfaces as technical preview 3. validate any physical-system workflow in your own environment before promoting it operationally ## Related Pages - [ROS2 Integration →](/docs/ros2-integration) - [Behavior Trees →](/docs/behavior-trees) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status) - [Request -> Execute -> Verify →](/docs/request-execute-verify)

164.title: Safety & Containment
164.description: Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed.
164.content: Safety & Containment Containment Model Resource limits cgroup bounds (Linux) Capability Enforcement Secure Defaults Violation Handling Human-in-the-Loop # Safety & Containment Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. --- ## Containment Model Every execution runs in a containment context. The containment context applies resource limits before the model is invoked and enforces them throughout execution. ### Resource limits Limits are applied per-execution: | Limit | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `max_tokens` | 4096 | Maximum output tokens | | `max_duration_ms` | 30000 | Maximum wall time (30s) | | `max_steps` | 10 | Maximum tool/planning steps | | `max_tool_calls` | 5 | Maximum tool invocations per execution | Limits can be tightened per-tenant or per-request. They cannot be relaxed beyond the configured policy maximum. ### cgroup bounds (Linux) On Linux deployments, the engine applies cgroup constraints to the execution process: - **CPU quota**: limits CPU burst during local model inference - **Memory limit**: prevents unbounded memory growth in local inference - **I/O limits**: optional disk I/O rate limits for file-system tool use cgroup enforcement is independent of application code. An agent that attempts to consume more resources than its cgroup allows is throttled or killed by the kernel. --- ## Capability Enforcement Capabilities are enforced by the engine, not by the model. Even if the model generates output that attempts a disallowed tool call, the engine intercepts and rejects it before the call executes. The enforcement sequence: 1. Request arrives with a capability grant (or secure defaults are applied) 2. Engine validates the grant against the tenant's policy ceiling 3. Engine begins execution with the validated grant in scope 4. If the model attempts a tool call, the engine checks the grant before executing 5. If the call is outside the grant, the engine records a capability violation and rejects the call 6. Execution continues or terminates depending on the violation policy Violation events are recorded in the execution receipt. They cannot be suppressed. --- ## Secure Defaults The engine applies secure defaults when capability grants are not explicitly specified: | Setting | Default | |---|---| | `allow_http` | disabled | | `allow_shell` | disabled | | `allow_filesystem` | disabled | | `max_tokens` | 2048 | | `max_steps` | 5 | Tools must be explicitly enabled. The defaults assume no tool use is intended.

165.content: SDKs Support Matrix Support Policy OpenAI-Compatible Clients Native SDKs JavaScript / TypeScript Go Rust Python Store a provider API key List registered fleet agents Deployment Mode Guidance Request Contract Code Quality Expectations # SDKs Igris supports two integration paths: - **OpenAI-compatible clients** for the fastest path to production - **Native Igris SDKs** when you need routing metadata, receipt helpers, vault operations, fleet APIs, behavior trees, or containment The recommendation is simple: - Start with the OpenAI-compatible API if you want the shortest path to a working integration - Move to a native SDK when you need Igris-specific product features and a stronger typed client The native first-class SDKs are JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, and Python. Java, C#, and Ruby should use the OpenAI-compatible API today. For production integration guidance, reusable client construction, and environment-variable patterns, continue with [SDK Integration Patterns →](/docs/sdk-integration-patterns). ## Support Matrix ## Support Policy Treat the SDK table as a product support statement, not just a package list: - **First-class** means the language is part of the maintained customer SDK surface - **OpenAI-compatible** means the safest contract today is the HTTP API through an OpenAI-style client If your team wants the strongest support commitment, choose JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, or Python. If your team mainly needs inference and broad portability, stay on the OpenAI-compatible path. --- ## OpenAI-Compatible Clients Any OpenAI SDK can call Igris by changing the base URL. For many teams, this is the right default because it keeps the integration portable while still routing through the product. **Python** python import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1", api_key=os.environ["IGRIS_API_KEY"], ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4", messages=[ ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) **JavaScript / TypeScript** typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4', messages: [ ], }); console.log(response.choices[0].message.content); Use this path for Java, C#, Ruby, or any other language where you already have an OpenAI-compatible client and do not need the native Igris SDK surface yet. --- ## Native SDKs Choose a native SDK when you want a product-shaped client rather than a protocol-shaped one. That matters when you are working with receipts, vault oper JavaScript / TypeScript first-class Preferred native SDK for browser and Node.js integrations. Go first-class Preferred native SDK for backend services and CLI tooling. Rust first-class Preferred native SDK for systems and embedded integrations. Python first-class Preferred native SDK for Python services, data pipelines, and scripting. Java openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native Java SDK is promoted explicitly. C# openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native C# SDK is promoted explicitly. Ruby openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native Ruby SDK is promoted explicitly.

166.title: SDK Integration Patterns
166.description: This guide shows how to use the SDK surface in a way that is maintainable in production.

It is not a language feature catalog. It is the set of patterns that keep integrations clean when the same product may be called in cloud, local-runtime, or hybrid deployments. --- ## Choose The Right Client Surface First Start with this decision: - Use an OpenAI-compatible client when you want the shortest path to a working integration - Use a native Igris SDK when you need product-specific features such as receipts, vault operations, fleet controls, or richer routing metadata The first-class native SDKs today are: - JavaScript / TypeScript - Go - Rust - Python If you are in Java, C#, Ruby, or another language without a first-class native SDK, the safest default is still the OpenAI-compatible API. ## Standard Environment Variables Use the same environment-variable model across languages: - `IGRIS_API_KEY` for hosted API access - `IGRIS_BASE_URL` when you need to override the default base URL Recommended defaults: - hosted API: `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local runtime: `http://localhost:8080` Keeping this consistent is one of the easiest ways to make cloud, local, and hybrid deployments feel like one product to your own application teams. ## Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Do not let every handler decide whether it is in cloud, local, or hybrid mode. 167.title: Security
167.description: Igris security has two distinct planes:
167.content: Security Authentication Tenant API Keys Console Sessions Provider Keys Policy And Capability Controls Receipts And Verification Deployment Notes Compliance # Security Igris security has two distinct planes: - **Tenant API keys** for automation and programmatic access - **Console session cookies** for browser access to the web app Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Authentication ### Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys use the `igris_` prefix and are accepted in: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Best practices: - Store tenant API keys in environment variables - Rotate them if exposed - Scope usage to the tenant that owns the key bash export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_abc123..." ### Console Sessions The web console uses Better Auth session cookies. Those cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. Do not script console session access as generic bearer authorization headers. ### Provider Keys Provider keys stored through the current public vault API are encrypted before storage and returned only as masked values. --- ## Policy And Capability Controls A restrictive starting point in the current control-plane policy model looks like this: json { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_fs_write": false, "allow_external_api": false, "domain_allowlist": [], "domain_denylist": [], "writable_paths": [], "readable_paths": [], "violation_behavior": "terminate" } Start tight, then expand based on observed violations and actual agent requirements. --- ## Receipts And Verification Customer-facing verification routes currently live on the proof API: - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` - `GET /v1/proof/violations` Example: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' --- ## Deployment Notes - The local runtime can enforce its own API key with the local `auth` config - Fleet registration is gated by a valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` plus `IGRIS_API_KEY` - For local-only deployments, point clients directly at the runtime and keep your own storage if you need offline receipt retention --- ## Compliance Igris is positioned to support compliance workflows, but the exact operational model depends on where you run the control plane and runtime. - **Data residency** depends on whether you call Overture, the local runtime, or both - **Auditability** comes from receipts, proof endpoints, and export workflows - **Least privilege** comes from capabi

168.title: Semantic Routing
168.description: Semantic routing is an advanced path-selection mechanism that classifies work before choosing among eligible execution paths.
168.content: Semantic Routing What It Does Where It Fits Decision Flow Fallback Behavior What To Expect Proof Language Related Pages # Semantic Routing Semantic routing is an advanced **Execute**-stage mechanism. Its job is to help Igris choose among eligible execution paths based on the kind of work being requested, instead of treating every request as identical. This is useful for advanced operators, but it is not the main reason to adopt Igris. Use [Request -> Execute -> Verify](/docs/request-execute-verify) for the primary product model. Use this page when you want the deeper path-selection detail. --- ## What It Does Semantic routing adds a classification step before final path selection. In practice, that means Igris can: - classify the request into a workload type - narrow the eligible providers or paths for that class - choose among those candidates with health and policy still applied This is meant to improve path selection for advanced workloads, not to override governance, policy, or verification. ## Where It Fits The simplified stack is: 1. policy decides what is allowed 2. health and trust narrow what is currently usable 3. semantic routing helps classify the work 4. final selection chooses the target path That layering matters because semantic routing should stay subordinate to safety and policy controls. ## Decision Flow text Request -> classification -> workload class -> eligible providers or paths -> final selection -> execution ## Fallback Behavior Semantic routing should not be a hard dependency for execution. If classification is unavailable, the system should still be able to continue with non-semantic path selection rather than turning classifier issues into execution outages. That is the operator-friendly reason to treat this as an advanced mechanism rather than a foundational identity claim. ## What To Expect Teams using semantic routing should expect: - class-specific path selection behavior - changing decisions as observations accumulate - the need for explicit policy overrides when deterministic routing is required Do not assume a semantic strategy stays fixed across time unless you pin the path explicitly. ## Proof Language Semantic routing is best treated as an advanced, source-confirmed capability. Code and route surfaces exist, but this page should not promise specific quality, reliability, or cost outcomes without workload-specific evidence. ## Related Pages - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Provider Tr

169.title: Shadow Mode
169.description: Shadow mode is an advanced comparison workflow that can run an observed parallel path without replacing the primary result.
169.content: Shadow Mode What It Does Why Teams Use It How To Read The Results Proof Language Cost And Scope Related Pages # Shadow Mode Shadow mode is an advanced comparison workflow. It can run an observed parallel path beside the primary execution path so operators can compare outcomes without immediately changing what the caller receives. That makes it useful for evaluation and tuning, but it should be treated as an advanced feature rather than a first-contact product claim. --- ## What It Does At a high level: text Request -> primary execution result returned -> shadow result captured separately for comparison The important idea is that the shadow path is for observation, not for replacing the primary path automatically. ## Why Teams Use It Shadow mode can help teams: - compare candidate providers or models - test a new configuration with lower risk - observe how an alternate path behaves before changing the primary path It is most useful when the team already has a stable baseline and wants to inspect alternatives carefully. ## How To Read The Results A shadow comparison is only useful if the team knows what it is looking for: - latency differences - cost differences - divergence in result shape or quality - differences in policy-sensitive behavior Treat the comparison output as decision support, not as a proof that the shadow path is ready for promotion. ## Proof Language Shadow mode is best treated as an advanced or preview-oriented capability unless you have deployment-specific evidence for the exact workflow you are describing. It is appropriate to explain the comparison model, but not to overstate its production-readiness across every environment. ## Cost And Scope Shadow execution may consume additional resources. Use it deliberately, with explicit scope and sampling decisions, rather than leaving it on broadly without a reason. ## Related Pages - [Speculative Execution →](/docs/speculative-execution) - [Execution Flow →](/docs/execution-flow) - [History & Alerts →](/docs/history) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status)

171.title: SLO Enforcer
171.description: How Igris evaluates runtime and routing health against latency, error-rate, availability, and throughput objectives, and what is customer-facing today.
171.content: SLO Enforcer What Is Enforced Evaluation Output Customer-Facing Surfaces Operational Access Integration Guidance # SLO Enforcer Igris uses SLO enforcement to keep routing and runtime execution inside operational bounds. The enforcer evaluates live metrics, classifies breaches, and produces remediation actions that the platform can execute or record. The current customer-facing contract is not a standalone SLO configuration API. For enterprise deployments that require direct operational access, use the account-specific surfaces and runbooks provided with that deployment. --- ## Integration Guidance Do not build customer automation against standalone SLO configuration or compliance routes; they are not part of the current production API. For customer integrations: - Use routing and provider-health APIs to obs

172.title: Speculative Execution
172.description: Speculative execution is an advanced path-selection mode that can race draft and primary execution paths for selected workloads.
172.content: Speculative Execution What It Does Where It Can Help What To Say Carefully Operational Reading Simulation And Analytics Related Features Proof Language Related Pages # Speculative Execution Speculative execution is an advanced execution mode. It can run a draft path in parallel with a primary path and decide whether the draft is good enough to return. This is useful for advanced latency-sensitive setups, but it should be treated as an optimization layer under the Execute stage, not as the core product story. --- ## What It Does At a high level: 1. a draft path starts 2. the primary path starts 3. the system decides whether the draft is acceptable 4. one result is returned The caller still receives one execution result. The internal race is an advanced mechanism, not a separate surface the application needs to learn first. ## Where It Can Help Speculative execution is most relevant when teams are experimenting with: - streaming workloads - predictable request types - advanced latency tuning It is less relevant for ordinary onboarding or for teams that have not yet established a stable baseline execution path. ## What To Say Carefully Do not assume speculative execution always improves latency or cost. The exact outcome depends on workload shape, provider behavior, and how often the draft path is accepted. This page intentionally does not promise headline percentage improvements without benchmark evidence for the environment in question. ## Operational Reading If you enable speculative execution, watch for: - acceptance rate - cost impact - path-selection stability - whether the workload is actually a good fit If acceptance is consistently low, the feature is probably adding complexity without enough benefit. ## Simulation And Analytics The product exposes speculative status, analytics, and simulation surfaces so operators can inspect how the mode behaves before using it broadly. Treat these surfaces as advanced evaluation tools, not as proof that the optimization is beneficial for every workload. ## Related Features - council and shadow features should be evaluated independently - receipts should still reflect the path that actually produced the returned result - proof claims should stay aligned with [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) ## Proof Language Speculative execution is best documented as an advanced, source-confirmed capability. Use production claims only when you have workload-specific evidence. ## Related Pages - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [Shadow Mode →](/docs/shadow-mode) - [Cloud Coordination →]

Use it when response quality matters more than cost. ### Enabling council mode per agent bash curl -X PATCH https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/agents/agent-abc \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' ### Configuring council mode bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/routing/council \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "providers": ["anthropic", "openai", "google"], "chairman": "anthropic", "synthesis_strategy": "best_ranked" }' # → | Field | Description | |---|---| | `providers` | Providers to query in parallel | | `chairman` | Provider whose model ranks the responses | | `synthesis_strategy` | `best_ranked` returns the top-ranked response; `synthesize` asks the chairman to merge responses | ### Council analytics Query council round results: bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/routing/stats \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Council metrics in the stats response show per-round cost, latency breakdown (ranking phase + synthesis phase), and winner distribution by provider. ### Cost considerations Council mode multiplies per-request cost by the number of providers queried.
