174.title: Tamper-Evident Logs
174.description: Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can
174.content: Tamper-Evident Logs How It Works Chain Verification What's Recorded Export GET /v1/receipts/export Console Retention Audit Workflow # Tamper-Evident Logs Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can be altered, deleted, or inserted without detection. --- ## How It Works Each execution receipt contains: 1. **Envelope hash** — SHA-256 hash of the canonical execution envelope 2. **Previous hash** — SHA-256 hash of the previous receipt (forming a chain) 3. **Signature** — Ed25519 signature of the envelope using a device-bound key Each receipt links to the previous receipt via hash, forming a chain. Each receipt is signed with a device-bound key that exists only on the originating runtime. Tampering with any receipt invalidates its signature and breaks the chain — both of which are detected by the verification API. --- ## Chain Verification Receipts can be verified at any time to confirm chain integrity: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' Response: json { "valid": true, "signature_valid": true, "chain_intact": true, "previous_hash_matches": true } If any link in the chain is broken, verification fails and the specific broken link is identified. --- ## What's Recorded Every receipt records: | Category | Fields | |---|---| | **Identity** | Request ID, tenant ID, agent ID, device ID, timestamp | | **Inputs** | Prompt, system message, parameters | | **Outputs** | Model response, tool call results | | **Resources** | Tokens consumed, wall time, CPU/memory usage | | **Capabilities** | Grants applied, violations recorded | | **Policy** | Policy hash at time of execution | | **Routing** | Provider selected, fallback count, latency | | **Chain** | Envelope hash, previous hash, signature | --- ## Export Receipts can be exported for external audit workflows: ### GET /v1/receipts/export Export receipts in the selected format and time range. bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=json&range=7d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ --output receipts_export.json Supported formats: - `json` — raw JSON array of receipts - `csv` — flattened CSV for spreadsheet analysis - `ndjson` — newline-delimited JSON for streaming processing --- ## Console View and verify receipts at `/proof/receipts`: - Receipt listing wit

175.description: Igris agents can call external tools: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. All tool use is governed by the execution envelope's capability grants and recorded in t
175.content: Tools Tool Overview HTTP Tool Shell Tool Filesystem Tool Tool Audit Trail # Tools Igris agents can call external tools: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. All tool use is governed by the execution envelope's capability grants and recorded in the execution receipt. --- ## Tool Overview | Tool | Capability required | Use | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | Call external APIs, webhooks, web services | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands in a sandboxed context | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, and list files | Tools are disabled by default. Each must be explicitly granted in the request's capability grant or in the tenant's policy. --- ## HTTP Tool The HTTP tool allows agents to make GET and POST requests to external endpoints. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true }, "tool_config": { "http": { "allowed_domains": ["api.example.com", "*.private.example.com"], "timeout_ms": 5000, "max_response_bytes": 65536 } } } **Security controls:** - **Domain allowlist**: agents can only reach configured domains. Wildcards are supported for subdomains. - **Timeout**: requests that exceed `timeout_ms` are aborted and the failure is recorded. - **Response size limit**: responses larger than `max_response_bytes` are truncated. If `allowed_domains` is empty, all domains are permitted. Leaving it empty is not recommended for production deployments. --- ## Shell Tool The shell tool allows agents to execute shell commands. Shell access is the most sensitive capability and should be granted only when necessary. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_shell": true }, "tool_config": { "shell": { "allowed_commands": ["ls", "cat", "grep", "python3"], "working_directory": "/workspace", "timeout_ms": 10000, "env_allowlist": ["PATH", "HOME"] } } } **Security controls:** - **Command allowlist**: only listed commands can be executed. Commands not on the list are rejected before execution. - **Working directory**: the shell is confined to the specified directory. Attempts to navigate outside it are blocked. - **Timeout**: commands that run longer than `timeout_ms` are killed. - **Environment**: only environment variables on the allowlist are passed to the child process. All shell executions — successful or rejected — are recorded in the execution receipt. --- ## Filesystem Tool The filesystem tool allows agents to read, write, and list files. **Configuration:** json { "capabiliti

177.description: This guide covers the most common issues encountered when running Igris. For each issue you will find the symptoms, the most likely cause, and the steps to fix it.
177.content: Troubleshooting Runtime Not Starting Port already in use Missing API key Config file not found Runtime Not Appearing in Fleet → Devices Network or firewall blocking outbound registration API key wrong or expired Registration call failing silently Provider Key Validation Failing Key copied incorrectly Key revoked or quota exhausted Network issue during validation Re-validating an existing key via API → {"valid": true, "provider": "openai"} Execution Runs Stuck in PAUSED Human review required High Violation Rate What violations mean Common patterns → list of your policies, find the one to update Requests Going to Wrong Provider How provider selection works Checking current routing behavior Overall routing statistics per provider Provider ranking as the router currently sees it Overriding routing behavior Local Model Not Loading or Slow Memory requirements Using quantized models Checking runtime health and load Basic health check Detailed metrics including model load status and memory usage Execution Runs Timing Out max_duration_ms limit hit List your policies API Rate Limit (HTTP 429) Receipt Verification Failing → {"valid": false, "reason": "signature_mismatch"} Getting More Help # Troubleshooting This guide covers the most common issues encountered when running Igris. For each issue you will find the symptoms, the most likely cause, and the steps to fix it. --- ## Runtime Not Starting ### Port already in use **Symptoms:** The runtime process exits immediately with an address binding error. Nothing appears in **Fleet → Devices**. **Cause:** Another process is already listening on the port the runtime is configured to use (default: 8080). **Fix:** Identify the conflicting process and stop it, or configure the runtime to use a different port. On Linux and macOS you can check what is using a port with: bash lsof -i :8080 After freeing the port or reconfiguring, restart the runtime. --- ### Missing API key **Symptoms:** The runtime starts but exits with an authentication error. No registration appears in the console. **Cause:** The runtime was started without a valid Igris API key in its configuration. **Fix:** Add your API key to the runtime's config file or pass it as the appropriate environment variable for your deployment method. Your API key is available in **Settings → Keys** in the console. If you do not see an API key, generate one from **Settings → Billing → Manage Account**. --- ### Config file not found **Symptoms:** The runtime exits with a message indicating it cannot find or parse the configuration file. **Cause:** The runtime is looking for its configuration file at the default path and it either does not exist or has a syntax error. **Fix:** Verify that the config file is present at the expected path. Check the file for YAML/TOML syntax errors — most runtimes print the line number of the first error. If you are using a custom path, confirm you are passing the correct path argument when starting the runtime. --- ## Runtime Not Appearing in Fleet → Devices ### Network or firewall blocking outbound registration **Symptoms:** The runtime starts and appears to be running (the local health endpoint responds) but never appears in **Fleet → Devices** in the console. **Cause:** Outbound HTTPS traffic to `overture.igrisinertial.com` is being blocked by a firewall rule, proxy, or network policy. **Fix:** Verify connectivity from the runtime host: bash curl -v https://overture.igrisinertial.com/health If this fails, work with your network administrator to allow outbound HTTPS (port 443) to `overture.igrisinertial.com`. 178.title: Upgrade & Migration
178.description: This guide covers how to upgrade between Igris versions, migrate data, and handle breaking changes.
178.content: Upgrade & Migration Versioning Upgrading the Runtime Automatic OTA Updates (Horizon+) Manual Upgrade Compare with the checksum shown in the console Or if running directly: pkill igris-runtime && igris-runtime serve Configuration Migration Config File Format Changes Backing Up Configuration Migrating Config Fields Data Migration Execution Receipts Fleet Configuration Provider Keys Behavior Tree Definitions Breaking Changes by Version Runtime v1.8.0 (March 2026) Runtime v1.7.x (March 2026) Runtime v1.6.0 (February 2026) Runtime v0.4.0 (November 2025) Rollback Checking for Updates Via Console Via API Via CLI Support # Upgrade & Migration This guide covers how to upgrade between Igris versions, migrate data, and handle breaking changes. --- ## Versioning Igris uses semantic versioning for the runtime binary: - **Major version** (v1 → v2): Breaking changes. Requires migration steps. - **Minor version** (v1.6 → v1.7): New features, backward compatible. - **Patch version** (v1.6.0 → v1.6.1): Bug fixes, backward compatible. The cloud API is versioned independently and maintains backward compatibility within a major version. --- ## Upgrading the Runtime ### Automatic OTA Updates (Horizon+) If you are on the Horizon or Infinite tier, you can push updates to your fleet from the console: 1. Navigate to **Fleet → Devices** 2. Select the instances to update 3. Click **Push Update** 4. Choose the target version and update strategy **Update strategies:** | Strategy | Behavior | |---|---| | `rolling` | Update instances one at a time (default) | | `canary` | Update one instance first, verify health, then proceed | | `all-at-once` | Update all instances simultaneously | ### Manual Upgrade For Seed tier or manual deployments: 1. Download the new binary: bash curl -fsSL https://igrisinertial.com/install | bash Or download from **Fleet → Downloads** in the console. 2. Verify the checksum: bash sha256sum /usr/local/bin/igris-runtime # Compare with the checksum shown in the console 3. Restart the runtime: bash sudo systemctl restart igris-runtime # Or if running directly: # pkill igris-runtime && igris-runtime serve 4. Verify the upgrade: bash igris-runtime --version curl http://localhost:8080/health --- ## Configuration Migration ### Config File Format Changes When upgrading between major versions, the configuration file format may change. The runtime will log warnings for deprecated fields and use defaults for new required fields. **Before upgrading, review the changelog for configuration changes.** ### Backing Up Configuration Always back up your configuration before upgrading: bash cp ~/.config/igris/config.json5 ~/.config/igris/config.json5.bak ### Migrating Config Fields If the upgrade includes config format changes, the runtime will: 1. Log a warning for each deprecated field 2. Use the default value for new required fields 3. Continue operating with the migrated configuration After upgrading, review the config file and update any deprecated fields to their new equivalents. --- ## Da

179.title: Verification
179.description: How to inspect execution metadata, signed records, receipt hashes, and current proof-route behavior in Igris.
179.content: Verification Verification Inputs Proven Local Verification Path Cloud Proof Route Semantics What To Check After A Run Choosing The Right Verification Surface Verification Language To Use Carefully # Verification Verification is the part of Igris that answers: what happened, what record came back, and what can actually be checked? The short version is: - some verification behavior is proven locally today - some proof-oriented routes are useful record-comparison surfaces - not every verification surface is equally strong --- ## Verification Inputs Depending on the route, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata such as route decisions and provider labels - a signed `execution_envelope` - a signed `execution_receipt` - receipt hashes - receipt-log entries and previous-hash linkage These are not interchangeable. Execution history is not the same thing as a signed receipt, and a proof-status lookup is not the same thing as cryptographic verification. ## Proven Local Verification Path The strongest demonstrated verification path today is the local unified proof: bash ./scripts/unified_execution_proof_demo.sh That flow verifies: - the returned execution envelope signature - the returned execution receipt signature - the returned execution receipt hash - receipt presence in the local receipt log - receipt-chain linkage This is the current **proven locally** path. ## Cloud Proof Route Semantics The hosted proof route is: text POST /proof/receipts/verify Its current handler compares submitted values against the stored receipt record and returns the current verification state. It is useful when you want to check whether a stored receipt matches a supplied hash or signature value. Important caveat: - The current handler does **not** perform full cryptographic signature verification by itself. - It compares stored versus submitted values and returns fields such as `verified`, `verification_status`, `hash_valid`, and `signature_matches`. That means you should not describe this route as a full public cryptographic verifier in first-contact docs. ## What To Check After A Run When a run matters, inspect at least these layers: 1. **Execution metadata** for route decision and provider context 2. **Signed records** for the returned envelope or receipt material 3. **Proof status** for what the current route can confirm 4. **Receipt export or storage path** if another system will depend on the record later ## Choosing The Right Verification Surface | Need | Best current path | |---|---| | Prove the repo's local execution flow end to end | [First Verified Run](/doc

Agent Lifecycle States State Transitions Querying Agent State Get the state for one local runtime agent Lifecycle Records Canceling In-Flight Work Safe Idle (Human-in-the-Loop) Recovery # Agent Lifecycle Every agent running on the execution engine has a tracked lifecycle. State transitions are deterministic, signed, and queryable — giving you a full audit trail of every agent's history from initialization to termination. --- ## States | State | Meaning | |---|---| | `INIT` | Agent registered, not yet started | | `RUNNING` | Actively processing a request | | `IDLE` | Waiting for the next request | | `DEGRADED` | Repeated failures; execution continues with reduced confidence | | `SAFE_IDLE` | Paused pending human review or approval | | `RECOVERING` | Restarting after a violation or crash | | `TERMINATED` | Permanently stopped; no further requests accepted | --- ## State Transitions INIT → RUNNING RUNNING → IDLE (request completed normally) RUNNING → DEGRADED (error threshold exceeded) RUNNING → SAFE_IDLE (human approval required) IDLE → RUNNING (new request received) DEGRADED → RECOVERING (recovery triggered) RECOVERING → IDLE (recovery succeeded) RECOVERING → TERMINATED (recovery failed) SAFE_IDLE → RUNNING (approval granted) SAFE_IDLE → TERMINATED (approval denied) * → TERMINATED (explicit shutdown or fatal error) --- ## Querying Agent State bash # Get the state for one local runtime agent curl http://localhost:8080/v1/runtime/agent/agent-abc/state \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "state": "IDLE", "created_at": "2026-03-01T10:00:00Z", "last_transition": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "total_requests": 47, "violations": 0 } The current local runtime API exposes state for a single known agent ID. Fleet-wide runtime lists are available through the swarm and fleet coordination APIs rather than the agent lifecycle endpoint. --- ## Lifecycle Records Each state transition is recorded as a signed lifecycle event: json { "agent_id": "agent-abc", "from_state": "RUNNING", "to_state": "IDLE", "trigger": "request_completed", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z", "signature": "sha256:d4e1..." } Lifecycle records are hash-chained and included in the audit log alongside execution receipts. --- ## Canceling In-Flight Work bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/runtime/task/task-abc/cancel \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Cancellation is task-scoped in the current runtime API. A canceled task is recorded in the runtime task history and its receipt/WAL evidence remains available for reconciliation. --- #

Agents Reflection Agents Planning Agents Tool-Use Agents Multi-Agent Swarms MCP Swarm Mode Agent Lifecycle Choosing the Right Agent Pattern Mode Flags Monitoring Agent State Context Engineering # Agents Igris supports four agent patterns: reflection, planning, tool use, and swarms. All run inside the execution envelope with full governance applied. --- ## Reflection Agents A reflection agent generates an initial response, evaluates its own quality, and regenerates if the quality score falls below a threshold. **Execution loop:** 1. Generate initial response 2. Score response on a 0.0–1.0 quality scale 3. If score ≥ threshold: return response 4. If score < threshold: regenerate with critique feedback 5. Repeat until threshold met or `max_steps` reached **Configuration:** json { "mode": "reflection", "reflection_threshold": 0.8, "max_reflection_steps": 3 } **When to use:** Tasks where response quality must meet a minimum bar before the result is returned — code generation, structured output, reasoning tasks. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Planning Agents A planning agent breaks down complex tasks into steps, executes each step, observes the result, and adjusts the plan before proceeding. **Execution loop:** Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect → Plan (repeat) The agent maintains a working plan that is revised after each step. Planning steps consume `max_steps` from the execution envelope. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "planning", "max_steps": 10 } **When to use:** Multi-step tasks where the approach depends on intermediate results — research, code generation with testing, multi-stage workflows. [Execution Model →](/docs/execution-model) --- ## Tool-Use Agents A tool-use agent can call external tools as part of inference: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. Tool calls are governed by the execution envelope's capability grants. Available tools (each requires an explicit capability grant): | Tool | Capability | What it does | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | GET/POST to external APIs | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands (sandboxed) | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, list files | Tool calls are recorded in the execution receipt including the call parameters, response, and latency. **Configuration:** json { "mode": "tools", "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": true } } [Tools →](/docs/tools) · [Capability Model →](/docs/capability-model) --- ## Multi-Agent Swarms A swarm executes a task using multiple specialized agents in parallel. The best way to read the architecture is not "which product do I buy?" but "how does a request move through Request -> Execute -> Verify?" At a high level: - **Request** enters through an Igris API surface. - **Execute** happens on the configured hosted or runtime path, with policy, capability, and routing decisions applied along the way. - **Verify** happens through execution metadata, signed records, and receipt-oriented audit material after the run. The hosted control plane and the runtime are implementation components inside that unified model. They matter for deployment and operations, but they should not be your first mental model. --- ## System Overview Start from the execution flow, then map it to components. This page covers how to access, query, and export audit data. --- ## Execution Receipts Every execution produces a signed execution receipt. The receipt is the primary audit artifact. A receipt contains: - **Request identity**: request ID, tenant ID, timestamp - **Inputs**: full prompt, system message, and parameters - **Outputs**: full model response - **Resource usage**: tokens consumed, wall time, tool calls - **Capability grants**: what the execution was permitted to do - **Capability violations**: any operations that were blocked - **Tool calls**: parameters, responses, and latency for each tool invocation - **Signature**: cryptographic seal over the canonical envelope The signature is computed over a deterministic serialization of all fields. An altered receipt will have an invalid signature. [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) --- ## Lineage Each receipt includes a `request_id` that traces back to the originating API call. For executions that went through the cloud coordination layer, the `request_id` links the routing decision to the execution record: API call → routing decision (request_id: abc123) │ ▼ Execution receipt (request_id: abc123, provider: anthropic) │ ▼ Signed envelope (canonical hash: sha256:...) Full lineage is queryable end-to-end by request ID. --- ## Querying Receipts Receipts are queryable through the cloud audit surfaces: - **Cloud receipt API** (`overture.igrisinertial.com`) — the central execution ledger - **Proof API** (`overture.igrisinertial.com/proof`) — verification and policy violation review The current runtime build returns execution receipt data from local execution responses, but it does not expose a public local receipt listing endpoint. bash # List receipts from the cloud ledger curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # Get a specific receipt by execution ID curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/exec-01HXYZ \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # Filter by time range curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts?from=2026-03-01T00:00:00Z&to=2026-03-02T00:00:00Z" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" --- ## Export Export receipts in bulk for external audit workflows: bash # Export as JSONL curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?fo

Authentication Tenant API Keys Session Cookies Runtime-local Auth Choosing a Credential Bearer Example Example JSON # Authentication Which credentials belong to automation, browser sessions, and runtime-local deployments, and how to choose the right one for each route. ## Tenant API Keys Customer automation should use tenant API keys with the `igris_` prefix. These keys are the default credential for server-side integrations, CI jobs, backend workers, and any script that is calling the hosted API outside the browser. Supply the key as `Authorization: Bearer ...` or `X-API-Key` if the endpoint allows it. Endpoint pages call out the expected model explicitly, so treat the endpoint page as authoritative over any generic assumption. ## Session Cookies Browser-driven console workflows use session cookies. These routes are designed for an authenticated user session rather than headless automation, so they should not be treated as generic bearer-token endpoints unless the endpoint page says an API key is also accepted. If you are building automation, prefer routes that are documented with API-key access. ## Runtime-local Auth The local runtime API follows the runtime `auth` configuration. Some deployments intentionally keep that surface inside a trusted network boundary with minimal local auth, while others front it with stricter controls. Because that access model depends on deployment, do not assume that a local runtime route behaves like the hosted API. ## Choosing a Credential Use tenant API keys for server-to-server automation. Use session cookies for browser experiences that are already inside the Igris console. Use runtime-local authentication only when the endpoint is explicitly local and you control the deployment boundary. ## Bearer Example text curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $IGRIS_API_KEY" \ https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/models ## Example JSON json { "error": "unauthorized", "code": "INVALID_API_KEY" } API authentication bearer api key session cookie runtime auth

Treat them as different layers of the product: - The **definition schema** used by the cloud control plane and console editor - The **runtime execution schema** used by the runtime API and native SDKs If you mix them up, validation will fail. --- ## 1. Igris's capability gates ensure that agents can only perform operations you explicitly authorize. --- ## The Capability Model Every execution in Igris runs with a **capability grant** — a declarative list of what the agent is permitted to do. The engine enforces these grants before any operation executes. ### Available Capabilities | Capability | Controls | |---|---| | `allow_http` | Outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | Specific domains the agent can call | | `allow_shell` | Shell command execution | | `allowed_shell_commands` | Specific commands the agent can run | | `allow_filesystem` | File read/write operations | | `allowed_filesystem_paths` | Specific paths the agent can access | | `max_file_write_bytes` | Maximum bytes the agent can write | --- ## Start Restrictive, Expand as Needed The safest approach is to start with no capabilities granted and add them incrementally: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 1: Deploy with No Capabilities Deploy your agent with all capabilities disabled. Run it against real traffic in **shadow mode** to observe what it would do without actually executing. ### Step 2: Review Violations Check the **Proof → Violations** page in the console. Each violation shows: - Which capability was attempted - Which agent attempted it - When it happened ### Step 3: Grant Legitimate Capabilities For violations that represent legitimate agent behavior, grant the specific capability: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true, "allowed_http_domains": ["api.example.com", "cdn.example.com"], "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } ### Step 4: Iterate Repeat steps 2–3 until your agent operates without violations. This process typically takes 1–3 iterations for well-designed agents. --- ## Capability Patterns by Agent Type ### Read-Only Analyst An agent that analyzes data and produces reports: json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_filesystem": false } } No tools needed. Capabilities & Limits Capability Fields Configuration Enforcement Points Violation Records Violation Types # Capabilities & Limits The execution engine enforces a capability model: every execution runs with an explicit set of permissions. If an agent tries to do something outside those permissions, the operation is blocked before it executes and the violation is recorded in the signed receipt. --- ## Capability Fields | Capability | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `allow_http` | bool | Allow outbound HTTP requests | | `allowed_http_domains` | string[] | Allowlist of domains for HTTP calls | | `allow_shell` | bool | Allow shell command execution | | `allow_filesystem` | bool | Allow filesystem read/write | | `max_file_write_bytes` | int | Maximum bytes the execution may write | --- ## Configuration Set capability limits in your `config.json5`: json5 { capabilities: { allow_http: true, allowed_http_domains: ["api.openweathermap.org", "api.github.com"], allow_shell: false, allow_filesystem: true, max_file_write_bytes: 1048576 // 1 MB } } Capabilities can also be set per-request via the `X-Igris-Capabilities` header for tenants with override permission. --- ## Enforcement Points **HTTP tool calls** — before each outbound request, the engine checks `allow_http` and that the target domain is in `allowed_http_domains`. Blocked calls produce a `HttpDomainNotAllowed` violation. **Shell commands** — if `allow_shell` is false and an agent attempts a shell invocation, the call is rejected with a `ShellNotAllowed` violation before the command is spawned. **Filesystem operations** — write operations are counted against `max_file_write_bytes`. Reads beyond the allowed path prefix produce a `FilesystemNotAllowed` violation. --- ## Violation Records Every blocked operation is recorded as a violation in the execution receipt: json { "capability_violations": [ { "kind": "HttpDomainNotAllowed", "detail": "Domain 'evil.com' not in allowed_http_domains", "timestamp": "2026-03-01T12:00:01Z" } ] } Violation records are included in the signed receipt and cannot be removed or suppressed. Compliance auditors can verify that policy enforcement was applied to every execution. --- ## Violation Types | Kind | Trigger | |---|---| | `HttpNotAllowed` | HTTP tool called but `allow_http` is false | | `HttpDomainNotAllowed` | Domain not in `allowed_http_domains` | | `ShellNotAllowed` | Shell command attempted but `allow_shell` is false | | `FilesystemNotAllowed` | Path outside allowed prefix |

Circuit Breaker Core States Why It Matters What It Does Not Mean How To Operate It Monitoring Related Pages # Circuit Breaker The circuit breaker is an advanced failure-aware execution mechanism. Its purpose is to reduce traffic to an upstream path that is repeatedly failing, then probe cautiously to see whether that path has recovered. This helps make failure paths more visible and controlled during execution. --- ## Core States The common state model is: - **closed** when the path is healthy enough for ordinary traffic - **open** when the path should stop receiving ordinary traffic - **half-open** when the system is probing recovery carefully This is a classic control mechanism, but in Igris it matters because it shapes which execution paths remain eligible during failure conditions. ## Why It Matters Without a breaker, the system may keep sending work into a failing path longer than it should. With a breaker, operators get: - clearer failure handling - reduced repeated attempts against a path that is already misbehaving - a more deliberate recovery probe before normal traffic resumes ## What It Does Not Mean The breaker is not a blanket guarantee that every execution survives every upstream issue. It is one mechanism in the larger Execute-stage control stack. Other layers still matter: - policy - health - trust - explicit deployment choices ## How To Operate It Use breaker settings to match your tolerance for: - repeated upstream failures - recovery probe frequency - flapping behavior If a path is bouncing rapidly between states, that is an operational signal worth inspecting rather than something to hide behind automation language. ## Monitoring Use console and API health views to inspect breaker state and recent failure behavior. Treat those views as execution diagnostics, not as proof that all survival scenarios are fully covered. ## Related Pages - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Provider Trust →](/docs/provider-trust) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination) - [SLO Enforcer →](/docs/slo-enforcer)

Receipts and audit context Choosing The Right Layer Implementation Checklist Common Patterns Hosted inference with light context Agent workflows with reusable state Hybrid deployments with shared device state Long-running workflows A Practical Product Pattern Common Mistakes What Good Context Engineering Looks Like Code And Workflow Quality Signals Related Guides # Context Engineering Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what the model should see, what the runtime should remember, and what the product should preserve across steps, failures, and deployments. In Igris, that choice matters because context can live in several different places: - the request itself - memory systems - MCP and shared context - durable-task checkpoints - receipts and audit records If you put the wrong information in the wrong layer, the system still works, but it becomes harder to reason about, more expensive to operate, and more fragile across retries, restarts, and handoffs. --- ## Start With The Smallest Useful Context The default rule is simple: give the model only the context required to succeed at the current step. That means: - put request-specific instructions and inputs in the request - put reusable knowledge in retrieval or memory - put shared operational state in an explicit shared context layer - put recovery-critical workflow state in durable tasks What you want to avoid is using the prompt as a dumping ground for everything the product knows. ## The Context Layers In Igris ### 1. Request-local context Request-local context belongs in the request payload itself: messages, task inputs, or tool-call inputs. This is the right place for information that matters only to the current call. Use this for: - the current user instruction - short-lived execution constraints - immediate tool-call inputs - one-off routing intent Do not use request-local context as a substitute for shared memory or durable state. ### 2. Retrieval and memory Use memory systems when context should survive beyond one request but does not need to become part of the durable workflow protocol. This includes: - semantic retrieval from vector memory - short-lived working state in KV-style memory - shared blackboard-style state when multiple agents need the same view Use this when the question is: "what should the next step be able to recall?" Use durable tasks instead when the question is: "what must survive an interruption and resume safely?" ### 3. MCP and shared context Use MCP when context should be shared across tools, sessions, or runtime instances in a structured way. MCP is the right layer for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented context - cross-instance context in swarm or multi-device operation Use MCP when context is part of the operating en

Nothing is transmitted to Igris servers unless you explicitly export it ### Data Retention Execution records are retained according to your tier: | Tier | Retention Period | |---|---| | Seed | 7 days | | Horizon | 30 days | | Infinite | 90 days (customizable) | After the retention period expires, execution data is automatically purged. ### Data Isolation All data is strictly scoped by tenant. Send A Local Request What To Say Carefully Common Mistakes Related Guides # Deploy Local Runtime Use this workflow when Igris should execute closer to where the work happens. Local runtime is not a separate product identity. It is an execution surface for workloads that benefit from locality, device-level boundaries, or reduced dependence on a hosted path. Choose this path when you need: - execution near the machine or device doing the work - local policy enforcement or bounded task handling - offline or low-connectivity operation - runtime-local behavior tree or tool execution If those properties are not central to the workload, start with the hosted integration first. --- ## 1. Download The Runtime Archive Use the runtime distribution endpoints for your platform and treat download as provisioning, not application traffic. bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-amd64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the archive checksum before installation. ## 2. Install The Binary bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ## 3. Configure Auth And Local Execution Behavior Create `~/.config/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/models/phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf", context_size: 4096, threads: 4, n_gpu_layers: 0 } } This configuration expresses how the runtime should execute work locally. Treat local GGUF fallback carefully in public claims: the code path exists, but reproducible proof should be checked against [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before you present it as a guaranteed behavior. ## 4. Start And Verify The Runtime bash igris-runtime serve curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health Once the runtime is healthy, use the runtime base URL for local requests: text http://localhost:8080/v1 ## 5. Send A Local Request typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'http://localhost:8080/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'phi3', messages: [ ], }); This is still the same execution model: - **Request** through an Igris API surf

Start the runtime Run As A Service Health And Monitoring # Deploying Igris on Edge Devices Running `igris-runtime` on edge hardware gives you local inference, local policy enforcement, and a clean path to hybrid cloud coordination. --- ## Supported Edge Platforms | Platform | Architecture | Minimum RAM | Recommended starting model | |---|---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4/5 | ARM64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano | ARM64 | 8 GB | Mistral 7B (Q4) | | Generic x86_64 host | x86_64 | 4 GB | Phi-3 Mini (Q4) | | GPU-backed x86_64 host | x86_64 | 16 GB | 7B to 8B GGUF | --- ## Install The Runtime ### 1. Download the archive bash export IGRIS_PLATFORM="linux-arm64" curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/install?platform=$ " \ -o /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz curl -fL "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/runtime/checksum?platform=$ " Verify the checksum output before extracting. ### 2. Extract and install bash tar -xzf /tmp/igris-runtime.tar.gz -C /tmp mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin" mv /tmp/igris-runtime "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" chmod +x "$HOME/.local/bin/igris-runtime" export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ### 3. Download a model bash mkdir -p /opt/igris/models wget -O /opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf \ "https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-gguf/resolve/main/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct-q4.gguf" ### 4. Configure the runtime Create `/etc/igris/config.json5`: json5 { server: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }, auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" }, local_fallback: { enabled: true, model_path: "/opt/igris/models/phi-3-mini-q4.gguf", n_gpu_layers: 0, threads: 4, context_size: 4096 } } Platform tuning: - **Raspberry Pi**: keep `n_gpu_layers` at `0`; tune `threads` to the available CPU cores - **Jetson**: raise `n_gpu_layers` for GPU offload and keep `threads` conservative - **GPU-backed x86_64**: increase `n_gpu_layers` based on VRAM capacity ### 5. Start the runtime bash igris-runtime serve If you want the device to appear in Fleet, also set `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` and `IGRIS_API_KEY` before startup. --- ## Run As A Service Example `systemd` unit: ini [Unit] Description=Igris Runtime After=network.target [Service] Type=simple ExecStart=/home/igris/.local/bin/igris-runtime serve Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 User=igris Group=igris [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target --- ## Health And Monitoring bash curl http://localhost:8080/v1/health curl http://localhost:8080/

Deployment Hosted Deployment Local Deployment Hybrid Deployment Local Models And Fallback Language Verifying A Deployment Common Deployment Issues Related Guides # Deployment Choose your deployment mode based on where execution should run. Igris is one execution system with multiple deployment modes: - **hosted** when provider-backed execution through the managed surface is enough - **local** when work should run closer to your machine or device - **hybrid** when hosted coordination and runtime participation both matter The deployment choice changes where execution happens. It does not create separate products. --- ## Hosted Deployment Use hosted deployment when you want the fastest provider-backed path with the least operational overhead. python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1", api_key="your-api-key" ) Hosted deployment is a good fit when you want: - managed API entry - provider-backed execution - simpler onboarding - customer-facing receipt and audit surfaces without local runtime operations Proof claims for specific real-provider paths should still follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status). ## Local Deployment Use local deployment when execution should happen closer to the environment doing the work. Typical reasons: - device or infrastructure locality - local tool or workflow integration - low-connectivity or offline-sensitive operation - runtime-side governance near the workload Start the runtime on your own infrastructure and point the client at the runtime base URL when the request belongs there. ## Hybrid Deployment Use hybrid deployment when you want one application-facing contract while allowing runtime participation underneath. This mode is useful when you need: - a hosted entry path for applications - runtime-backed execution in selected environments - operator visibility into registered execution environments Keep the proof language careful: - hybrid architecture is supported - not every failover or recovery behavior should be described as proven without the matching artifact See [Hybrid Deployment Workflow](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow) for the staged operator view. ## Local Models And Fallback Language Local model configuration is part of the deployment story, but language here should stay disciplined: - local execution is real - local fallback paths exist in the product model - failure-to-local-model proof should follow [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) before being described as proven behavior ## Verifying A Deployment After you deploy,

Durable Task Execution What Durable Tasks Add How To Think About The Lifecycle Submitting A Task Example Tracking Task Status Checkpoints And Recovery Language Durable Streaming Common Mistakes Related Guides # Durable Task Execution Durable tasks are for long-running AI work that should not be treated like a single short request. Use them when the workload needs: - multiple steps - explicit state progression - bounded execution over time - records that remain inspectable after the task completes or fails This page explains the durable-task model in practical terms and keeps recovery claims aligned with current proof status. --- ## What Durable Tasks Add Compared with a short synchronous request, a durable task adds: - task identity - execution-state tracking across steps - checkpoint and WAL-oriented structures - follow-up inspection through task status and receipt-oriented workflows That makes durable tasks the right fit for longer-running governed work. ## How To Think About The Lifecycle The durable-task lifecycle is still Request -> Execute -> Verify: - Errors Status Codes Validation Errors Authentication Failures Server Errors Handling Strategy Error Envelope Example JSON Common Status Codes # Errors How to read error responses across the API reference and what to expect from validation, authentication, throttling, and server failures. ## Status Codes The HTTP status code tells you what class of failure happened before you look at the JSON body. Treat 4xx responses as request, authentication, or access problems that your client should handle directly, and treat 5xx responses as server-side failures that may require retry, fallback, or operator attention. The most common patterns are 400 for invalid request shape, 401 for missing or invalid credentials, 403 for an authenticated request that still is not allowed, 404 when the addressed resource does not exist, 429 when throttling is applied, and 500-level codes when the server cannot complete a valid request. ## Validation Errors Validation failures usually mean the request shape was wrong for the route you called. Many handlers return a compact JSON envelope with `error` and sometimes a more specific `message` or `code` value that tells you what part of the request could not be accepted. ## Authentication Failures Authentication failures typically return HTTP 401. Session-based handlers often use codes such as `MISSING_SESSION` or `INVALID_SESSION`, while API-key handlers more commonly return `INVALID_API_KEY`. ## Server Errors Server-side failures commonly return a generic error such as `internal_error` or a route-specific code such as `registration_failed` or `STORAGE_FAILED`. These responses indicate that the server accepted the route contract but could not complete the operation. ## Handling Strategy Good clients do not handle every error the same way. Fix the request for 400-class validation issues, refresh or replace credentials for 401 responses, stop and inspect authorization assumptions on 403 responses, and apply controlled retry or fallback only for the routes and statuses that are documented as retry-safe. ## Error Envelope text { "error": "invalid_request", "message": "Failed to parse request body" } ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 400 | Bad Request | The route was reached, but the request body, query, or path data did not match the endpoint contract. | | 401 | Unauth API errors error codes invalid request unauthorized internal error

Execution Model Request Execute Boundaries Verify Signed Records Deployment Modes Fit Under The Same Model What To Treat Carefully # Execution Model The Igris execution model is: 1. **Request** 2. **Execute** 3. **Verify** Everything else on this page is a more detailed explanation of those three stages. --- ## Request Request is how work enters Igris. That can be an OpenAI-compatible call, a task-oriented request, or another documented surface. The key idea is consistency: the request enters one execution system, not a collection of unrelated product identities. At request time, Igris establishes the context that matters for the run: - identity and tenant scope - input payload and parameters - capability expectations - applicable limits or policy boundaries ## Execute Execution is where the request becomes governed work. During execution, Igris can: - apply capability and policy checks - enforce budgets and other boundaries - capture execution events and state - run on the hosted or runtime-backed path configured for the workload - record violations or failure outcomes instead of hiding them This is the layer that turns a plain model response into an inspectable run. ### Boundaries Typical execution boundaries include: | Boundary | What it restricts | |---|---| | Capability gates | What the run is allowed to do | | Token or resource limits | How much work the run can consume | | Time limits | How long execution is allowed to continue | | Tool restrictions | Which external actions are allowed | If execution exceeds an allowed boundary, that outcome should be recorded as part of the run. ## Verify Verification is how you inspect what happened after execution. Depending on the path, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt hashes - proof-status information That is what makes the system useful for review, governance, and post-run analysis. ## Signed Records The model is not complete until the run produces something you can inspect later. In Igris terms, that can include: - the execution envelope for the run context - the execution receipt for the final record - hash-linked receipt material for downstream audit workflows Use [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) and [Verification](/docs/verification) for the public-facing receipt and proof workflows. ## Deployment Modes Fit Under The Same Model Hosted, local, and hybrid setups all fit under the same execution model: - the request still enters through Igris

Keep Rollback Simple Common Mistakes Related Guides # Fleet Rollout Workflow Use this workflow when you want to introduce runtime-backed execution environments in stages instead of turning on broad rollout all at once. The goal is simple: 1. start small 2. observe execution behavior 3. verify the records that matter 4. expand only after the first slice is stable This page is about staged rollout of execution environments. --- ## 1. Start With A Small Environment Set Before expanding rollout, make sure each target environment can: - start cleanly - register successfully - remain visible through heartbeat reporting - execute the workload shape you care about If those basics are not healthy, rollout is the wrong next step. ## 2. Observe Execution Before Expanding Do not treat rollout as a blind infrastructure action. Use the first slice to inspect: - whether environments stay registered - whether requests route the way you expect - whether execution events and receipts remain available - whether customer-facing traffic is unaffected This is the practical operator version of Request -> Execute -> Verify. ## 3. Roll Configuration Deliberately If you use config-push surfaces, separate configuration changes from binary updates whenever possible. That makes it easier to answer: - did the environment change break execution behavior - did the binary change introduce the issue - which step should be rolled back first Config-push surfaces exist, but broad rollout success should still be described carefully unless you have reproducible evidence for the exact pattern you are using. ## 4. Governance What Governance Covers Before Execution: Permissions And Scope During Execution: Boundaries And Events After Execution: Signed Records Capability Boundaries Review And Follow-Up What To Avoid Claiming Related Guides # Governance Governance in Igris starts with the Request -> Execute -> Verify model. - **Request** defines what work is being asked for and under which context. - **Execute** applies permissions, boundaries, and runtime checks while the work runs. - **Verify** makes the resulting events and signed records available for inspection later. This page is about the practical controls around execution, not about broad unsupported governance claims. --- ## What Governance Covers Governance answers four operator questions: 1. what was requested 2. what the run was allowed to do 3. what happened during execution 4. what record is available afterward That maps directly to: - permissions and capability checks - execution boundaries - execution events and outcome state - signed records and receipt-oriented inspection ## Before Execution: Permissions And Scope Before the main work runs, Igris can apply controls such as: - tenant or deployment scope - capability grants - allowed tools or access paths - duration or resource expectations This is the part of governance that decides whether the request is allowed to become execution at all. ## During Execution: Boundaries And Events While the run is active, governance is about keeping execution inside its declared boundaries and making the outcome inspectable. Examples include: - capability checks during tool or action attempts - resource boundaries such as duration or token limits - recording violations or rejected actions - surfacing execution events that help operators understand what happened That is why governance belongs to execution itself, not just to a static policy document. ## After Execution: Signed Records Governance is only useful if the result can be checked later. Depending on the path, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt-oriented audit records Use these pages for the public-facing workflow: - [Verification →](/docs/verification) - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status) ## Capability Boundaries Governance often starts with capability scope. Typical controls include: | Control | What it governs | |---|---| | Tool permissions | Which external actions are allowed | | Domain or path limits | Where an execution may reach | | Resource limits | How much work the execution may consume | | Re

How Adaptive Routing Works The Problem How It Works Why This Matters for Your Workload Automatic Adaptation Handles New Providers Gracefully Balances Cost and Performance Configuration Monitoring # How Adaptive Routing Works When you configure multiple AI providers with Igris, you face a fundamental question: which provider should handle each request? The answer depends on constantly changing factors — provider latency, error rates, cost, and your specific workload patterns. Igris solves this automatically using an adaptive routing algorithm that learns from every request. --- ## The Problem Imagine you have three providers configured: | Provider | Avg Latency | Cost per 1K tokens | |---|---|---| | Anthropic Claude | 280ms | $0.015 | | OpenAI GPT-4 | 350ms | $0.030 | | Google Gemini | 200ms | $0.010 | A naive approach might always pick the fastest (Gemini) or the cheapest (Gemini). But what if: - Gemini occasionally times out under load? - Claude produces higher-quality responses for your specific prompts? - OpenAI is faster for certain model types? Static rules can't adapt to these dynamics. Igris's adaptive routing can. --- ## How It Works Igris maintains real-time performance statistics for each configured provider: latency, success rate, and cost. On each request, the routing engine selects the best provider based on recent observations — automatically balancing between providers it knows are reliable and occasionally trying others to keep its data fresh. After each request completes, the provider's statistics are updated with the observed result. A provider that performs well receives more traffic. A provider that degrades is automatically routed around. --- ## Why This Matters for Your Workload ### Automatic Adaptation If a provider's latency degrades, the router automatically reduces its traffic share. No manual intervention needed. When the provider recovers, traffic gradually returns. ### Handles New Providers Gracefully When you add a new provider, the router explores it to gather performance data, then settles into a steady pattern once it understands the provider's characteristics. ### Balances Cost and Performance The algorithm naturally finds the sweet spot between cost and performance for your specific workload. If a cheaper provider is "good enough," it will receive more traffic. If quality matters most, higher-performing providers dominate. --- ## Configuration Adaptive routing is the default. You can also select a specific strategy: json { "routing": { "strategy": "thompson-sampling", "fallback_chain": ["anthropic", "openai", "local

A reviewer must explicitly approve or reject the run before execution continues. The full approval event — who made the decision, when, and why — is recorded in the signed execution receipt and cannot be altered after the fact. --- ## How Executions Get Paused for Review The execution engine evaluates review triggers as each run progresses. Triggers are configured in your policy and can match on tool call targets, output classifications, capability combinations, or custom conditions. When a trigger fires, the run transitions from RUNNING to **PAUSED** with `pause_reason: human_review_required`. The run holds open in that state indefinitely — it does not time out and does not progress — until a human makes a deliberate approve or reject decision. The execution envelope remains intact while the run is paused. Resources are reserved and the agent's context is preserved. Once a decision is made, the run either continues (approve) or terminates (reject) from exactly the point where it was paused. --- ## Finding Runs Waiting for Approval Query paused runs via the API: bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/execution/runs?status=PAUSED" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "execution_id": "exec-01HXYZ", "agent_id": "agent-abc", "status": "PAUSED", "pause_reason": "human_review_required", "paused_at": "2026-03-31T10:14:22Z", "prompt_preview": "About to POST to https://payments.example.com/disburse with amount: 4500", "runtime_id": "runtime-01" } ] The `prompt_preview` field is a brief description of what the execution was about to do at the point it was paused. It is generated by the execution engine and is not the raw model input — it is a structured summary of the pending action, designed to give a reviewer enough context to make an informed decision. --- ## Reviewing in the Console The **Execution Runs** page in the console shows all paused runs in a dedicated review queue at the top of the list. Each row shows a **Review** badge and the time the run has been waiting. Click a paused run to open its detail panel. You will see: - **Prompt preview** — the pending action description - **Agent ID** — which agent initiated this run - **Pause reason** — always `human_review_required` for HITL items - **Paused

Treat Failure Paths Carefully Common Mistakes Related Guides # Hybrid Deployment Workflow Use this workflow when one Igris execution model needs to span hosted and local environments. Hybrid deployment is still one product story: - **Request** enters through a stable application-facing Igris surface - **Execute** can involve hosted coordination and runtime-backed execution - **Verify** stays tied to the same records, receipts, and inspection workflows This model is useful when you care about: - governance across hosted and local environments - running execution closer to devices or private infrastructure - clearer failure-path handling between application traffic and runtime operations - verification-ready records even when execution topology is mixed --- ## 1. Keep One Application-Facing Contract In most hybrid setups, the application still points at the hosted base URL: text https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1 That keeps the application contract stable while allowing runtime participation underneath. ## 2. Start Runtimes With The Right Registration Context Hybrid deployment only works when the runtime can start and register correctly. bash export IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY="YOUR_LICENSE_KEY" export IGRIS_API_KEY="YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY" igris-runtime serve This is the operational step that makes runtime-backed participation possible. It does not create a second product surface for the application team. ## 3. Verify Hosted And Runtime Health Separately Check both sides of the system deliberately: - hosted API calls succeed with your tenant API key - the runtime answers `http://localhost:8080/v1/health` - runtime registration and visibility succeed where your workflow depends on them Hybrid works best when execution traffic and runtime operations are both observable. ## 4. Identity & Access Two Access Planes Console Identity Tenant API Keys Tenant Roles Higher-Assurance Access Controls 2FA SSO Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Identity & Access Igris separates **human access** from **programmatic access**. - **Console identity** is for people using the web app - **Tenant API keys** are for applications, automation, and deployed runtimes Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Two Access Planes | Plane | Used by | Primary credential | Scope | |---|---|---|---| | **Console** | Human operators | Session cookie | Browser session tied to a tenant user | | **API** | Apps, agents, runtimes | `igris_` API key | Tenant-scoped machine access | Console cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. For scripts and integrations, use tenant API keys. --- ## Console Identity The console uses a session-based sign-in model. A user signs in once, receives a session cookie, and then operates inside one tenant context at a time. Current product behavior: - Console access is designed for interactive human use - Session state is separate from tenant API-key auth - Tenant context is applied before policy, billing, and audit logic This keeps browser access and machine access cleanly separated. --- ## Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys are the automation contract for the coordination layer. Accepted forms: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Use tenant API keys for: - server-side application calls - CI/CD or operational automation - provisioning and runtime registration flows - customer-visible integrations that should not depend on browser cookies Do not reuse one tenant's API key across other tenants. Keys are tenant-scoped by design. --- ## Tenant Roles Igris distinguishes between ordinary tenant access and elevated administrative access. In practical terms, roles matter for: - tenant administration - sensitive configuration changes - identity and security operations - management actions that should not be available to every authenticated caller When you design operational workflows, treat roles as part of the product boundary that customers and operators can reason about directly. --- ## Higher-Assurance Access Controls Igris includes stronger access controls for deployments that need more than basic session auth plus API keys. ### 2FA Two-factor authentication is available for tenant-level console access hardening. Use it when console operators can perform security-sensitive actions such as reviewing paused executions, rotating provider keys, or chang

Igris Request -> Execute -> Verify Request Execute Verify What To Expect From The Current Product Recommended Path Find By Goal Advanced Directions # Igris Igris helps engineers run AI tasks with governed, verifiable execution. Direct provider calls are still the right tool for simple chat or one-off prompting. Igris becomes useful when AI output starts doing work: calling tools, crossing system boundaries, touching customer data, or triggering decisions that need to be reviewed later. The simplest mental model is: 1. **Request** through one Igris API surface. 2. **Execute** with governance, routing, events, and failure handling. 3. **Verify** with signed records and verification-ready receipts. --- ## Request -> Execute -> Verify ### Request Send a request once. The surface can be OpenAI-compatible chat, a task submission, or another documented Igris endpoint. The point is not "many products." The point is one execution system that can accept work in a stable, inspectable way. ### Execute Igris decides how the run should proceed for the deployment you have configured. That can include routing to a runtime, applying capability and policy boundaries, capturing execution events, and surfacing failure paths instead of hiding them behind a plain model response. ### Verify Igris returns more than output text. The system can also return execution metadata, signed execution records, and receipt material that can be checked after the run. That is the difference between "the model answered" and "the execution can be inspected." --- ## What To Expect From The Current Product **Governed execution.** Igris is built for runs that need boundaries, not just completions. Capability checks, policy controls, and execution-state visibility are part of the product story. **Execution visibility.** The system tracks route decisions, execution metadata, and receipt-oriented records so engineers can inspect what happened after a run. **Verification-ready records.** Signed envelopes and receipts are part of the product today, and the local unified proof demonstrates signature and hash verification on the proof-backed path. **Honest proof status.** The strongest proven path today is the local unified proof with a mock upstream. Real-provider mode is wired, but it requires sanctioned credentials and was not proven in the prior environment. Advanced areas such as local GGUF fallback, checkpoint recovery, fleet failover, robotics, and multimodal should be treated according to their page-level proof labels. ## Recommended Path Start

Use the hosted API at `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` when your integration needs account, fleet, billing, receipt, or policy capabilities. Use the local runtime API at `http://localhost:8080` by default when the request belongs on the machine where Igris is running. This split is about where the request executes, not about two different products. The API reference groups endpoints by capability so you can navigate by task first and only think about the base URL when you are ready to make the call. ## How Endpoint Pages Work Every endpoint has its own page. That page tells you what the route is for, which authentication model it expects, the path and query parameters it accepts, the request body fields that matter, and the status codes you should plan for in a real client. Use the overview page to browse by capability, then switch to endpoint pages when you are implementing or debugging a specific call. ## SDK Guidance JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, and Python are the first-class SDK languages today. When an endpoint is covered by a native SDK, prefer that SDK for application code because it gives you a cleaner call surface and reduces request-shape drift over time. Some management routes are still best treated as direct HTTP integrations. Licensing & Activation Product Model Tenant Activation Runtime Admission Device Identity And Heartbeats What The License Controls Recommended Operating Model Related Pages # Licensing & Activation Igris licensing is not just a billing flag. It is part of the runtime bootstrap path. There are two distinct surfaces: - **Tenant activation in the console** associates a purchased license with a tenant - **Runtime validation and heartbeat** determine whether a deployed runtime is allowed to stay active Treat those as one lifecycle. --- ## Product Model At a high level, the licensing flow works like this: 1. A tenant activates a license key from the console. 2. The runtime validates that license during startup. 3. The runtime registers a device identity under that license. 4. The runtime sends periodic heartbeats to remain counted as active. If validation fails, the runtime should not be treated as fully admitted into the platform. --- ## Tenant Activation The console exposes a tenant-facing activation flow so an operator can bind a license to the current tenant account. From a product perspective, that does three things: - sets the active plan for the tenant - determines the feature set and quota envelope - establishes the license record that runtimes will validate against The console also exposes plan and quota state, including: - current plan - license status - request quota - device quota - active device count That means licensing is visible to both finance and operations, not just procurement. --- ## Runtime Admission The runtime performs license validation during startup before it proceeds with its normal cloud-registration path. In practical terms, runtime admission depends on: - a valid license key - a generated device identity - the runtime version reported during validation The runtime then attempts device registration under that license. This is important operationally because a license is not only "valid" or "invalid"; it also tracks how many active devices are attached to it. --- ## Device Identity And Heartbeats Each runtime derives a device ID from local machine characteristics and registers that device against the license. Once registered, the runtime sends periodic heartbeats. This gives Igris an operational answer to questions like: - which runtimes are still alive - how many devices are currently consuming the license - whether a device should be treated as stale or deregistered If you are operating a fleet, heartbeats are part of capacity accounting, not just health reporting. --- ## What The License Controls Lice

MCP Guide Pages Transport Surfaces Method Families Session and Transport Context and Resource Operations Tooling and Agent Workflows How MCP Fits In # MCP MCP is the structured context layer in Igris. Use it when context belongs to the operating environment and must move between tools, agents, sessions, or runtimes without becoming accidental prompt state. This section documents MCP as part of the product contract. Start with the overview pages below if you are orienting yourself, then move to the transport and integration guides when you are shaping production workflows. ## Guide Pages - [MCP Server](/docs/mcp-server): customer-facing transport and method model - [MCP Swarm Mode](/docs/mcp-swarm): how shared context behaves in multi-agent execution - [MCP Integration Patterns](/docs/mcp-integration-patterns): practical patterns for durable, auditable context usage ## Transport Surfaces - [`POST /v1/mcp`](/docs/mcp-server): hosted transport for customer-facing MCP requests - [`POST /v1/mcp/stream`](/docs/mcp-server): streaming transport when MCP exchange needs incremental output ## Method Families ### Session and Transport - initialize session state - advertise capabilities - establish request and response shape ### Context and Resource Operations - list available context resources - read resource content - push or refresh context into the shared working surface ### Tooling and Agent Workflows - expose tools to participating agents - share execution context across swarm members - coordinate working context without confusing it with receipts or durable checkpoints ## How MCP Fits In Use MCP for shared working context. MCP Integration Patterns Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Related Guides # MCP Integration Patterns This guide shows how to use MCP as part of a production integration rather than as an isolated protocol feature. --- ## Pattern: Separate Working Context From Audit Data Use MCP for working state that tools, agents, or runtimes need to share. Do not use MCP as the place where audit evidence lives. Keep audit and receipt workflows separate so the system remains understandable. ## Pattern: Give Shared Context A Schema Avoid dumping arbitrary JSON into a few generic keys. Define stable keys and value shapes for shared context that your application team can reason about. Good: - `mission_state` - `dispatch_plan` - `device_role` Weak: - `state` - `payload` - `latest_data` ## Pattern: Pair MCP With Durable Tasks Deliberately MCP and durable tasks solve different problems: - MCP shares structured state - durable tasks preserve progress and resume semantics Use both when a long-running workflow needs shared context and safe recovery. Do not force one to replace the other. ## Pattern: Keep The Product Boundary Clean Your application should still think in terms of one product: - hosted coordination when the application contract belongs in the cloud - runtime-local execution when work belongs on-device - MCP for shared operational state across those boundaries ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Durable Tasks →](/docs/durable-tasks) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

MCP Server What The MCP Server Is For Customer Contract Request Shape Core Method Families Integration Guidance Related Guides # MCP Server This page documents the MCP server surface that Igris exposes through the product. Treat MCP as part of the product contract rather than as a generic tool-call side channel. --- ## What The MCP Server Is For Use the MCP server when context needs to move between agents, tools, sessions, or runtimes in a structured way. That makes it useful for: - shared mission state - tool-oriented working context - multi-agent coordination - runtime-local or cross-runtime context exchange If the problem is only one request deep, keep the data in the request instead. Use MCP when the context belongs to the operating environment. ## Customer Contract The customer-facing hosted entry points are: - `POST /v1/mcp` for request/response JSON-RPC calls - `POST /v1/mcp/stream` for streaming MCP interactions The product forwards those calls to the appropriate runtime MCP server where needed, so the customer can keep thinking in terms of one product surface. ## Request Shape The MCP request body follows JSON-RPC 2.0: json { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "context/write", "params": { "key": "mission_state", "value": { "step": 3, "status": "navigating" } }, "id": 1 } ## Core Method Families The main MCP method families exposed through Igris today are: - `context/*` for structured shared context - `tools/*` for tool discovery and invocation Treat the specific method contract as part of your application integration, not as an undocumented side channel. ## Integration Guidance - keep request-local prompt data out of MCP unless it truly belongs in shared state - prefer explicit keys and schemas for shared context - do not mix audit evidence with working context - use durable tasks when progress recovery matters more than context recall ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering) - [Hybrid Deployment Workflow →](/docs/hybrid-deployment-workflow)

MCP Swarm Mode What It Solves Operational Model Configuration Design Boundaries Common Mistakes Related Guides # MCP Swarm Mode MCP Swarm Mode extends structured context across multiple runtimes on the same network. Use it when context must move between devices or runtime instances without turning every exchange into an application-managed synchronization problem. --- ## What It Solves Swarm Mode is useful when: - multiple runtimes need the same operational context - one runtime should be able to continue after another runtime wrote the latest shared state - distributed planning or robotics coordination needs a shared context layer ## Operational Model In Swarm Mode: - runtimes discover peers - shared context is replicated across the swarm - reads can be served from a peer that did not originate the write That makes Swarm Mode a context-sharing mechanism, not a replacement for durable workflow recovery or audit evidence. ## Configuration toml [mcp_swarm] enabled = true discovery = "mdns" encryption_key_path = "/path/to/swarm.key" ## Design Boundaries Use Swarm Mode for shared operational state. Do not use it for: - signed audit records - long-term business data retention - progress recovery that should be modeled as a durable task ## Common Mistakes - treating swarm replication as if it were a durable checkpoint protocol - storing too much request-local prompt state in the shared swarm context - using swarm state where one runtime-local value would be simpler ## Related Guides - [MCP →](/docs/mcp) - [MCP Server →](/docs/mcp-server) - [Context Engineering →](/docs/context-engineering)

It gives agents access to a long-term knowledge base without including everything in the context window. **How it works:** 1. Documents are embedded and stored in the local vector index 2. At query time, the agent provides a query string 3. The vector store returns the top-K most similar documents 4.
