Igris supports federated learning across your fleet of Runtime devices, enabling collaborative model improvement without sharing raw data between devices. --- ## What It Is Model Aggregation (federated learning) allows multiple Runtime devices to train local model updates (LoRA adapters) and aggregate them into a global model improvement — all without sending training data off-device. Device A: trains local adapter ──┐ Device B: trains local adapter ──┼──► Aggregator → Global model update Device C: trains local adapter ──┘ Each device: 1. Trains a LoRA adapter on its local execution history 2. Sends only the adapter weights (encrypted) to the aggregator 3. Receives the aggregated global model update 4. Applies the update to its local model Raw execution data never leaves the device. --- ## Architecture ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer (Cloud) │ │ │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Federated Coordinator │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ Round Manager → Aggregator → Model Distributor│ │ │ └──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ │Device A │ │Device B │ │Device C │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ │(LoRA) │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ --- ## Aggregation Rounds Federated learning operates in rounds: 1. **Round Start** — The coordinator triggers a new aggregation round 2. **Local Training** — Each participating device trains its LoRA adapter 3. **Weight Upload** — Devices upload encrypted adapter weights 4. **Aggregation** — The coordinator computes a weighted average of all adapters 5. **Distribution** — The aggregated model is sent back to all participants 6. **Application** — Each device loads the updated model ### Round Configuration json { "federated_learning": { "enabled": true, "min_participants": 3, "round_interval_mins": 60, "max_rounds_per_day": 12, "privacy_budget": 1.0, "noise_scale": 0.1 } } | Field | Type | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | `enabled` | bool | `false` | Enable federated learning | | `min_participants` | int | 3 | Minimum devices required to start a round | | `round_interval_mins` | int | 60 | Time between aggregation rounds | | `max_rounds_p

Multi-Tenancy Architecture Isolation guarantees Tenant Identification Tenant Configuration Resource Quotas Cross-Tenant Isolation Data isolation Network isolation Key isolation Billing # Multi-Tenancy Igris supports multi-tenant deployments where a single infrastructure serves multiple isolated tenants. Each tenant has its own execution space, policies, keys, and audit trail. --- ## Architecture Multi-tenancy in Igris is enforced at every layer: ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Coordination Layer │ │ │ │ Tenant A │ Tenant B │ │ Tenant C │ Tenant D │ └────────┬────────────────┘ │ ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ ┌─────┴─────┐ │ Runtime A │ │ Runtime B │ │ Runtime C │ │ (Tenant A) │ │ (Tenant B) │ │ (Tenant C) │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ ### Isolation guarantees | Layer | Isolation method | |---|---| | **Inference** | Separate API keys, separate provider configurations | | **Execution** | Separate execution envelopes with tenant-scoped IDs | | **Data** | Tenant-scoped storage — no cross-tenant data access | | **Policies** | Per-tenant policy envelopes | | **Audit** | Per-tenant receipt chains | | **Keys** | Per-tenant vault — keys are never shared | --- ## Tenant Identification Every request is associated with a tenant via the API key used for authentication. The API key maps to exactly one tenant. There is no cross-tenant key. API Key → Tenant ID → Execution Context The tenant ID is embedded in every execution receipt, ensuring full traceability from receipt back to tenant. --- ## Tenant Configuration Each tenant has an independent configuration: json { "tenant": { "id": "tenant-abc123", "name": "Acme Corp", "tier": "horizon", "providers": ["anthropic", "openai"], "policy": { "max_tokens": 4096, "max_steps": 10, "allow_http": true, "allow_shell": false }, "slo": { "latency_p99_ms": 2000, "max_cost_per_request_usd": 0.05 } } } --- ## Resource Quotas Tenants are allocated resource quotas based on their tier: | Resource | Seed | Horizon | Infinite | |---|---|---|---| | Runtime instances | 3 | 50 | 500 | | Receipt retention | 7 days | 30 days | 90 days | | Federated learning | — | — | ✓ | | SLO enforcement | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | Routing advisor | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | When a tenant exceeds its quota, requests are rejected with HTTP 429. The `X-RateLimit-Remaining` header indicates remaining capacity. --- ## Cross-Tenant Isolation ### Data isolation - Execution receipts are scoped to tenant — no tenant can query another tenant's receipts - Vector store indexes are tenant-scoped - KV cache entries are tenant-scoped -

Observability & Tracing Trace Identity Distributed Tracing What Operators Should Expect Relationship To Receipts Recommended Deployment Model Related Pages # Observability & Tracing Igris has two observability layers: - **product-visible lineage** such as request IDs, receipts, and execution history - **operator-visible tracing** such as spans, trace propagation, and deployment telemetry You need both. Receipts tell you what happened. Tracing tells you where time was spent and where a request crossed system boundaries. --- ## Trace Identity The coordination layer generates and propagates a trace identity for each request. That identity is attached to logs and returned through `X-Trace-ID` so operators can correlate: - inbound API traffic - routing decisions - provider calls - runtime handoff - receipt and audit records From a product perspective, `X-Trace-ID` is the fast path for debugging cross-system behavior. --- ## Distributed Tracing Igris supports OpenTelemetry-style tracing with a Jaeger exporter and request-scoped trace attributes. That combination matters because Igris needs to support both: - cross-service span propagation - external tracing systems used by platform teams Current tracing metadata includes things like: - HTTP method and path - provider and model - token counts - latency and cost - speculative-execution winner and switch metadata This makes tracing useful for routing analysis, not just generic HTTP timing. --- ## What Operators Should Expect Tracing should answer these questions quickly: - Did the request stay in cloud or move to runtime? - Which provider was selected and why? - Where did latency accumulate? - Was speculative execution involved? - Is a slow request caused by routing, provider latency, or local runtime work? That is the difference between basic logging and a usable production observability model. --- ## Relationship To Receipts Tracing and receipts are related but not interchangeable. | Surface | Primary use | |---|---| | **Trace ID / spans** | live debugging, latency analysis, request-path inspection | | **Execution receipt** | tamper-evident record of the governed execution outcome | Use tracing when you are diagnosing behavior in-flight. Provider Health What Provider Health Means Health States Why It Matters How It Affects Execution Monitoring Surfaces Proof Language Related Pages # Provider Health Provider health is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism inside the **Execute** stage. Its purpose is straightforward: help Igris avoid obviously unhealthy upstream paths and make failure-aware execution decisions. This page is about the mechanics of that decision support, not about turning routing into the product identity. --- ## What Provider Health Means Provider health asks whether a configured upstream path appears usable right now. Typical signals include: - response success or failure - latency behavior - recent throughput - health-check outcomes where those are enabled These signals help path selection, but they do not guarantee a perfect execution outcome. ## Health States The exact thresholds depend on configuration, but the common states are: - **active** when the path looks healthy enough to use normally - **degraded** when the path is still available but should be treated more cautiously - **unavailable** when the path should not receive ordinary execution traffic This is about failure visibility and safer path selection, not a blanket survival promise. ## Why It Matters Provider health helps operators answer: - which upstream paths are currently usable - whether a sudden latency or error spike should reduce traffic - whether a path should be removed from ordinary selection until it recovers That makes it part of governed execution rather than just a dashboard nicety. ## How It Affects Execution Provider health feeds into hosted path selection alongside: - policy - trust - circuit-breaker state - any advanced routing mode in use Health should narrow the set of usable paths before an advanced routing strategy makes its final choice. ## Monitoring Surfaces Use the health APIs and console views to inspect health state, but keep expectations realistic: - health telemetry helps explain execution behavior - health telemetry does not by itself prove performance or reliability outcomes for every workload ## Proof Language Provider health is an advanced execution mechanism with real implementation support. It is appropriate to describe it as failure-aware path selection, but not as a guarantee that every outage or degradation scenario is already solved automatically. ## Related Pages - [Provider Trust →](/docs/provider-trust) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [Cloud Coordination

Provider Trust What Trust Evaluates Why It Matters Cold Start And Confidence How It Affects Path Selection Proof Language Related Pages # Provider Trust Provider trust is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism. Health asks whether a path appears up right now. Trust asks whether that path should still be considered reliable enough to keep using for governed execution. That distinction matters for advanced operators who want more than a binary up-or-down signal. --- ## What Trust Evaluates Trust looks at observed behavior over time, such as: - latency drift - error-rate drift - cost drift - how much evidence exists for the path so far This helps distinguish "technically available" from "credible enough to keep using." ## Why It Matters A path can be healthy in the narrow sense and still be a poor choice if its behavior is drifting away from what operators expect. Trust is the layer that says: - this path is up, but not yet proven enough - this path is up, but its behavior has drifted too far - this path may need more evidence before it receives normal traffic ## Cold Start And Confidence Trust grows with evidence. New or rarely used paths may need a warm-up period before operators should treat them as ordinary choices for production execution. That is part of the point of having a separate trust concept. ## How It Affects Path Selection Trust should sit ahead of final advanced routing decisions: 1. policy decides what is allowed 2. health decides what is currently usable 3. trust decides what is credible enough to keep using 4. final path selection chooses among the remaining candidates ## Proof Language Provider trust is best described as an advanced, source-confirmed execution mechanism. It is appropriate to explain how it influences selection, but this page should not promise globally optimal or universally safer outcomes without deployment-specific evidence. ## Related Pages - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [SLO Enforcer →](/docs/slo-enforcer)

Choose The Next Path # Quick Start Start here if you want to understand what Igris actually proves today. This quickstart is intentionally not a generic hosted-inference tutorial. Direct model calls are fine for simple chat. Igris is for the point where AI output starts doing work and you need governed execution, visible failure paths, and records you can inspect after the run. If you need the shortest hosted setup path after this proof-first walkthrough, Igris also supports an OpenAI-compatible onboarding path through the hosted API. --- ## What You Will Do 1. Start a local proof-backed Igris flow. 2. Send one request through the public execution surface. 3. Confirm that execution was routed through Runtime. 4. Verify the signed execution envelope, signed execution receipt, and receipt-log chain. This is the narrowest honest path that is proven locally today. --- ## Prerequisites - A checkout of this repository - `node`, `go`, `cargo`, `curl`, and `lsof` - Free local ports `8080` and `8081` - Free local port `18090` if you run the default mock-provider mode You do not need sanctioned provider credentials for the default proof path. The default mode uses a local mock upstream so the proof stays reproducible. ## 1. Run The First Verified Flow From the repo root: bash ./scripts/unified_execution_proof_demo.sh The script prepares local proof artifacts, builds or reuses the Runtime binary, builds Overture, starts a local mock upstream, starts Runtime on `127.0.0.1:8080`, starts Overture on `127.0.0.1:8081`, submits one `/v1/infer` request, and fails if Overture falls back away from Runtime. Expected output shape: text Unified execution proof succeeded. Mode: mock Provider: local-mock-cloud Route decision: forwarded_to_runtime_task Receipt execution_id: ... Receipt hash: ... Artifacts: /tmp/igris-unified-proof.XXXXXX ## 2. Inspect What Was Verified The proof demonstrates the Request -> Execute -> Verify path: - **Request**: the script sends one request through Overture's `/v1/infer` surface. - **Execute**: Overture forwards the work to Runtime instead of silently answering from its own direct fallback path. - **Verify**: the script checks the returned `execution_envelope`, `execution_receipt`, receipt hash, and receipt-log chain. If the script succeeds, you have a local proof that: - Runtime handled the execution authority for the request - execution metadata captured the route decis

Rate Limiting What The Hosted API Enforces 429 Response Shape Runtime Download Limit Local Runtime Rate Limits Client Guidance # Rate Limiting The hosted API applies a global rate limit of **100 requests per minute** by default. Runtime binary downloads also have a dedicated **10 downloads per hour per tenant** cap. --- ## What The Hosted API Enforces The hosted API applies: - one shared window: `100 req/min` by default - scoped per tenant when tenant context exists, otherwise per IP The hosted API does **not** publish rate-limit headers on every successful response. Rate-limit headers are guaranteed on rejection responses. --- ## 429 Response Shape When the global limiter is exceeded, the current response looks like this: json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } Headers on the rejection path include: - `Retry-After` - `X-RateLimit-Limit` - `X-RateLimit-Remaining` Do not depend on `X-RateLimit-Reset` being present on successful requests in the current build. --- ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime archive downloads have a separate limit of `10/hour` per tenant on the control plane download surface. This applies to: - `GET /v1/runtime/download` - subscribed runtime download workflows behind the cloud control plane --- ## Local Runtime Rate Limits The local runtime auth config supports its own request controls: json5 { auth: { enabled: true, api_key: "YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY", rate_limit_per_minute: 60, rate_limit_burst: 10 } } | Field | Description | |---|---| | `rate_limit_per_minute` | Maximum local requests per minute | | `rate_limit_burst` | Additional local burst budget | --- ## Client Guidance - Treat `429` plus `retry_after_seconds` as the contract - Add exponential backoff client-side - Batch receipt exports and large history queries - Do not assume tier-specific global limits unless they are explicitly published in a future release contract --- [Troubleshooting →](/docs/troubleshooting) · [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference)

Rate Limits Global Control-plane Limit Runtime Download Limit Client Behavior 429 Example Example JSON Common Status Codes # Rate Limits What throttling exists today, where it applies, and how clients should behave when they receive a 429 response. ## Global Control-plane Limit The hosted API currently applies a default limiter of 100 requests per minute. Endpoint pages call out the exceptions that matter more than the global default. Response headers are only guaranteed on the 429 path right now. Clients should not assume that every successful response carries full rate-limit metadata. ## Runtime Download Limit Runtime download endpoints use a tighter subscription-aware throttle. Treat binary download as a provisioning or rollout action, not as a hot-path request that your application makes repeatedly during normal traffic. ## Client Behavior Build clients so that a 429 is expected and handled, not treated as an exceptional edge case. Honor `Retry-After` when it is present, apply backoff with jitter for repeated retries, and avoid running parallel request bursts that all wake up at the same second. ## 429 Example text Retry-After: 60 X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 ## Example JSON json { "error": { "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again later.", "type": "rate_limit_error", "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" }, "retry_after_seconds": 60 } ## Common Status Codes | Code | Title | Description | |---|---|---| | 429 | Too Many Requests | Retry after the advertised cooldown window. | API rate limits retry-after 429 throttle

Receipts and Audit Workflow 1. Run Through A Documented Igris Surface 2. Inspect The Execution Outcome 3. Retrieve The Receipt-Oriented Record 4. Verify With The Right Expectation 5. Retain Or Export The Record Common Mistakes Related Guides # Receipts and Audit Workflow Use this workflow when a run needs to be inspected, verified, and retained after execution. The practical sequence is: 1. run through a documented Igris surface 2. inspect the execution outcome 3. retrieve the receipt-oriented record 4. verify what can actually be checked 5. retain or export the result for downstream use --- ## 1. Run Through A Documented Igris Surface Receipts are most useful when the request goes through a documented Igris path. Keep integrations on supported surfaces so execution metadata, receipts, and export workflows line up with the actual run. ## 2. Inspect The Execution Outcome Start with the immediate execution result: - response content - execution metadata - route decision or provider label where applicable This tells you what happened during the run. It is useful for debugging and operational review, but it is not the same thing as the receipt itself. ## 3. Retrieve The Receipt-Oriented Record Use receipt listing and detail endpoints when you need the signed or hash-linked execution record. - [Execution Receipts →](/docs/execution-receipts) - [API Reference →](/docs/api-reference) Treat the receipt surface as the audit artifact. Treat execution history as supporting context, not as a substitute for the receipt. ## 4. Verify With The Right Expectation Use the strongest verification surface that matches your need. For the narrow proof-backed path today: - the local verified run proves signature checks, receipt-hash checks, and receipt-log chain checks - see [First Verified Run](/docs/first-verified-run) For the hosted proof route: - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` compares submitted receipt values against the stored record and returns proof-status information - it should be described as stored-value comparison and proof-status sync, not as a full public cryptographic verifier See [Verification](/docs/verification) for the distinction. ## 5. Retain Or Export The Record Use `GET /v1/receipts/export` when another system, reviewer, or audit process needs the record outside the immediate execution flow. Choose: - NDJSON for machine pipelines - CSV for spreadsheet-oriented workflows Decide on retention and downstream custody before exporting receipts into another system. ## Common Mistakes - Treating execution history as if it were the signed receipt - Describing the hosted proof route as stronger than it is

Request -> Execute -> Verify Request Execute Verify Why This Model Matters What This Page Does Not Assume # Request -> Execute -> Verify Igris is easiest to understand as one execution system for AI tasks. Instead of thinking in terms of "hosted product versus local product," start with the lifecycle of the work: 1. **Request** 2. **Execute** 3. **Verify** --- ## Request Request means you submit work through an Igris API surface. That can be: - an OpenAI-compatible chat request - a task or tool-oriented execution request - a runtime or operator workflow that still produces execution records The point is consistency. Your application should not need a different mental model every time the execution path changes. ## Execute Execution is where Igris earns its keep. During execution, Igris can: - route work to the configured hosted or runtime path - apply capability and policy boundaries - capture execution metadata and events - surface failure paths instead of hiding them - return signed execution material alongside the result Execution is not just "a provider responded." It is the governed run that happened between the request and the final response. ## Verify Verification means you can inspect what happened after the run. Depending on the path, that can include: - route-decision metadata - execution metadata - signed execution envelopes - signed execution receipts - receipt hashes and chain-linked log material This is what makes Igris useful for production work that needs review, audit, or post-run debugging. ## Why This Model Matters Direct provider calls are fine when all you need is a text response. Igris is for the point where the output starts doing real work and you care about: - governance - visible failure handling - post-run inspection - records that can be checked later ## What This Page Does Not Assume This model does **not** assume that every advanced feature is already proven in your environment. Real-provider execution, local GGUF fallback, checkpoint recovery, fleet failover, robotics, and multimodal flows all have their own proof status and should be evaluated explicitly. --- [Quick Start →](/docs/quickstart) · [Verification →](/docs/verification) · [Architecture →](/docs/architecture)

Routing Advisor How It Works Proposals GET /v1/cognitive/proposals GET /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id POST /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id/apply → {"status": "applied", "applied_at": "2026-03-01T12:05:00Z"} Auto-Apply Configuration GET /v1/cognitive/config PUT /v1/cognitive/config # Routing Advisor The Routing Advisor analyzes your routing history and proposes configuration changes — adjusting provider weights, enabling speculative execution, or switching routing strategy — based on observed performance. Auto-apply can be configured to apply proposals automatically when they meet your confidence and risk thresholds. --- ## How It Works 1. The advisor monitors routing telemetry continuously 2. When it detects an optimization opportunity, it generates a **proposal** with a confidence score and a risk score 3. You can review and apply proposals manually, or configure auto-apply thresholds 4. Applied changes take effect immediately; a rollback window is available --- ## Proposals ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals List pending and recent proposals. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json [ { "id": "prop-01HXYZ", "type": "routing_strategy", "description": "Switch to latency-optimized routing — Anthropic p50 has dropped 18% over 24h", "confidence": 0.91, "risk_score": 0.12, "estimated_improvement": "~18% latency reduction", "proposed_at": "2026-03-01T12:00:00Z", "status": "pending" } ] | Field | Description | |---|---| | `confidence` | 0–1 — how certain the advisor is this change helps | | `risk_score` | 0–1 — estimated risk of degradation | | `status` | `pending`, `applied`, `rejected`, `rolled_back` | --- ### GET /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id Get a single proposal with full detail. --- ### POST /v1/cognitive/proposals/:id/apply Apply a proposal immediately. bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/proposals/prop-01HXYZ/apply \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" # → The change takes effect on the next request. If performance degrades within the rollback window, you can revert via the console or by applying the previous configuration manually. --- ## Auto-Apply Configuration The advisor can apply proposals automatically when they meet configured thresholds. Set `enabled: true` in the auto-apply config to activate. ### GET /v1/cognitive/config Returns the current auto-apply configuration. bash curl https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/cognitive/config \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" Response: json { "enabled": false, "confidence_threshold": 0.85, "max_risk_score": 0.25, "eval_interval_mins": 60, "rollback_window_mins": 30,

Routing Engine What It Is What It Considers Strategy Layer Relationship To Other Controls Console And Inspection Proof Language Related Pages # Routing Engine The routing engine is an advanced path-selection layer inside Igris execution. Its job is to choose among the execution paths that remain allowed and usable after policy, health, and trust have already narrowed the field. This makes it important to advanced operators, but it should not be read as the primary product identity. --- ## What It Is At a simple level: text Request -> policy and boundary checks -> health and trust filters -> routing engine -> selected execution path That means the routing engine is not a standalone product story. It is one layer inside the broader Execute stage. ## What It Considers Depending on configuration, the engine may consider: - latency behavior - success or failure history - cost signals - availability - strategy-specific selection logic Different deployment modes may expose different routing behavior, but the core idea is the same: choose an execution path under governance, not by ad hoc client-side guessing. ## Strategy Layer Different strategy modes can exist on top of the engine, such as adaptive, cost-aware, or latency-aware selection. Those strategies are advanced operator tools and should be evaluated with workload-specific evidence rather than broad assumptions. ## Relationship To Other Controls The engine sits behind: - policy - health - trust - circuit-breaker state That ordering matters. Advanced path selection should not override the safety and governance layers that determine whether a path should even be considered. ## Console And Inspection Routing dashboards can help explain which path was chosen and why, but they should be treated as advanced execution diagnostics. They are useful after you already understand the main product model. ## Proof Language The routing engine is a real advanced control layer, but this page should not promise globally optimal provider choice, automatic savings, or universal reliability gains without evidence for the specific workload and environment. ## Related Pages - [Semantic Routing →](/docs/semantic-routing) - [Provider Health →](/docs/provider-health) - [Circuit Breaker →](/docs/circuit-breaker) - [Cloud Coordination →](/docs/cloud-coordination)

Safety & Containment Containment Model Resource limits cgroup bounds (Linux) Capability Enforcement Secure Defaults Violation Handling Human-in-the-Loop # Safety & Containment Igris enforces safety limits at the execution engine level — not at the application layer, where they could be bypassed. --- ## Containment Model Every execution runs in a containment context. The containment context applies resource limits before the model is invoked and enforces them throughout execution. ### Resource limits Limits are applied per-execution: | Limit | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `max_tokens` | 4096 | Maximum output tokens | | `max_duration_ms` | 30000 | Maximum wall time (30s) | | `max_steps` | 10 | Maximum tool/planning steps | | `max_tool_calls` | 5 | Maximum tool invocations per execution | Limits can be tightened per-tenant or per-request. They cannot be relaxed beyond the configured policy maximum. ### cgroup bounds (Linux) On Linux deployments, the engine applies cgroup constraints to the execution process: - **CPU quota**: limits CPU burst during local model inference - **Memory limit**: prevents unbounded memory growth in local inference - **I/O limits**: optional disk I/O rate limits for file-system tool use cgroup enforcement is independent of application code. An agent that attempts to consume more resources than its cgroup allows is throttled or killed by the kernel. --- ## Capability Enforcement Capabilities are enforced by the engine, not by the model. Even if the model generates output that attempts a disallowed tool call, the engine intercepts and rejects it before the call executes. The enforcement sequence: 1. Request arrives with a capability grant (or secure defaults are applied) 2. Engine validates the grant against the tenant's policy ceiling 3. Engine begins execution with the validated grant in scope 4. If the model attempts a tool call, the engine checks the grant before executing 5. If the call is outside the grant, the engine records a capability violation and rejects the call 6. Execution continues or terminates depending on the violation policy Violation events are recorded in the execution receipt. They cannot be suppressed. --- ## Secure Defaults The engine applies secure defaults when capability grants are not explicitly specified: | Setting | Default | |---|---| | `allow_http` | disabled | | `allow_shell` | disabled | | `allow_filesystem` | disabled | | `max_tokens` | 2048 | | `max_steps` | 5 | Tools must be explicitly enabled. The defaults assume no tool use is intended.

It is not a language feature catalog. It is the set of patterns that keep integrations clean when the same product may be called in cloud, local-runtime, or hybrid deployments. --- ## Choose The Right Client Surface First Start with this decision: - Use an OpenAI-compatible client when you want the shortest path to a working integration - Use a native Igris SDK when you need product-specific features such as receipts, vault operations, fleet controls, or richer routing metadata The first-class native SDKs today are: - JavaScript / TypeScript - Go - Rust - Python If you are in Java, C#, Ruby, or another language without a first-class native SDK, the safest default is still the OpenAI-compatible API. ## Standard Environment Variables Use the same environment-variable model across languages: - `IGRIS_API_KEY` for hosted API access - `IGRIS_BASE_URL` when you need to override the default base URL Recommended defaults: - hosted API: `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local runtime: `http://localhost:8080` Keeping this consistent is one of the easiest ways to make cloud, local, and hybrid deployments feel like one product to your own application teams. ## Pattern: Choose A Mode Once Do not let every handler decide whether it is in cloud, local, or hybrid mode. Make that a startup concern: - cloud mode points to `https://overture.igrisinertial.com` - local mode points to `http://localhost:8080` - hybrid mode usually still keeps application traffic on the hosted API, while Igris coordinates work with runtimes behind that surface The goal is to keep your business logic unaware of deployment details whenever possible. ## Pattern: Centralize Client Construction Do not scatter client creation across handlers and jobs. Create one small constructor per service and keep the auth/base-URL decision there. ### JavaScript / TypeScript typescript export function createIgrisClient() { const apiKey = process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY; if (!apiKey) { throw new Error('IGRIS_API_KEY is required'); } return new IgrisClient({ baseUrl: process.env.IGRIS_BASE_URL ?? 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com', apiKey, }); } ### Go go package igrisclient import ( "os" igris "github.com/igris-inertial/go-sdk" ) func New() *igris.Client { baseURL := os.Getenv("IGRIS_BASE_URL") if baseUR

Java, C#, and Ruby should use the OpenAI-compatible API today. For production integration guidance, reusable client construction, and environment-variable patterns, continue with [SDK Integration Patterns →](/docs/sdk-integration-patterns). ## Support Matrix ## Support Policy Treat the SDK table as a product support statement, not just a package list: - **First-class** means the language is part of the maintained customer SDK surface - **OpenAI-compatible** means the safest contract today is the HTTP API through an OpenAI-style client If your team wants the strongest support commitment, choose JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, Rust, or Python. If your team mainly needs inference and broad portability, stay on the OpenAI-compatible path. --- ## OpenAI-Compatible Clients Any OpenAI SDK can call Igris by changing the base URL. For many teams, this is the right default because it keeps the integration portable while still routing through the product. **Python** python import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1", api_key=os.environ["IGRIS_API_KEY"], ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4", messages=[ ], ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) **JavaScript / TypeScript** typescript const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: 'https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1', apiKey: process.env.IGRIS_API_KEY, }); const response = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4', messages: [ ], }); console.log(response.choices[0].message.content); Use this path for Java, C#, Ruby, or any other language where you already have an OpenAI-compatible client and do not need the native Igris SDK surface yet. --- ## Native SDKs Choose a native SDK when you want a product-shaped client rather than a protocol-shaped one. That matters when you are working with receipts, vault oper JavaScript / TypeScript first-class Preferred native SDK for browser and Node.js integrations. Go first-class Preferred native SDK for backend services and CLI tooling. Rust first-class Preferred native SDK for systems and embedded integrations. Python first-class Preferred native SDK for Python services, data pipelines, and scripting. Java openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native Java SDK is promoted explicitly. C# openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native C# SDK is promoted explicitly. Ruby openai-compatible Use the OpenAI-compatible API until a native Ruby SDK is promoted explicitly.

Security Authentication Tenant API Keys Console Sessions Provider Keys Policy And Capability Controls Receipts And Verification Deployment Notes Compliance # Security Igris security has two distinct planes: - **Tenant API keys** for automation and programmatic access - **Console session cookies** for browser access to the web app Treat those as different contracts. --- ## Authentication ### Tenant API Keys Tenant API keys use the `igris_` prefix and are accepted in: - `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` - `X-API-Key: YOUR_IGRIS_API_KEY` Best practices: - Store tenant API keys in environment variables - Rotate them if exposed - Scope usage to the tenant that owns the key bash export IGRIS_API_KEY="igris_abc123..." ### Console Sessions The web console uses Better Auth session cookies. Those cookies are not a published bearer-token contract. Do not script console session access as generic bearer authorization headers. ### Provider Keys Provider keys stored through the current public vault API are encrypted before storage and returned only as masked values. --- ## Policy And Capability Controls A restrictive starting point in the current control-plane policy model looks like this: json { "allow_http": false, "allow_shell": false, "allow_fs_write": false, "allow_external_api": false, "domain_allowlist": [], "domain_denylist": [], "writable_paths": [], "readable_paths": [], "violation_behavior": "terminate" } Start tight, then expand based on observed violations and actual agent requirements. --- ## Receipts And Verification Customer-facing verification routes currently live on the proof API: - `GET /proof/receipts` - `POST /proof/receipts/verify` - `GET /v1/proof/violations` Example: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' --- ## Deployment Notes - The local runtime can enforce its own API key with the local `auth` config - Fleet registration is gated by a valid `IGRIS_LICENSE_KEY` plus `IGRIS_API_KEY` - For local-only deployments, point clients directly at the runtime and keep your own storage if you need offline receipt retention --- ## Compliance Igris is positioned to support compliance workflows, but the exact operational model depends on where you run the control plane and runtime. - **Data residency** depends on whether you call Overture, the local runtime, or both - **Auditability** comes from receipts, proof endpoints, and export workflows - **Least privilege** comes from capabi

Semantic Routing What It Does Where It Fits Decision Flow Fallback Behavior What To Expect Proof Language Related Pages # Semantic Routing Semantic routing is an advanced **Execute**-stage mechanism. Its job is to help Igris choose among eligible execution paths based on the kind of work being requested, instead of treating every request as identical. This is useful for advanced operators, but it is not the main reason to adopt Igris. Use [Request -> Execute -> Verify](/docs/request-execute-verify) for the primary product model. Use this page when you want the deeper path-selection detail. --- ## What It Does Semantic routing adds a classification step before final path selection. In practice, that means Igris can: - classify the request into a workload type - narrow the eligible providers or paths for that class - choose among those candidates with health and policy still applied This is meant to improve path selection for advanced workloads, not to override governance, policy, or verification. ## Where It Fits The simplified stack is: 1. policy decides what is allowed 2. health and trust narrow what is currently usable 3. semantic routing helps classify the work 4. final selection chooses the target path That layering matters because semantic routing should stay subordinate to safety and policy controls. ## Decision Flow text Request -> classification -> workload class -> eligible providers or paths -> final selection -> execution ## Fallback Behavior Semantic routing should not be a hard dependency for execution. If classification is unavailable, the system should still be able to continue with non-semantic path selection rather than turning classifier issues into execution outages. That is the operator-friendly reason to treat this as an advanced mechanism rather than a foundational identity claim. ## What To Expect Teams using semantic routing should expect: - class-specific path selection behavior - changing decisions as observations accumulate - the need for explicit policy overrides when deterministic routing is required Do not assume a semantic strategy stays fixed across time unless you pin the path explicitly. ## Proof Language Semantic routing is best treated as an advanced, source-confirmed capability. Shadow Mode What It Does Why Teams Use It How To Read The Results Proof Language Cost And Scope Related Pages # Shadow Mode Shadow mode is an advanced comparison workflow. It can run an observed parallel path beside the primary execution path so operators can compare outcomes without immediately changing what the caller receives. That makes it useful for evaluation and tuning, but it should be treated as an advanced feature rather than a first-contact product claim. --- ## What It Does At a high level: text Request -> primary execution result returned -> shadow result captured separately for comparison The important idea is that the shadow path is for observation, not for replacing the primary path automatically. ## Why Teams Use It Shadow mode can help teams: - compare candidate providers or models - test a new configuration with lower risk - observe how an alternate path behaves before changing the primary path It is most useful when the team already has a stable baseline and wants to inspect alternatives carefully. ## How To Read The Results A shadow comparison is only useful if the team knows what it is looking for: - latency differences - cost differences - divergence in result shape or quality - differences in policy-sensitive behavior Treat the comparison output as decision support, not as a proof that the shadow path is ready for promotion. ## Proof Language Shadow mode is best treated as an advanced or preview-oriented capability unless you have deployment-specific evidence for the exact workflow you are describing. It is appropriate to explain the comparison model, but not to overstate its production-readiness across every environment. ## Cost And Scope Shadow execution may consume additional resources. Use it deliberately, with explicit scope and sampling decisions, rather than leaving it on broadly without a reason. ## Related Pages - [Speculative Execution →](/docs/speculative-execution) - [Execution Flow →](/docs/execution-flow) - [History & Alerts →](/docs/history) - [Proof Status →](/docs/proof-status)

The enforcer evaluates live metrics, classifies breaches, and produces remediation actions that the platform can execute or record. The current customer-facing contract is not a standalone SLO configuration API. Customers see SLO outcomes through routing behavior, provider health, execution receipts, history, and observability views. --- ## What Is Enforced The production enforcer evaluates these metric inputs: | Metric | Target | Warning | Critical | |---|---:|---:|---:| | `p99_latency_ms` | `100` | `130` | `150` | | `p95_latency_ms` | `50` | `80` | `100` | | `error_rate` | `0.001` | `0.01` | `0.02` | | `availability` | `0.9999` | `0.999` | `0.99` | | `throughput_rps` | `10000` | `8000` | `5000` | The enforcer is configured with a 20-second evaluation interval and a 300-second breach cooldown. Auto-remediation is enabled in the default production configuration. --- ## Evaluation Output SLO evaluations are exposed to customers through supported product surfaces rather than a standalone public SLO API. Use provider-health state, routing statistics, execution receipts, history, and observability exports to understand when the platform detected degraded behavior and how traffic was handled. --- ## Customer-Facing Surfaces Use these documented surfaces to understand SLO behavior: - [Provider Health](/docs/provider-health) for provider status and degradation signals. - [Circuit Breaker](/docs/circuit-breaker) for provider trip state and recovery behavior. - [Routing Control & Analytics](/docs/api-reference/routing-control-analytics/get-v1-routing-stats) for routing telemetry. - [Execution Receipts](/docs/execution-receipts) for receipt-level evidence that an execution completed, failed, or violated policy. - [Observability & Tracing](/docs/observability-tracing) for deployment-level monitoring. --- ## Operational Access SLO administration is not part of the public API reference. Speculative Execution What It Does Where It Can Help What To Say Carefully Operational Reading Simulation And Analytics Related Features Proof Language Related Pages # Speculative Execution Speculative execution is an advanced execution mode. It can run a draft path in parallel with a primary path and decide whether the draft is good enough to return. This is useful for advanced latency-sensitive setups, but it should be treated as an optimization layer under the Execute stage, not as the core product story. --- ## What It Does At a high level: 1. a draft path starts 2. the primary path starts 3. the system decides whether the draft is acceptable 4. one result is returned The caller still receives one execution result. The internal race is an advanced mechanism, not a separate surface the application needs to learn first. ## Where It Can Help Speculative execution is most relevant when teams are experimenting with: - streaming workloads - predictable request types - advanced latency tuning It is less relevant for ordinary onboarding or for teams that have not yet established a stable baseline execution path. ## What To Say Carefully Do not assume speculative execution always improves latency or cost. The exact outcome depends on workload shape, provider behavior, and how often the draft path is accepted. This page intentionally does not promise headline percentage improvements without benchmark evidence for the environment in question. ## Operational Reading If you enable speculative execution, watch for: - acceptance rate - cost impact - path-selection stability - whether the workload is actually a good fit If acceptance is consistently low, the feature is probably adding complexity without enough benefit. ## Simulation And Analytics The product exposes speculative status, analytics, and simulation surfaces so operators can inspect how the mode behaves before using it broadly. Treat these surfaces as advanced evaluation tools, not as proof that the optimization is beneficial for every workload. ## Related Features - council and shadow features should be evaluated independently - receipts should still reflect the path that actually produced the returned result - proof claims should stay aligned with [Proof Status](/docs/proof-status) ## Proof Language Speculative execution is best documented as an advanced, source-confirmed capability. Use production claims only when you have workload-specific evidence. ## Related Pages - [Routing Engine →](/docs/escapevector) - [Shadow Mode →](/docs/shadow-mode) - [Cloud Coordination →]

Tamper-Evident Logs How It Works Chain Verification What's Recorded Export GET /v1/receipts/export Console Retention Audit Workflow # Tamper-Evident Logs Every execution in Igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. The tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can be altered, deleted, or inserted without detection. --- ## How It Works Each execution receipt contains: 1. **Envelope hash** — SHA-256 hash of the canonical execution envelope 2. **Previous hash** — SHA-256 hash of the previous receipt (forming a chain) 3. **Signature** — Ed25519 signature of the envelope using a device-bound key Each receipt links to the previous receipt via hash, forming a chain. Each receipt is signed with a device-bound key that exists only on the originating runtime. Tampering with any receipt invalidates its signature and breaks the chain — both of which are detected by the verification API. --- ## Chain Verification Receipts can be verified at any time to confirm chain integrity: bash curl -X POST https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' ' Response: json { "valid": true, "signature_valid": true, "chain_intact": true, "previous_hash_matches": true } If any link in the chain is broken, verification fails and the specific broken link is identified. --- ## What's Recorded Every receipt records: | Category | Fields | |---|---| | **Identity** | Request ID, tenant ID, agent ID, device ID, timestamp | | **Inputs** | Prompt, system message, parameters | | **Outputs** | Model response, tool call results | | **Resources** | Tokens consumed, wall time, CPU/memory usage | | **Capabilities** | Grants applied, violations recorded | | **Policy** | Policy hash at time of execution | | **Routing** | Provider selected, fallback count, latency | | **Chain** | Envelope hash, previous hash, signature | --- ## Export Receipts can be exported for external audit workflows: ### GET /v1/receipts/export Export receipts in the selected format and time range. bash curl "https://overture.igrisinertial.com/v1/receipts/export?format=json&range=7d" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \ --output receipts_export.json Supported formats: - `json` — raw JSON array of receipts - `csv` — flattened CSV for spreadsheet analysis - `ndjson` — newline-delimited JSON for streaming processing --- ## Console View and verify receipts at `/proof/receipts`: - Receipt listing wit

Tools Tool Overview HTTP Tool Shell Tool Filesystem Tool Tool Audit Trail # Tools Igris agents can call external tools: HTTP APIs, shell commands, and filesystem operations. All tool use is governed by the execution envelope's capability grants and recorded in the execution receipt. --- ## Tool Overview | Tool | Capability required | Use | |---|---|---| | HTTP | `allow_http` | Call external APIs, webhooks, web services | | Shell | `allow_shell` | Execute shell commands in a sandboxed context | | Filesystem | `allow_filesystem` | Read, write, and list files | Tools are disabled by default. Each must be explicitly granted in the request's capability grant or in the tenant's policy. --- ## HTTP Tool The HTTP tool allows agents to make GET and POST requests to external endpoints. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_http": true }, "tool_config": { "http": { "allowed_domains": ["api.example.com", "*.private.example.com"], "timeout_ms": 5000, "max_response_bytes": 65536 } } } **Security controls:** - **Domain allowlist**: agents can only reach configured domains. Wildcards are supported for subdomains. - **Timeout**: requests that exceed `timeout_ms` are aborted and the failure is recorded. - **Response size limit**: responses larger than `max_response_bytes` are truncated. If `allowed_domains` is empty, all domains are permitted. Leaving it empty is not recommended for production deployments. --- ## Shell Tool The shell tool allows agents to execute shell commands. Shell access is the most sensitive capability and should be granted only when necessary. **Configuration:** json { "capabilities": { "allow_shell": true }, "tool_config": { "shell": { "allowed_commands": ["ls", "cat", "grep", "python3"], "working_directory": "/workspace", "timeout_ms": 10000, "env_allowlist": ["PATH", "HOME"] } } } **Security controls:** - **Command allowlist**: only listed commands can be executed. Commands not on the list are rejected before execution. - **Working directory**: the shell is confined to the specified directory. Attempts to navigate outside it are blocked. - **Timeout**: commands that run longer than `timeout_ms` are killed. - **Environment**: only environment variables on the allowlist are passed to the child process. For each issue you will find the symptoms, the most likely cause, and the steps to fix it. --- ## Runtime Not Starting ### Port already in use **Symptoms:** The runtime process exits immediately with an address binding error. Nothing appears in **Fleet → Devices**. **Cause:** Another process is already listening on the port the runtime is configured to use (default: 8080). **Fix:** Identify the conflicting process and stop it, or configure the runtime to use a different port. On Linux and macOS you can check what is using a port with: bash lsof -i :8080 After freeing the port or reconfiguring, restart the runtime. --- ### Missing API key **Symptoms:** The runtime starts but exits with an authentication error. No registration appears in the console. **Cause:** The runtime was started without a valid Igris API key in its configuration. **Fix:** Add your API key to the runtime's config file or pass it as the appropriate environment variable for your deployment method. Your API key is available in **Settings → Keys** in the console. If you do not see an API key, generate one from **Settings → Billing → Manage Account**. --- ### Config file not found **Symptoms:** The runtime exits with a message indicating it cannot find or parse the configuration file. **Cause:** The runtime is looking for its configuration file at the default path and it either does not exist or has a syntax error. **Fix:** Verify that the config file is present at the expected path. Check the file for YAML/TOML syntax errors — most runtimes print the line number of the first error. If you are using a custom path, confirm you are passing the correct path argument when starting the runtime. --- ## Runtime Not Appearing in Fleet → Devices ### Network or firewall blocking outbound registration **Symptoms:** The runtime starts and appears to be running (the local health endpoint responds) but never appears in **Fleet → Devices** in the console. **Cause:** Outbound HTTPS traffic to `overture.igrisinertial.com` is being blocked by a firewall rule, proxy, or network policy. **Fix:** Verify connectivity from the runtime host: bash curl -v https://overture.igrisinertial.com/health If this fails, work with your network administrator to allow outbound HTTPS (port 443) to `overture.igrisinertial.com`. Choose the target version and update strategy **Update strategies:** | Strategy | Behavior | |---|---| | `rolling` | Update instances one at a time (default) | | `canary` | Update one instance first, verify health, then proceed | | `all-at-once` | Update all instances simultaneously | ### Manual Upgrade For Seed tier or manual deployments: 1. Verification Verification Inputs Proven Local Verification Path Cloud Proof Route Semantics What To Check After A Run Choosing The Right Verification Surface Verification Language To Use Carefully # Verification Verification is the part of Igris that answers: what happened, what record came back, and what can actually be checked? The short version is: - some verification behavior is proven locally today - some proof-oriented routes are useful record-comparison surfaces - not every verification surface is equally strong --- ## Verification Inputs Depending on the route, Igris can return or persist: - execution metadata such as route decisions and provider labels - a signed `execution_envelope` - a signed `execution_receipt` - receipt hashes - receipt-log entries and previous-hash linkage These are not interchangeable. Execution history is not the same thing as a signed receipt, and a proof-status lookup is not the same thing as cryptographic verification. ## Proven Local Verification Path The strongest demonstrated verification path today is the local unified proof: bash ./scripts/unified_execution_proof_demo.sh That flow verifies: - the returned execution envelope signature - the returned execution receipt signature - the returned execution receipt hash - receipt presence in the local receipt log - receipt-chain linkage This is the current **proven locally** path. ## Cloud Proof Route Semantics The hosted proof route is: text POST /proof/receipts/verify Its current handler compares submitted values against the stored receipt record and returns the current verification state. It is useful when you want to check whether a stored receipt matches a supplied hash or signature value. Important caveat: - The current handler does **not** perform full cryptographic signature verification by itself. - It compares stored versus submitted values and returns fields such as `verified`, `verification_status`, `hash_valid`, and `signature_matches`. That means you should not describe this route as a full public cryptographic verifier in first-contact docs. ## What To Check After A Run When a run matters, inspect at least these layers: 1. **Execution metadata** for route decision and provider context 2. **Signed records** for the returned envelope or receipt material 3. **Proof status** for what the current route can confirm 4. **Receipt export or storage path** if another system will depend on the record later ## Choosing The Right Verification Surface | Need | Best current path | |---|---| | Prove the repo's local execution flow end to end | [First Verified Run](/doc

circuit breaker circuit-breaker circuit breaker core states why it matters what it does not mean how to operate it monitoring related pages  # circuit breaker the circuit breaker is an advanced failure-aware execution mechanism. its purpose is to reduce traffic to an upstream path that is repeatedly failing, then probe cautiously to see whether that path has recovered. this helps make failure paths more visible and controlled during execution. --- ## core states the common state model is: - **closed** when the path is healthy enough for ordinary traffic - **open** when the path should stop receiving ordinary traffic - **half-open** when the system is probing recovery carefully this is a classic control mechanism, but in igris it matters because it shapes which execution paths remain eligible during failure conditions. ## why it matters without a breaker, the system may keep sending work into a failing path longer than it should. with a breaker, operators get: - clearer failure handling - reduced repeated attempts against a path that is already misbehaving - a more deliberate recovery probe before normal traffic resumes ## what it does not mean the breaker is not a blanket guarantee that every execution survives every upstream issue. it is one mechanism in the larger execute-stage control stack. other layers still matter

multimodal inference (technical preview) multimodal multimodal inference (technical preview) how it fits what to expect related pages  # multimodal inference (technical preview) multimodal inference is a **technical preview** surface. use this page when you need to understand how multimodal execution could fit into igris. do not treat it as a broadly proven or customer-ready default path. check [proof status](/docs/proof-status) before promoting multimodal behavior beyond preview language. --- ## how it fits multimodal work still belongs under the same request -> execute -> verify model: - **request** includes text plus one or more additional modalities - **execute** depends on the configured multimodal-capable path - **verify** depends on the execution record that comes back from that run the preview status is about maturity, not about a different product identity. ## what to expect this surface is appropriate for evaluation when teams want to explore: - text-plus-image workflows - text-plus-audio workflows - how multimodal requests should be represented in execution and verification workflows use careful language: - multimodal support should be treated as preview-oriented - provider-backed proof should be checked before making stronger readiness claims - stub-heavy or partial behavior should be assumed possible

observability & tracing observability-tracing observability & tracing trace identity distributed tracing what operators should expect relationship to receipts recommended deployment model related pages  # observability & tracing igris has two observability layers: - **product-visible lineage** such as request ids, receipts, and execution history - **operator-visible tracing** such as spans, trace propagation, and deployment telemetry you need both. receipts tell you what happened. tracing tells you where time was spent and where a request crossed system boundaries. --- ## trace identity the coordination layer generates and propagates a trace identity for each request. that identity is attached to logs and returned through `x-trace-id` so operators can correlate: - inbound api traffic - routing decisions - provider calls - runtime handoff - receipt and audit records from a product perspective, `x-trace-id` is the fast path for debugging cross-system behavior. --- ## distributed tracing igris supports opentelemetry-style tracing with a jaeger exporter and request-scoped trace attributes. that combination matters because igris needs to support both: - cross-service span propagation - external tracing systems used by platform teams current tracing metadata includes things like: - http method and path - provider and model - token counts - latency and cost - speculative-execution winner

overview index igris request -> execute -> verify request execute verify what to expect from the current product recommended path find by goal advanced directions  # igris igris helps engineers run ai tasks with governed, verifiable execution. direct provider calls are still the right tool for simple chat or one-off prompting. igris becomes useful when ai output starts doing work: calling tools, crossing system boundaries, touching customer data, or triggering decisions that need to be reviewed later. the simplest mental model is: 1. **request** through one igris api surface. 2. **execute** with governance, routing, events, and failure handling. 3. **verify** with signed records and verification-ready receipts. --- ## request -> execute -> verify ### request send a request once. the surface can be openai-compatible chat, a task submission, or another documented igris endpoint. the point is not "many products." the point is one execution system that can accept work in a stable, inspectable way. ### execute igris decides how the run should proceed for the deployment you have configured. that can include routing to a runtime, applying capability and policy boundaries, capturing execution events, and surfacing failure paths instead of hiding them behind a plain model response. ### verify igris returns more than output text. the system can also re

policy policy policy what policy controls tool and permission boundaries execution-time effects policy and records routing policy should stay secondary here common mistakes related guides  # policy policy in igris is the mechanism for controlling what ai tasks are allowed to do. in request -> execute -> verify terms: - **request** carries intent and scope - **execute** applies policy checks and boundaries - **verify** exposes the resulting events and records for review this page is about execution control, not about presenting policy as a broad platform claim detached from execution behavior. --- ## what policy controls policy helps determine: - which tools or actions are allowed - which boundaries apply to the run - what should happen when the run exceeds those boundaries - what review signals should be available afterward that makes policy a live part of execution, not just static configuration. ## tool and permission boundaries policy can express boundaries such as: | area | what it controls | |---|---| | tool access | which tools or external actions are allowed | | domain or target restrictions | where http or similar actions may reach | | resource limits | duration, step, or token limits | | review expectations | which outcomes should trigger operator follow-up | when a run exceeds these boundaries, that result should appear in the execution record and follow-up

provider health provider-health provider health what provider health means health states why it matters how it affects execution monitoring surfaces proof language related pages  # provider health provider health is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism inside the **execute** stage. its purpose is straightforward: help igris avoid obviously unhealthy upstream paths and make failure-aware execution decisions. this page is about the mechanics of that decision support, not about turning routing into the product identity. --- ## what provider health means provider health asks whether a configured upstream path appears usable right now. typical signals include: - response success or failure - latency behavior - recent throughput - health-check outcomes where those are enabled these signals help path selection, but they do not guarantee a perfect execution outcome. ## health states the exact thresholds depend on configuration, but the common states are: - **active** when the path looks healthy enough to use normally - **degraded** when the path is still available but should be treated more cautiously - **unavailable** when the path should not receive ordinary execution traffic this is about failure visibility and safer path selection, not a blanket survival promise. ## why it matters provider health helps operators answer: - which upstream paths are currently

provider trust provider-trust provider trust what trust evaluates why it matters cold start and confidence how it affects path selection proof language related pages  # provider trust provider trust is an advanced hosted coordination mechanism. health asks whether a path appears up right now. trust asks whether that path should still be considered reliable enough to keep using for governed execution. that distinction matters for advanced operators who want more than a binary up-or-down signal. --- ## what trust evaluates trust looks at observed behavior over time, such as: - latency drift - error-rate drift - cost drift - how much evidence exists for the path so far this helps distinguish "technically available" from "credible enough to keep using." ## why it matters a path can be healthy in the narrow sense and still be a poor choice if its behavior is drifting away from what operators expect. trust is the layer that says: - this path is up, but not yet proven enough - this path is up, but its behavior has drifted too far - this path may need more evidence before it receives normal traffic ## cold start and confidence trust grows with evidence. new or rarely used paths may need a warm-up period before operators should treat them as ordinary choices for production execution. that is part of the point of having a separate trust concept. ## how it

semantic routing semantic-routing semantic routing what it does where it fits decision flow fallback behavior what to expect proof language related pages text # semantic routing semantic routing is an advanced **execute**-stage mechanism. its job is to help igris choose among eligible execution paths based on the kind of work being requested, instead of treating every request as identical. this is useful for advanced operators, but it is not the main reason to adopt igris. use [request -> execute -> verify](/docs/request-execute-verify) for the primary product model. use this page when you want the deeper path-selection detail. --- ## what it does semantic routing adds a classification step before final path selection. in practice, that means igris can: - classify the request into a workload type - narrow the eligible providers or paths for that class - choose among those candidates with health and policy still applied this is meant to improve path selection for advanced workloads, not to override governance, policy, or verification. ## where it fits the simplified stack is: 1. policy decides what is allowed 2. health and trust narrow what is currently usable 3. semantic routing helps classify the work 4. final selection chooses the target path that layering matters because semantic routing should stay subordinate to safety and policy co

shadow mode shadow-mode shadow mode what it does why teams use it how to read the results proof language cost and scope related pages text # shadow mode shadow mode is an advanced comparison workflow. it can run an observed parallel path beside the primary execution path so operators can compare outcomes without immediately changing what the caller receives. that makes it useful for evaluation and tuning, but it should be treated as an advanced feature rather than a first-contact product claim. --- ## what it does at a high level: text request -> primary execution result returned -> shadow result captured separately for comparison the important idea is that the shadow path is for observation, not for replacing the primary path automatically. ## why teams use it shadow mode can help teams: - compare candidate providers or models - test a new configuration with lower risk - observe how an alternate path behaves before changing the primary path it is most useful when the team already has a stable baseline and wants to inspect alternatives carefully. ## how to read the results a shadow comparison is only useful if the team knows what it is looking for: - latency differences - cost differences - divergence in result shape or quality - differences in policy-sensitive behavior treat the comparison output as decision support,

speculative execution speculative-execution speculative execution what it does where it can help what to say carefully operational reading simulation and analytics related features proof language related pages  # speculative execution speculative execution is an advanced execution mode. it can run a draft path in parallel with a primary path and decide whether the draft is good enough to return. this is useful for advanced latency-sensitive setups, but it should be treated as an optimization layer under the execute stage, not as the core product story. --- ## what it does at a high level: 1. a draft path starts 2. the primary path starts 3. the system decides whether the draft is acceptable 4. one result is returned the caller still receives one execution result. the internal race is an advanced mechanism, not a separate surface the application needs to learn first. ## where it can help speculative execution is most relevant when teams are experimenting with: - streaming workloads - predictable request types - advanced latency tuning it is less relevant for ordinary onboarding or for teams that have not yet established a stable baseline execution path. ## what to say carefully do not assume speculative execution always improves latency or cost. the exact outcome depends on workload shape, provider behavior, and how often the draft path is accepted. this page intentionally does not promise

tamper-evident logs tamper-evident-logs tamper-evident logs how it works chain verification what's recorded export get /v1/receipts/export console retention audit workflow bash json bash # tamper-evident logs every execution in igris produces a cryptographically signed receipt that forms part of an immutable audit trail. the tamper-evident log system ensures that no execution record can be altered, deleted, or inserted without detection. --- ## how it works each execution receipt contains: 1. **envelope hash** — sha-256 hash of the canonical execution envelope 2. **previous hash** — sha-256 hash of the previous receipt (forming a chain) 3. **signature** — ed25519 signature of the envelope using a device-bound key each receipt links to the previous receipt via hash, forming a chain. each receipt is signed with a device-bound key that exists only on the originating runtime. tampering with any receipt invalidates its signature and breaks the chain — both of which are detected by the verification api. --- ## chain verification receipts can be verified at any time to confirm chain integrity: bash curl -x post https://overture.igrisinertial.com/proof/receipts/verify \ -h "authorization: bearer your_api_key" \ -h "content-type: application/json" \ -d ' ' response: json { "valid": true, "signature_valid": true, "chain_intact": true, "previous_hash_matches": true } if any l

runtime not starting ### port already in use **symptoms:** the runtime process exits immediately with an address binding error. nothing appears in **fleet → devices**. **cause:** another process is already listening on the port the runtime is configured to use (default: 8080). **fix:** identify the conflicting process and stop it, or configure the runtime to use a different port. on linux and macos you can check what is using a port with: bash lsof -i :8080 after freeing the port or reconfiguring, restart
